# Backend deep audit — 2026-08-04

Comprehensive multi-round adversarial audit of the ENTIRE Orbetra backend — ingest, worker pipeline, api, db, codec, shared, infra

**268 agents**, 2 rounds, every finding adversarially verified before it appears here. **113 confirmed findings.** Remediation status: `backend-audit-remediation.md`.

## Health summary

The core of this backend is genuinely well built. Ingest's framing/CRC/ACK contract, the ACK-after-XADD ordering, the invalid-fix seam (I5), idempotent position writes with ON CONFLICT, the scoped-repository layer with `scopedWhere`, the per-shard leasing with a fencing check before durable effects, the argon2 concurrency semaphore, the audit-coverage meta-test and the tenant isolation suite are all real engineering, and the in-code comments show the authors reasoning about the right invariants. Most of what follows is not sloppiness — it is a small number of recurring blind spots applied consistently across an ambitious surface area.

Five patterns account for nearly every finding. (1) **Guards measured on the wrong axis or clock**: shard depth measured as XLEN of a stream nothing trims, rule cooldowns in wall-clock against fix_time-stamped events, report windows built in the browser zone against account-zone buckets, Stripe ordering on second-granular `event.created`, offline detection as `now − device clock`, `pipeline_lag_ms` computed from fix_time. (2) **Non-atomic dual-write seams with no compensation**: Redis registry + Postgres, claim-then-write in SMS, revoke-then-insert in refresh rotation, delete-then-rebuild in trip recompute, LPOP-then-record in command dispatch. (3) **Unbounded caller input on hot paths**: geofence vertex counts, rule `scope.deviceIds`, angle/speed into smallint, report spans, CSV field lengths, request bodies on the pre-limiter routes. (4) **Fail-open, silently**: discarded return values, `catch`-and-continue with no counter, and — the biggest one — a dozen failure counters that exist in `prom.ts` but are exported by nothing and alerted on by nothing. (5) **Second-tier surfaces skip the conventions the core enforces**: affiliates/commissions have no audit rows, scheduled_reports/push_subscriptions/api_keys have no FKs, SMS and geofence creation have no rate limit or quota, and GDPR erase/export were never updated for tables added after they shipped. Before real customer traffic, fix in this order: the XLEN backpressure latch (#1 — this is a guaranteed total-ingest outage within days of go-live, not a risk), the poison-batch/no-dead-letter path (#2), the UDP limiter and codec-16 wedge, the fix_time clamp, then the auth/session-revocation cluster (API-key WS, refresh fencing, body limits, signup argon2), then the money bugs (past_due metering, unmetered SMS), and then observability — because today the API exports one metric and no worker failure counter is alerted on, so none of the above would page anyone.

## Findings

### 1. [CRITICAL] I4 backpressure uses XLEN of raw:{shard}, which never shrinks — every socket permanently pauses and every UDP datagram is permanently dropped once a shard has ever held 50k records

**Subsystem:** ingest · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/session.ts:327`

`getCachedShardDepth` (apps/ingest/src/session.ts:318-330) defines "shard depth" as `XLEN raw:{shard}`. XLEN is the number of *retained* entries, not the unprocessed backlog: XACK does not remove stream entries. I verified this against one of the repo's own Redis 7.4.8 containers — after XADDing 5 entries, reading them through the `pipeline` consumer group and XACKing all 5, `XLEN` still returned 5 with `XPENDING` = 0.

Nothing in production code ever removes entries from `raw:{shard}`. `grep -rn 'xdel|XDEL|xtrim|XTRIM'` over the repo returns exactly one hit, and it is in a test (apps/ingest/__tests__/ingest.spec.ts:173). The worker only XACKs (apps/worker/src/consumer.ts:195 and :217) and its own comment (consumer.ts:191) states the design assumption: "ingest trims raw:{shard} with MAXLEN ~100k". Ingest's only trim is the `MAXLEN ~ 100_000` on each XADD (apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:56-60), and `~` guarantees Redis never trims *below* 100 000. Redis is configured `maxmemory-policy noeviction` with AOF (infra/compose/docker-compose.yml:30), so nothing else prunes it and a restart does not reset it.

Therefore `XLEN raw:{shard}` is monotonically non-decreasing up to a ~100 000 plateau, and it crosses the `pauseAboveDepth: 50_000` threshold (apps/ingest/src/server.ts:20 — hardcoded, no env override in apps/ingest/src/main.ts:17-21) after the shard has *cumulatively* received 50 001 records. From that moment the depth check can never clear:

- TCP (session.ts:279-292): after the first AVL frame every session sets `paused = true`, calls `socket.pause()`, and enters `pollForDrain()` (session.ts:295-312), which re-reads XLEN every 500 ms forever and never resumes.
- UDP (apps/ingest/src/udp.ts:138-142): every datagram is dropped without an ACK — 100% loss on the UDP channel.

A second consequence: because XLEN is not a backlog measure and XPENDING/`XINFO GROUPS ... lag` is never read anywhere, there is no actual protection against `MAXLEN` trimming entries the worker has not consumed, even though those records were already ACKed to the device (I1).

This also disables the alerting built on the same number: `stream_depth` (apps/worker/src/prom.ts:51-56) is the same XLEN, so `StreamDepthHigh` (>50 000) and `StreamDepthCritical` (>90 000) at infra/prometheus/alerts.yml:10 and :17 fire permanently, as does `BackpressureSustained` (infra/prometheus/alerts.yml:61).

The only test that exercises the drain path hides the bug: apps/ingest/__tests__/ingest.spec.ts:173 simulates "the pipeline consumer draining the shard" with `setInterval(() => redis.xtrim('raw:'+SHARD,'MAXLEN',0), 200)` — it deletes the stream, which is something no production component does.

**failureScenario:** Go-live with a 1 000-device fleet reporting every 30 s. Each shard receives ~120 records/min, so shard N accumulates 50 000 entries after ~7 hours (a 100-device pilot takes ~3 days; a busy shard is faster). At that instant every device that connects gets exactly one packet ACKed, then `maybeBackpressure()` pauses its socket; `pollForDrain()` re-reads XLEN every 500 ms and never resumes because the stream is now permanently ~100k entries. The device's next packet sits unread in the kernel buffer, it never sees an ACK, its own timeout fires and it reconnects — delivering one packet per reconnect cycle while the paused socket lingers for the 40-minute read-idle timeout, burning the 20 000-connection / 200-per-IP caps and issuing 2 XLEN/s per paused socket against the same Redis the ACK path uses. Any device configured for UDP loses 100% of its data (`udpBackpressureDropsTotal`) with no ACK at all. Operators see StreamDepthCritical and BackpressureSustained firing continuously with a healthy, idle worker. (The W7 load test's 'sustained-rate gate generator-limited' result is the same symptom seen from the sender side.)

**suggestedFix:** Stop using XLEN as the depth signal. Measure the actual backlog with `XINFO GROUPS raw:{shard}` → the `lag` field (Redis 7) or `XPENDING raw:{shard} pipeline` plus the entries-added/entries-read delta, and compare *that* against `pauseAboveDepth`. Export the same number as `stream_depth` in apps/worker/src/prom.ts so the alerts in infra/prometheus/alerts.yml keep their intended meaning. Independently, have the worker XDEL (or periodically XTRIM MINID to the group's last-delivered id) after XACK so the stream stops holding a permanent 16×100 000-entry retention buffer in a `noeviction` Redis shared with BullMQ. Add a regression test that fills a shard above the threshold, drains it through a real consumer group (XREADGROUP + XACK only, no XTRIM), and asserts the socket resumes.

### 2. [CRITICAL] Backpressure drain-poll has no error handling — a rejected XLEN kills the whole ingest process

**Subsystem:** ingest · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/session.ts:298`

`pollForDrain()` builds a self-rescheduling poll loop (`setTimeout(() => void tick(), 500)`, lines 308 and 311). `tick()` is an `async` function whose only awaited call, `getCachedShardDepth(...)` → `redis.xlen('raw:{shard}')` (line 298), is NOT wrapped in try/catch, and the scheduled invocation is `void tick()` — the returned promise has no rejection handler.

This is the ONE Redis call in the whole session that escapes the session's error net: every other async path runs inside the `socket.on('data')` chain, which has an explicit `.catch()` (session.ts:75-88) that increments `sessionErrorsTotal` and destroys just that socket. `maybeBackpressure()` (line 280) is inside that chain; `pollForDrain()'s tick is not.

There is no `process.on('unhandledRejection')` handler anywhere in the repo (`grep -rn 'unhandledRejection' apps packages infra tools` → no matches), so on Node 22 the default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` turns the rejection into an uncaught exception and terminates the process.

ioredis rejects in-flight commands with `Error: Connection is closed.` when the socket drops (flushQueue on close), and returns error replies for WRONGTYPE / CLUSTERDOWN / a replica-side failure — so `xlen` rejecting is not hypothetical. Crucially, this poll loop only RUNS when the shard stream is above `pauseAboveDepth`, i.e. exactly when the worker is behind and Redis is under the most stress.

If the process somehow survives the rejection (e.g. a future global handler), the second failure mode still applies: the retry chain stops. `this.paused` stays true and `socket.pause()` is never undone, so `maybeBackpressure()` (guarded by `!this.paused`) can never re-arm the poll and the data handler's `.finally()` (guarded by `!this.paused`) can never resume — the device's socket is dead-but-open until the read-idle timer fires.

**failureScenario:** A fleet burst pushes `raw:7` past `pauseAboveDepth`; 300 sockets on shard 7 call `maybeBackpressure()` → `paused = true` → `pollForDrain()`. 500 ms later all 300 `tick()`s issue an XLEN. At that instant the Redis primary restarts (or a failover drops the connection); ioredis flushes the in-flight command queue and rejects every XLEN with `Connection is closed.`. Each rejection is unhandled → the ingest process throws and exits, dropping ALL ~20k live TCP sessions at the moment the pipeline was already backed up. Devices reconnect en masse into a still-degraded Redis; the un-ACKed packets are re-sent, amplifying the burst that caused the pause in the first place.

**suggestedFix:** Wrap the body of `tick()` in try/catch: on error, log + increment `sessionErrorsTotal` and re-arm `setTimeout(() => void tick(), 500)` (never leave the socket paused with no pending poll). Independently, add a `process.on('unhandledRejection')` handler in `apps/ingest/src/main.ts` (and api/worker mains) that logs the reason before deciding to exit, so a single stray rejection is diagnosable rather than an unexplained restart.

### 3. [CRITICAL] Unvalidated uint16 angle/speed written into smallint columns poisons an entire batch — no dead-letter for write failures

**Subsystem:** worker/consumer (I1 durability, poison-batch) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/writer.ts:46`

The codec parses `angle` and `speed` as unsigned 16-bit (`packages/codec/src/parse.ts:91` `raw.readUInt16BE(19)`, `:93` `raw.readUInt16BE(22)`), so both have range 0..65535. `normalize()` copies them verbatim (`apps/worker/src/normalize.ts:69` `course: p.angle`, `:68` speed) with no bound, `rawStreamPayloadSchema` only asserts `z.number()` (`packages/shared/src/records.ts:16,18`), and ingest's sanity gate only bounds `tsMs`/`lat`/`lon` (`apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:15-19`). `writePositions` then binds them into `speed smallint, course smallint` (`packages/db/sql/001_positions.sql:9`) whose range is -32768..32767. Any value >= 32768 makes PostgreSQL raise 22003 `smallint out of range` for the WHOLE multi-row INSERT — all 200 records in the batch fail. There is no try/catch and no dead-letter for DB-write failures: `normalize()` failures go to `raw:dead` (`consumer.ts:188-199`) but a `writePositions` throw propagates out of `process()`, so the batch can never be quarantined and is retried forever. The UDP transport makes this trivially reachable because it performs no integrity check at all — `wrapAsTcpFrame` computes the CRC over the payload it just received (`packages/codec/src/udp.ts:79-85`), so a corrupt or spoofed datagram carrying angle=0xFFFF passes `parseFrame` unchallenged.

**failureScenario:** A single UDP datagram for any registered IMEI (or a TCP frame from a device with a firmware quirk) carries angle=0xFFFF. Ingest sanity-checks only timestamp/lat/lon, XADDs it to raw:{shard}, and ACKs. The worker reads a 200-record batch containing it; `INSERT INTO positions ... VALUES (...,65535,...)` fails with 22003; `process()` throws; the 200 entries stay PENDING and none of the 199 innocent records are written. 30 s later XAUTOCLAIM reclaims the same batch and it fails identically — forever. Combined with the `lastAutoclaim` defect (consumer.ts:124) the shard stops reading new entries entirely and 1/16 of the fleet's positions are silently trimmed away by ingest's `MAXLEN ~ 100000`.

**suggestedFix:** Clamp/validate in `normalize()` (or in `rawStreamPayloadSchema`): `course = p.angle > 32767 ? null : p.angle`, same for speed — or widen the columns to `integer` in a new numbered migration. Independently, wrap `writePositions` so a batch that fails to INSERT is bisected and the offending row(s) dead-lettered to `raw:dead` instead of being retried forever.

### 4. [HIGH] POST /v1/devices/:id/sms is an unbounded open SMS relay: both the message body and the destination number are caller-controlled, with no quota or rate limit

**Subsystem:** api — SMS gateway authz · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:618`

The send route takes `data.body` straight from `smsSendRequestSchema` (packages/shared/src/sms.ts:20-23 — `body: z.string().min(1).max(320).optional()`, no content constraint) and uses it verbatim: `const bodyText = data.body ?? sheet.smsAuto` (crud.ts:618). The destination is `device.simMsisdn` (crud.ts:620/622), which the SAME role tier can set to any E.164 number via `PATCH /v1/devices/:id` — `simMsisdn` is in `deviceUpdateSchema` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:57) and `PATCH /v1/devices/:id` is `WRITE_POLICY.device = ACCOUNT_WRITERS` (crud.ts:127), the same tier as `WRITE_POLICY.sms` (crud.ts:141). So the "config SMS to a device's SIM" framing bounds nothing: an account_manager fully controls both `To` and `Body`. There is no per-tenant SMS quota, no per-user rate limit and no daily cap anywhere in apps/api (grep for limit/quota/throttle across the SMS path returns nothing); the only gates are the `smsGateway` entitlement (any `tsp_*` plan) and the ACCOUNT_WRITERS role. V1 sends every tenant through ONE platform Twilio account with a platform `TWILIO_FROM` (ADR-032 §4, apps/worker/src/sms/drivers.ts:77-86), and the worker's SETNX guard (smsWorker.ts:74) only prevents re-charging the SAME delivery id — a fresh `POST` is a fresh delivery id and a fresh charge. ADR-032 documents the per-send charge as the reason for the entitlement gate but never accepts an arbitrary-destination relay.

**failureScenario:** An account_manager in any `tsp_*` tenant (or anyone who phishes one such session) loops: `PATCH /v1/devices/{id} {"simMsisdn":"+1555…"}` then `POST /v1/devices/{id}/sms {"body":"Your bank account is locked, verify at http://…"}`. Each iteration enqueues one SMS job that Twilio bills to the platform and delivers from the platform's sender id to an arbitrary worldwide number. With `concurrency: 4` on the sms worker and no API-side limiter, a single authenticated low-tier user can burn the founder's Twilio balance and get the platform's sender number blocked for smishing — while every send is attributed to the platform, not the tenant.

**suggestedFix:** (a) Reject a caller-supplied `body` in V1 (send only `sheet.smsAuto`/`sheet.sms*`), or restrict it to a server-side allowlist of Teltonika command templates; (b) add a per-tenant AND per-device fixed-window quota in Redis before `smsDeliveries.create` (the same atomic INCR+EXPIRE Lua used by reports.ts/routing.ts), plus a platform-wide circuit breaker like signup.ts:81; (c) require an explicit re-verification (or restrict to TENANT_ADMINS) when `simMsisdn` changes, so the destination is not mutable by the same role that triggers the send.

### 5. [HIGH] Revoking an API key never terminates the live WebSocket stream it opened — full tenant position feed keeps flowing forever

**Subsystem:** api/auth + ws gateway · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/apiKeys.ts:53`

`DELETE /v1/api-keys/:id` only sets `revokedAt` on the row (`apiKeys.ts:53` → `packages/db/src/repos/apiKeys.ts:97-104`). It never calls `markSessionsRevoked`, unlike every other credential-invalidation path (logout `auth/login.ts:251`, self password change `:309`, reset `:395`, admin PATCH user `routes/crud.ts:331`, DELETE user `:349`).

An API key CAN open a stream: `GET /v1/ws-ticket` (`app.ts:209`) carries no `requireRole`, and the X-Api-Key branch of `authMiddleware` (`auth/middleware.ts:53-63`) sets a full `AuthContext` with `role:'viewer'`. The B1 staleness guard on that route is a no-op for keys — `revokedAfter` returns `false` immediately when `tokenIssuedAtS` is undefined (`ws.ts:62`), and the API-key context never sets it (`auth/apiKey.ts:51-58`).

The WS gateway's only teardown mechanism is the periodic sweep at `ws.ts:104-133`, which closes a socket solely when a `ws:revoke:{userId}` marker exists with `t >= establishedAt` (`ws.ts:124`). For an API key the principal id is the key id (`apiKey.ts:53`), and no code path ever writes `ws:revoke:{apiKeyId}`. Sockets have no TTL, no re-auth, and no expiry of their own.

Same hole applies to the plan axis: `authMiddleware` re-checks `apiAccess` per REST request (`app.ts:189`), but a downgrade/lapse to `FLOOR_ENTITLEMENTS` (apiAccess:false) leaves an already-open key-authenticated stream running.

**failureScenario:** A TSP hands an integration partner a read-only `orb_live_…` key. The partner (or an attacker who exfiltrates the key from a CI log) calls `GET /v1/ws-ticket` and opens `wss://app/v1/stream?ticket=…`. The leak is discovered and the admin revokes the key via `DELETE /v1/api-keys/:id` — REST returns 401 immediately, so the admin believes containment is complete. The already-established socket is subscribed to `live:{tenantId}` and, because the key's accountId is null (tenant-wide), receives every device position event for the entire tenant. It keeps streaming for as long as the TCP connection is held open — days or weeks — with no metric, log, or UI showing it. Verified reachable: no role gate on /v1/ws-ticket, `revokedAfter` short-circuits on undefined `tokenIssuedAtS`, and grep shows `markSessionsRevoked` is called from exactly 5 sites, none of them the api-keys route.

**suggestedFix:** In the `DELETE /v1/api-keys/:id` handler, after a successful `revoke`, call `markSessionsRevoked(redis, keyId)` (mountApiKeys needs `redis` threaded in from `createApp`). The sweep already keys on `ctx.userId`, which for a key IS the key id, so the marker will match. Additionally, either refuse `GET /v1/ws-ticket` for the API-key principal (integration keys arguably should not hold long-lived streams) or have the gateway's 15 s sweep re-validate key-backed sockets against `apiKeys.findActiveByHash`/`revokedAt`.

### 6. [HIGH] An account-scoped tenant admin can re-point or delete a TENANT-SHARED webhook — the generic repo mutates with the READ scope, the exact asymmetry geofences were fixed for

**Subsystem:** api/db — tenant-shared row mutation scope · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/generic.ts:88`

`createGenericRepo` builds one `scopedById()` (generic.ts:62-65) from `scopedWhere(scope, cfg.scopeOpts)` and uses it for BOTH the read and the mutate pre-check. Webhooks are registered with `scopeOpts: { nullableAccount: true }` (packages/db/src/repos/webhooks.ts:26), so for an account-scoped caller that where-clause is `tenantId=T AND (accountId=A OR accountId IS NULL) AND id=W` — it matches a TENANT-SHARED webhook (accountId NULL). `update` (generic.ts:88-91) then runs `delegate.update({ where: { id } })` with no scope predicate at all, and `remove` (generic.ts:101-107) the same. The geofence repo explicitly fixed this exact class with a separate `mutateScopeSql` (packages/db/src/repos/geofences.ts:88-98, comment: "Reusing the read scope here let an account_manager PATCH/DELETE a shared geofence… cross-account sabotage"); webhooks and api_keys (repos/apiKeys.ts:98-105) were never given the same asymmetry. Creation IS pinned (crud.ts:1027 `a.accountId !== undefined ? a.accountId : data.accountId`), so an account-scoped admin cannot make a shared webhook but can freely mutate one — the precise asymmetry the geofence comment says must not exist. `webhookUpdateSchema` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:348-350) permits changing `url`, and the worker's `loadWebhooks` (apps/worker/src/jobs/webhookWorker.ts:36) selects `("accountId" = $2 OR "accountId" IS NULL)` for EVERY device's account, so a tenant-shared hook carries every sibling account's events.

**failureScenario:** TSP tenant T has accounts A1 (customer 1) and A2 (customer 2) plus a tenant-shared webhook W (accountId NULL) pointing at the TSP's own integration. Bob is a `tsp_admin` narrowed to A1 (a supported configuration — crud.ts:317 explicitly handles "a tsp_admin narrowed to one account"). Bob calls `PATCH /v1/webhooks/{W}` with `{"url":"https://bob.evil/collect"}`. The scoped findFirst matches W via the `accountId IS NULL` OR-branch, the unscoped `prisma.webhook.update({where:{id}})` rewrites the URL, and from the next event onward Bob receives geofence crossings, overspeed, panic and power-cut payloads (device ids, lat/lon, timestamps) for A2's whole fleet — a cross-account live-telemetry leak. `DELETE /v1/webhooks/{W}` likewise silently kills the tenant's integration for every account. The same read-scope-for-mutation hole lets Bob revoke a tenant-wide API key via `DELETE /v1/api-keys/{id}` (repos/apiKeys.ts:100).

**suggestedFix:** Add a `mutateScopeOpts` (or a `mutateScopedById` that never applies the `nullableAccount` OR-branch) to `createGenericRepo`, mirroring `mutateScopeSql` in geofences.ts, and make `update`/`remove` use it — and additionally scope the final `delegate.update`/`delegate.delete` by re-using `before.id` plus the scope predicate. Apply the same to `apiKeys.revoke`. Extend the isolation suite's existing "account_manager cannot MUTATE a tenant-shared fence" test to webhooks/api-keys with an account-scoped tsp_admin token.

### 7. [HIGH] WS gateway has no heartbeat, no send-backpressure guard and no client cap — a half-open socket buffers the tenant's entire live feed in the API heap forever

**Subsystem:** api/websocket-resources · **Location:** `apps/api/src/ws.ts:95`

`attachWsGateway` builds `new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })` (ws.ts:95) with no `maxPayload`, no ping/pong keepalive loop and no cap on concurrent clients. The fanout does `ws.send(message)` for every `live:{tenantId}` pmessage with only a `readyState === OPEN` check (ws.ts:154-158) — `ws.bufferedAmount` is never consulted and there is no per-socket drop/close policy. Registry entries are removed only on the `close` event (ws.ts:186-190).

`ws` fires `close` only when the peer sends a FIN/RST or when a ping times out. Because no ping interval is configured and node's HTTP server does not enable TCP keepalive on upgraded sockets, a client that vanishes silently (mobile NAT/carrier timeout, laptop sleep, VPN drop — the normal case for a fleet dashboard on a phone) leaves the socket in `OPEN` state indefinitely. The entry stays in `subscribers`, so every position published for that tenant is written into a socket whose TCP window is closed; the bytes accumulate in the node stream buffer inside the API process, unbounded.

The periodic revocation sweep (ws.ts:104-135) walks the same registry but only *closes revoked* users' sockets, so it does not reap dead ones either.

**failureScenario:** A 2,000-device tenant reports every 30 s → ~67 live messages/s at ~300 bytes each on its `live:` channel. A dispatcher has the map open on a phone; the phone goes through a tunnel and the TCP connection dies without a FIN. The socket never emits `close`, so the entry stays in `subscribers`. The API keeps calling `ws.send()` ~67×/s into a socket that can never drain: ~20 KB/s → ~72 MB/hour of heap per dead socket. A handful of such sockets across a workday exhausts the container's memory and the API is OOM-killed, taking down REST auth, the Stripe webhook and every other tenant's stream. Because the API exports no metrics beyond `ws_clients` (apps/api/src/app.ts:99), the only symptom before the kill is rising RSS that nothing is watching.

**suggestedFix:** Add a heartbeat: `ws.on('pong', ...)` plus a ~30 s interval that `ws.ping()`s every entry and `ws.terminate()`s any socket that missed the previous pong (this is the documented `ws` pattern and it also fixes the never-draining `httpServer.close()` on SIGTERM). Guard the fanout with `if (ws.bufferedAmount > SOME_LIMIT) { ws.terminate(); continue }` so a slow consumer is dropped rather than buffered. Set `maxPayload` on the WebSocketServer (the gateway never reads client messages, so a few KB is plenty) and cap total clients per tenant/process.

A peer that vanishes without FIN causes retransmission (or zero-window probe) exhaustion, and the kernel aborts on tcp_retries2 (~15 min on Linux defaults) with ETIMEDOUT. ws 8.21 handles that via `socketOnError` (node_modules/.pnpm/ws@8.21.0/.../lib/websocket.js:1397-1407) which destroys the socket → \'close\' fires → the map entry is deleted. So exposure per silently-dead client is bounded at roughly rate × 15 min (~18 MB in the claim\'s own 2000-device example), then reclaimed. "72 MB/hour forever" and "a handful across a workday exhausts memory" do not follow.\n3. "no maxPayload" is literally true but the ws server default is 100 MiB (websocket-server.js:74), not unbounded.\n\nWHAT IS GENUINELY LEFT (why not REJECTED):\n- The unbounded variant is real but needs an adversary, not a tunnel: an authenticated client that keeps ACKing with a zero window (or reads a byte occasionally) resets the persist counter, so no timeout ever fires and node\'s writable buffer grows without limit inside the API heap. Any ticket-holder qualifies — /v1/ws-ticket (apps/api/src/app.ts:209) has no rate limit and there is no per-user/per-tenant socket cap, so one viewer-role account on a busy fleet can also open N sockets and multiply the fanout. Blast radius is the shared API process (REST auth, Stripe webhook, every other tenant\'s stream), and the container has no mem_limit, so it is host memory.\n- The operational path is real but self-limiting: apps/web/src/lib/ws.ts auto-reconnects with backoff, so each network flap opens a fresh socket while leaving the zombie buffering for the TCP abort window — concurrent flaps stack, they just don\'t accumulate all day.\nRight-sized severity: MEDIUM. The fix is still the one implied (ping/pong sweep + bufferedAmount ceiling with terminate + per-user socket cap).\n\nADJACENT, SHARPER DEFECT ON THE SAME LINES (found while verifying, not part of this claim): no `ws.on(\'error\')` is registered at ws.ts:182-193, and ws adds no default error listener in `completeUpgrade` (websocket-server.js:438-450). `receiverOnError` (websocket.js:1201-1219) does `websocket.emit(\'error\', err)` for any protocol-level fault — an unmasked frame, a bad opcode, a payload over 100 MiB. With no listener the EventEmitter throws, and apps/api/src/main.ts registers no `uncaughtException` handler, so the API process exits. Any holder of a single ws-ticket (obtainable via the public self-serve signup path) can kill the whole API with one malformed frame; `restart: unless-stopped` just restarts it. That is a cheaper and more certain DoS than the buffering scenario and deserves its own finding.']

### 8. [HIGH] Signup honeypot branch runs argon2 before the rate limiter, letting an unauthenticated caller saturate the process-wide argon2 semaphore and stall every login

**Subsystem:** apps/api — public signup / argon2 semaphore · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/signup.ts:66`

`POST /v1/public/signup` parses the body (signup.ts:58) and then, if `hp_field` is non-empty, immediately does `await hashPassword(body.password)` and returns a fake 201 (signup.ts:65-68). The per-IP + global fail-closed rate limiter is at signup.ts:77-86 — i.e. AFTER that early return, so the honeypot path is completely unrate-limited. The route's own comment at signup.ts:75-76 states the global bucket exists specifically 'to protect the shared argon2 semaphore (hashPassword) that login depends on'; the honeypot branch escapes it.

`hashPassword` (apps/api/src/auth/passwords.ts:39) runs inside a process-wide semaphore of `ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT` (default 8) with ARGON2ID_PARAMS m=64 MB / t=3 / p=4. Excess calls are pushed onto an unbounded `waiters` array (passwords.ts:25,29) and served FIFO. That same semaphore is shared by tenant login (login.ts:181,184 via verifyPassword), self-service password change (login.ts:294,297), password reset (login.ts:389+), partner login (partner.ts:91) and user create/update (crud.ts:269,310).

`password` is only constrained by `z.string().min(8).max(1024)` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts, signupSchema), so each request costs a full 64 MB / t=3 argon2 hash. Note that Caddy's 64 KB `/v1/public/*` cap does not help — the payload is tiny by design.

**failureScenario:** An attacker sends a sustained ~50 rps of `POST /v1/public/signup` with body `{"name":"a","email":"a@b.com","password":"<1024 chars>","hp_field":"x"}` from a single IP. Each request bypasses signup's own 5/hour per-IP and 200/hour global buckets, immediately claims (or queues for) one of the 8 argon2 slots at ~150-400 ms each. Within seconds all 8 slots are permanently occupied and the FIFO `waiters` array grows without bound. Every legitimate `POST /v1/auth/login`, `/v1/auth/password` and `/v1/partner/login` queues behind the attacker's backlog and effectively never completes — a full authentication outage for all tenants — while the unbounded waiter array plus 8×64 MB of in-flight argon2 memory adds heap pressure.

**suggestedFix:** Move the rate-limit block (signup.ts:77-86) above the honeypot branch so the honeypot path is subject to the same per-IP and global buckets. To preserve the timing-equalisation the honeypot was written for, keep the argon2 burn but only after the limiter admits the request (i.e. reorder, do not delete the hash). Consider also bounding `waiters` in passwords.ts:25 so a saturated semaphore sheds load (503) rather than queueing indefinitely.

### 9. [HIGH] Global 1 MB body limit does not cover any route registered before it — unauthenticated /v1/auth/*, /v1/public/pilot-request and /v1/webhooks/stripe buffer arbitrarily large bodies

**Subsystem:** apps/api — request pipeline / body limits · **Location:** `apps/api/src/app.ts:205`

Hono composes matched handlers in registration order, so `app.use('/v1/*', pickBodyLimit)` at app.ts:205 only guards handlers registered AFTER it. Everything mounted earlier is unprotected: `createAuthRoutes` (app.ts:150 → login.ts:162 `c.req.json()`, :274, :289, :321, :384), `createPilotRequestRoute` (app.ts:168 → pilotRequest.ts:44), and `mountStripeWebhook` (app.ts:175 → billing.ts:238 `await c.req.text()` — read BEFORE signature verification). signup.ts:55 and partner.ts:69 explicitly added their own 64 KB `bodyLimit` for exactly this reason; auth, pilot-request and the Stripe webhook were missed.

The edge does not compensate. In infra/Caddyfile only the marketing-site block has `request_body { max_size 64KB }`, and it applies to `/v1/public/*` only. The app-host block (`{$ORBETRA_APP_HOST}`), the staging-host block, and the tenant custom-domain `https://` block all `handle /v1/*` → `reverse_proxy api:3010` with no cap. `@hono/node-server` (apps/api/src/main.ts:121) imposes no default body size, and neither does node:http.

I verified the Hono ordering behaviour empirically against the repo's own hono version: a route registered before `app.use(bodyLimit({maxSize:100}))` accepted a 50 000-byte body (200), while a route registered after it returned 413. apps/api/__tests__/apiHardening.spec.ts:158 only exercises `PATCH /v1/users/:id`, which is registered after the limiter, so the gap is not test-caught.

**failureScenario:** Unauthenticated attacker POSTs to https://dash.orbetra.com/v1/auth/login (no Origin header, so login.ts:161 `sameOriginOk` returns true) with a 1.5 GB chunked JSON body. `c.req.json()` at login.ts:162 reads the whole stream into the heap before zod ever runs and before the per-IP lockout at login.ts:168-174. A handful of concurrent such requests exhausts the API container's memory and the process is OOM-killed — taking down the REST API, the WS gateway and the Caddy on-demand-TLS `ask` endpoint with it. The same works on /v1/auth/forgot-password, /v1/auth/reset-password, /v1/public/pilot-request and /v1/webhooks/stripe (the latter before any signature check).

**suggestedFix:** Register the body limiter (or a per-route one) before these routes. Simplest: move `app.use('/v1/*', pickBodyLimit)` above the `app.route('/v1/auth', ...)` / pilot-request / Stripe-webhook mounts in createApp, keeping the import-route carve-out; the auth middleware ordering is unaffected because bodyLimit is not an auth gate. Alternatively add `bodyLimit({maxSize: 64*1024})` inside createAuthRoutes and createPilotRequestRoute, and a ~1 MB cap on the Stripe webhook, mirroring signup.ts:55. Also add `request_body { max_size ... }` to the app-host and custom-domain `handle /v1/*` blocks in infra/Caddyfile, and extend apiHardening.spec.ts to assert 413 on a pre-limiter route.

### 10. [HIGH] All unauthenticated /v1/auth/* routes bypass the global request-body limit (unbounded memory buffering)

**Subsystem:** auth/http-surface · **Location:** `apps/api/src/app.ts:150`

Hono composes matched handlers in REGISTRATION order and stops at the first handler that returns a Response. `app.route('/v1/auth', createAuthRoutes(...))` is registered at app.ts:150, while `app.use('/v1/*', pickBodyLimit)` is registered at app.ts:205 — so the body limiter never runs for any /v1/auth route. I verified this empirically against the vendored hono@4.12.27: a sub-app mounted with `app.route()` before `app.use('/v1/*', bodyLimit({maxSize:100}))` accepted a 50 KB body (200) while a route registered after the limiter got 413.

Every one of these handlers calls `await c.req.json()` (login.ts:162, 213 via cookie only, 274, 289, 321, 384), which buffers the entire body into V8 memory before zod ever runs. `POST /v1/auth/login`, `/forgot-password` and `/reset-password` are fully unauthenticated. `signup.ts:55` and `partner.ts:68` explicitly added their own 64 KB `bodyLimit` for exactly this reason; the auth sub-app was missed.

The edge does not compensate: infra/Caddyfile applies `request_body { max_size 64KB }` ONLY inside `handle /v1/public/*` on the marketing-site host. The app host block, the staging-by-IP block and the tenant custom-domain block all `handle /v1/* { reverse_proxy api:3010 }` with no cap.

**failureScenario:** An unauthenticated attacker runs `curl -X POST https://dash.orbetra.com/v1/auth/login -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @1gb.json` (no Origin header, so `sameOriginOk` at login.ts:161 returns true). `c.req.json()` at login.ts:162 buffers the full gigabyte before the zod parse rejects it. A handful of concurrent such requests exhausts the API container's heap and OOM-kills the single API process — taking down REST, the WS gateway and Caddy's on-demand-TLS `ask` endpoint with it. Cost to the attacker is one upload; no credentials, no rate limit, and the 1 MB `GLOBAL_BODY_LIMIT` the code believes is protecting it never executes.

**suggestedFix:** Move `app.use('/v1/*', pickBodyLimit)` (and the security-relevant part of the chain) above `app.route('/v1/auth', ...)`, or — minimal diff, matching the pattern already used in signup.ts/partner.ts — add `app.use('*', bodyLimit({ maxSize: 64*1024, onError }))` as the first line of `createAuthRoutes`. Add a regression test asserting a 2 MB body to `POST /v1/auth/login` returns 413 (and add the same to `/v1/public/pilot-request` and the Stripe webhook, which are registered before line 205 too).

### 11. [HIGH] Affiliate email is stored verbatim against a case-sensitive unique column while partner login lowercases — any mixed-case partner can never log in

**Subsystem:** auth/partner · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/affiliates.ts:133`

Three places disagree on email casing on the partner auth path:
- `affiliates.create` (affiliates.ts:133) writes `email: data.email` with no normalization; `affiliateCreateSchema` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:254) is a plain `z.string().email()` with no `.toLowerCase()` transform, and the `POST /v1/affiliates` handler (crud.ts:1264-1283) passes it straight through.
- `Affiliate.email` is `String @unique` (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:128) — a plain btree unique on the raw value, case-SENSITIVE. (Contrast `code`, which the team explicitly fixed with a functional `lower(code)` unique index, affiliates.ts:117-127.)
- `findByEmailForAuth` (affiliates.ts:206-207) is `prisma.affiliate.findUnique({ where: { email } })` — exact match — and `POST /v1/partner/login` lowercases before calling it (partner.ts:76).

The tenant-user path does not have this bug: `packages/db/src/repos/users.ts:51` stores `data.email.trim().toLowerCase()`. Every email in apps/api/__tests__/partner.spec.ts is already lowercase, so the whole partner surface is untested for this.

**failureScenario:** A platform_admin creates a partner via `POST /v1/affiliates {"name":"Jonas","email":"Jonas@Partner.lt"}` — the row stores `Jonas@Partner.lt`. The admin issues a set-password token (`POST /v1/affiliates/:id/set-password-token`), the partner redeems it successfully (partner.ts:100 keys on the token, not the email) and sets a password. The partner then tries to log in with their own address: partner.ts:76 lowercases it to `jonas@partner.lt`, `findUnique` finds nothing, `partner` is null, and partner.ts:89 returns 401 `invalid credentials` — forever, for every casing they try, with 10 attempts per hour before a 429. Secondarily, the case-sensitive unique lets `A@x.com` and `a@x.com` coexist as two distinct affiliates with two distinct referral codes, so commission attribution and the `?ref` self-referral guard can be pointed at the wrong row.

**suggestedFix:** Normalize on write and add a functional unique index, mirroring the fix already applied to `code`: store `data.email.trim().toLowerCase()` in `affiliates.create` (and in `update` if email ever becomes updatable), add an append-only migration creating `UNIQUE (lower(email))` on `affiliates` after collapsing existing duplicates, and change `findByEmailForAuth` to a `lower("email") = lower($1)` raw query so pre-existing mixed-case rows keep working. Add a partner.spec case that creates `Mixed@Case.co` and logs in as `mixed@case.co`.

### 12. [HIGH] Signup honeypot runs argon2 BEFORE the rate limiter, letting anonymous traffic starve the shared argon2 semaphore used by login

**Subsystem:** auth/rate-limiting · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/signup.ts:65`

The honeypot branch at signup.ts:65-68 does `await hashPassword(body.password)` and returns 201 — but the per-IP + platform-wide fail-closed rate limiter is at signup.ts:77-86, i.e. AFTER that early `return`. The honeypot path therefore executes an unbounded number of full argon2id operations.

`hashPassword` (apps/api/src/auth/passwords.ts:38) goes through `withSlot`, a process-global semaphore of `ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT` (default 8, passwords.ts:23) that is SHARED with `verifyPassword` — which is what `POST /v1/auth/login` (login.ts:181,184), `POST /v1/auth/password` (login.ts:294) and `POST /v1/partner/login` (partner.ts:87) all use. Excess callers queue in `waiters` (passwords.ts:25,28) with no bound and no timeout.

The route's own comment at signup.ts:76 states the global bucket exists "to protect the shared argon2 semaphore (hashPassword) that login depends on" — the honeypot branch escapes precisely that protection. `signupSchema` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:280) permits `hp_field` up to 200 chars, so triggering the branch is trivial, and the 64 KB `bodyLimit` at signup.ts:55 does not slow it down.

**failureScenario:** Attacker sends `POST /v1/public/signup {"name":"a","email":"a@b.co","password":"<8 chars>","hp_field":"x"}` at ~50 rps from a single host. Each request occupies one of the 8 argon2 slots for the full m=64MB,t=3,p=4 hash (~100-300 ms), so all 8 slots stay permanently saturated. Every real `POST /v1/auth/login` then blocks in `waiters` behind the flood — no tenant user, admin, or partner can sign in for as long as the flood runs, and no rate limit, lockout, or metric ever fires because the honeypot returns 201 before any of them.

**suggestedFix:** Move the per-IP + global rate-limit block (signup.ts:77-86) ABOVE the honeypot branch so the honeypot is also throttled, and replace the honeypot's real `hashPassword` with a fixed sleep of comparable duration (the branch only needs timing parity, not a real hash). Add a test asserting that N+1 honeypot posts from one IP return 429.

### 13. [HIGH] Revoking an API key never terminates the live WebSocket stream it opened — the leaked key keeps streaming positions forever

**Subsystem:** auth/session-revocation · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/apiKeys.ts:50`

`DELETE /v1/api-keys/:id` (apiKeys.ts:50-55) sets `revokedAt` in Postgres and nothing else. It never calls `markSessionsRevoked` — a grep over apps/api/src shows the only callers are login.ts:251/309/395 and crud.ts:331/349 (all human-user paths).

An API key CAN open a live stream: `authMiddleware` (middleware.ts:53-63) is mounted on `/v1/*` at app.ts:189 with the `apiKey` branch enabled, and `GET /v1/ws-ticket` is registered after it at app.ts:209. For an API key, `AuthContext.userId` is the key id (apiKey.ts:53) and `tokenIssuedAtS` is never set, so `revokedAfter` at app.ts:214 returns `false` immediately (ws.ts:62) and a ticket is always issued.

Once upgraded, the only teardown mechanism is the periodic sweep at ws.ts:104-133, which closes a socket only if `ws:revoke:<userId>` exists and is `>= establishedAt`. No code ever writes that marker for an API-key id. There is also no heartbeat, no idle timeout and no maximum socket lifetime in ws.ts, and Caddy's `handle /v1/* { reverse_proxy api:3010 }` blocks set no proxy timeout for the upgrade.

**failureScenario:** A tenant's `orb_live_…` key leaks (committed to a repo, CI log, or a partner integration). The attacker calls `GET /v1/ws-ticket` with `X-Api-Key`, then connects `wss://dash.orbetra.com/v1/stream?ticket=…`. The tenant notices, and the admin does `DELETE /v1/api-keys/:id` — every REST call with that key now 401s, the audit log records the revocation, and the dashboard shows the key as revoked. The attacker's WebSocket is untouched and keeps receiving every `live:{tenantId}` position event for the whole fleet, indefinitely, until the API process is restarted. The tenant has no way to observe or stop it.

**suggestedFix:** In `apiKeys.revoke`'s route handler, call `await markSessionsRevoked(deps.redis, id)` after a successful revoke (the WS sweep already keys on `ctx.userId`, which is the key id — no gateway change needed). Independently, add a hard maximum socket lifetime / periodic re-authorization in `attachWsGateway` so no credential can produce an unbounded-lifetime stream, and add a test that a socket opened with an API key closes with `WS_REVOKED_CLOSE` after the key is deleted.

### 14. [HIGH] Refresh rotation is not fenced against revocation — a refresh in flight during a password reset re-mints a live token in the just-revoked family

**Subsystem:** auth/session-revocation · **Location:** `apps/api/src/auth/login.ts:231`

`POST /v1/auth/refresh` performs three unrelated statements with no transaction and no revocation fence: `claimForRotation` (login.ts:213), `findByIdForAuth` (:224), then `issueSession` → `refreshTokens.create` (:231 → :140-146). `create` inserts a row with `revokedAt: null` unconditionally — it never re-checks whether the family or the user was revoked between the claim and the insert.

Every eviction path in the product is an `UPDATE ... WHERE revokedAt IS NULL` over rows that already exist: `revokeAllForUser` (packages/db/src/auth.ts:162-164) used by `/v1/auth/password` (login.ts:306), `/v1/auth/reset-password` (login.ts:394) and the admin `PATCH /v1/users/:id` (routes/crud.ts:326); and `revokeFamily` (auth.ts:159-161). A row inserted *after* that UPDATE is simply not covered by it, so the new refresh token is fully live for the whole `REFRESH_TTL` (14 days by default) and keeps rotating indefinitely.

There is also no rate limit anywhere on `POST /v1/auth/refresh` (it is registered at app.ts:150, before both `authMiddleware` and `pickBodyLimit`), so an attacker can keep a request permanently in flight in the claim→create window.

The WS side is defeated too: the racing refresh mints an access token whose `iat` is at or after the revoke second, so `revokedAfter` (ws.ts:61-71, `Math.floor(revokedAtMs/1000) > tokenIssuedAtS`) returns false and `GET /v1/ws-ticket` (app.ts:214) issues a ticket; the resulting socket's `establishedAt` is newer than the marker so the sweep at ws.ts:124 never closes it.

**failureScenario:** An attacker holds a stolen `orb_refresh` cookie and loops `POST /v1/auth/refresh` continuously (no rate limit on that route). The victim notices and does the documented remedy — `POST /v1/auth/reset-password` (or an admin does `PATCH /v1/users/:id` with a new password). At that instant one attacker request has already passed `claimForRotation` (login.ts:213) but has not yet reached `refreshTokens.create` (login.ts:140). `revokeAllForUser` marks every existing row revoked; ~2 ms later the attacker's insert lands with `revokedAt: null`, `rotatedAt: null`, `expiresAt = now + 14d`. The attacker's session survives the reset, keeps rotating forever, and — because the new access token's `iat` is not older than the revoke marker — can still mint ws-tickets and open live position streams. The victim's password reset evicted nobody. The same race fires benignly for an honest user whose second browser tab auto-refreshes during a "log out everywhere", silently resurrecting a session they believe they killed.

**suggestedFix:** Make claim+create one atomic, revocation-aware step: run `claimForRotation` and `refreshTokens.create` inside a single `prisma.$transaction`, and inside it re-assert the family is still live (`SELECT ... FROM refresh_tokens WHERE familyId = $1 AND revokedAt IS NOT NULL LIMIT 1` → abort). Better: add a `users.sessionsRevokedAt` column, set it in the same statement as `setPassword`, and have `claimForRotation` reject any token whose family `createdAt < sessionsRevokedAt` — that also removes the 15-minute access-token blind spot. Additionally add a per-cookie/per-IP rate limit to `POST /v1/auth/refresh` so the window cannot be held open at will.

A rate limit on `/v1/auth/refresh` is worth adding regardless (it is an unauthenticated 2-query-per-request DB amplifier today), but it narrows the odds rather than closing the race.']

### 15. [HIGH] WS ticket revocation is checked at issuance but not at redemption — a pre-fetched ticket survives logout/password-reset permanently

**Subsystem:** auth/ws-session · **Location:** `apps/api/src/ws.ts:183`

Revocation is enforced in two places that leave a gap. At issuance, `app.ts:214` runs `revokedAfter(redis, auth.userId, auth.tokenIssuedAtS)` and refuses a ticket for a token minted before the marker. At redemption, `ws.ts:174` only does `GETDEL ticket:<t>` and then `ws.ts:183` stamps `establishedAt = Date.now()` — the revocation marker is never consulted, and neither the token's `iat` nor the ticket's issuance time is carried into the entry (the ticket JSON does contain `tokenIssuedAtS`, since `issueTicket` serializes the whole `AuthContext`, but the gateway ignores it).

The sweep at ws.ts:121-130 closes a socket only when `revokedAt >= establishedAt`. A ticket minted BEFORE the revoke but redeemed AFTER it produces `establishedAt > revokedAt`, so the sweep permanently considers that socket authorized. Tickets live 30 s (`WS_TICKET_TTL`, app.ts:217), so the window is up to 30 s wide and is trivially kept open by continuously pre-fetching tickets.

**failureScenario:** An attacker holds a stolen access token (XSS, leaked log, shared machine). They run a loop: every 25 s call `GET /v1/ws-ticket` and hold the ticket unredeemed. The victim logs out (login.ts:251 writes `ws:revoke:<uid>` = T) or resets their password (login.ts:395). The attacker's next ticket fetch 401s with `session_revoked` — that is their signal — so they immediately redeem the ticket they already hold. `handleUpgrade` succeeds, `establishedAt = T+2s > T`, and the 15 s sweep never closes it. The attacker now has a live, indefinitely-lived feed of every position in the tenant that survived both the logout and the password reset, while the user's REST access token expires normally in 15 min and every UI signal says the session was terminated.

**suggestedFix:** Re-check revocation at redemption: after `GETDEL`, read `ws:revoke:<ctx.userId>` and refuse the upgrade if the marker is newer than the ticket's issuance instant; simplest correct form is to stamp the ticket with `issuedAtMs` in `issueTicket` and set `establishedAt = ctx.issuedAtMs` (not `Date.now()`) at ws.ts:183, so the existing `revokedAt >= establishedAt` sweep closes it on the very next tick. Add a test: mint ticket → `markSessionsRevoked` → redeem → assert the socket is closed with `WS_REVOKED_CLOSE`.

### 16. [HIGH] POST /v1/devices/:id/sms sends an arbitrary body to an arbitrary E.164 number with no rate limit, quota, or metering — unbounded platform Twilio spend

**Subsystem:** billing / SMS cost · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:592`

The SMS send route (`crud.ts:592-632`) is gated only by role (`sms: ACCOUNT_WRITERS` — crud.ts:143, i.e. account_manager and up) and the `smsGateway` entitlement. Nothing else bounds it:

- The destination is `device.simMsisdn` (crud.ts:620), which the same ACCOUNT_WRITERS role can set to any value matching `/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/` via `deviceCreateSchema`/`deviceUpdateSchema` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:48,57) — any international or premium-rate number.
- The message text is fully caller-controlled: `const bodyText = data.body ?? sheet.smsAuto` (crud.ts:618), with `body: z.string().min(1).max(320)` (packages/shared/src/sms.ts:21) — up to 3 SMS segments per request.
- There is no per-tenant/per-device cooldown or quota anywhere: `smsDeliveries.create` (packages/db/src/repos/smsDeliveries.ts:56) is an unconditional insert, and `app.ts` applies no rate limiter to this path (the only limiters configured are caddy-ask, share, api-key, signup, routing, reports — app.ts:48-88).
- The worker's charge guard is per-`smsDeliveryId` only (apps/worker/src/jobs/smsWorker.ts:73 `SET NX sms:sent:{id}`) — it prevents charging one delivery twice, but every POST mints a NEW delivery id, so it does not bound the number of paid sends at all.
- SMS is never metered or billed back: it produces no `usage_daily` row, no Stripe meter event, and does not appear in `reportDailyOverage`. It is 100% unrecoverable platform cost.

**failureScenario:** A TSP tenant's `account_manager` (or anyone with a stolen session/password for such a user) PATCHes one device's `simMsisdn` to a premium-rate international number they control, then loops `POST /v1/devices/{id}/sms {"body":"<320 chars>"}`. Each request is a 201 and a fresh Twilio charge. At a few requests/second with 3 segments per message, the platform's Twilio account bleaks hundreds of euros per hour to a number the attacker collects revenue-share on (classic SMS pumping). Nothing rate-limits it, nothing alerts on it, and none of it is billed to the tenant — the first signal is the Twilio invoice. The same loop with no attacker at all (a buggy retry in a customer's integration) produces the same bill.

**suggestedFix:** Bound the endpoint before the delivery row is created: (a) a per-device cooldown (config SMS is an onboarding action — one per device per N minutes is plenty) and a per-tenant daily send cap, both Redis-backed and fail-closed; (b) restrict `data.body` to the generated onboarding text (or an allowlist of Teltonika config commands) rather than free text; (c) restrict destinations to the ICCID/MSISDN ranges of SIMs actually provisioned to the tenant, or at minimum an allowlist of dialing prefixes; (d) record each send in `usage_daily`/a Stripe meter so the cost is at least attributable.

### 17. [HIGH] Strict `lt` monotonic guard silently drops a genuinely newer Stripe event that shares the same `created` SECOND

**Subsystem:** billing / Stripe webhook · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:250`

`applySubscriptionEvent` guards with `{ OR: [{ lastBillingEventAt: null }, { lastBillingEventAt: { lt: eventAt } }] }` (tenants.ts:250) where `eventAt = new Date(event.created * 1000)` (billing.ts:256). Stripe's `event.created` is Unix SECONDS. The guard therefore cannot distinguish 'this is a replay of the event I already applied' from 'this is a DIFFERENT, later event that happens to fall in the same second' — the second one matches zero rows and is dropped with no error, no retry and no log (the route still returns 200 at billing.ts:280). The in-code comment at tenants.ts:242 conflates the two cases. Nothing ever reconciles tenant billing state against Stripe afterwards, so the divergence is permanent.

**failureScenario:** A customer completes Checkout. Stripe emits `customer.subscription.created` (status `incomplete`) and, once the first invoice is paid, `customer.subscription.updated` (status `active`) — routinely within the same second. If `created` is applied first, `lastBillingEventAt` is stamped with that second and the `active` event's `lt` predicate fails → dropped. The tenant is permanently recorded as `subscriptionStatus='incomplete'`. Consequences: (a) `GET /v1/billing` reports `active:false` and `canSubscribe:false` (billing.ts:81-84) and `POST /v1/billing/checkout` returns 409 `already_subscribed` (billing.ts:123), so the paying customer has no self-service recovery; (b) `listActiveSubscribers()` filters `subscriptionStatus in ['active','trialing']` (tenants.ts:280-286), so this tenant is excluded from `reportDailyOverage` FOREVER — every device-day of overage goes unbilled, silently.

**suggestedFix:** Dedupe replays on the Stripe `event.id` (a `processed_billing_events` table or a Redis SET NX on the id) and change the ordering guard to `lte`, or carry a finer ordering key. At minimum, when the update matches zero rows and the event id has not been seen before, log/metric it instead of acking silently.

### 18. [HIGH] `past_due` tenants keep full entitlements but are excluded from overage metering — free overage for the entire dunning window

**Subsystem:** billing / usage metering · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:282`

`listActiveSubscribers` selects only `subscriptionStatus IN ('active','trialing')`, so it is the sole input to `reportDailyOverage` (`apps/worker/src/billing/usageReporter.ts:73`). The entitlement layer takes the opposite position on the same status: `LAPSED_SUBSCRIPTION_STATUSES` in `packages/shared/src/plans.ts:64` deliberately EXCLUDES `past_due`, with the comment "it is Stripe's dunning grace window, so a temporary card failure keeps access while retries run". The result is a direct contradiction: during dunning the tenant keeps white-label, sub-accounts, API, webhooks, SMS gateway and an uncapped device count, while their device-day overage is not metered at all. Combined with finding #1 (a day is never re-reported), those days are lost permanently even after the card is fixed and the status flips back to `active`.

**failureScenario:** A tsp_grow tenant with 260 active devices (200 included) has its card expire on 2026-08-01. Stripe marks the subscription `past_due` and retries for the configured dunning window (commonly 2–3 weeks). Every day in that window `listActiveSubscribers` omits the tenant, so no meter event is created for ~60 devices/day. On 2026-08-18 the customer updates the card, the subscription returns to `active`, and Stripe invoices the period — with roughly 17 × 60 = 1020 device-days of overage missing, which no code path can recover.

**suggestedFix:** Align the metering predicate with the entitlement predicate: report overage for any status that is NOT in `LAPSED_SUBSCRIPTION_STATUSES` (i.e. include `past_due`), or derive both from one shared helper so the grace-window decision cannot be made twice with opposite answers.

### 19. [HIGH] `/v1/internal/caddy-ask` is publicly reachable through every Caddy host block; its per-domain 10/min bucket is an anonymous kill-switch for a tenant's white-label TLS

**Subsystem:** caddy/api-exposure · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/caddyAsk.ts:48`

`createPublicRoutes` registers `GET /v1/internal/caddy-ask` before `authMiddleware`, so it is unauthenticated by design — it is only meant to be called by Caddy over the internal compose network (`ask http://api:3010/v1/internal/caddy-ask`, infra/Caddyfile:7). But every public site block in infra/Caddyfile proxies the whole `/v1/*` prefix straight to the api: the app host (Caddyfile:58), the staging-by-IP host (Caddyfile:81) and the on-demand-TLS tenant-custom-domain block (Caddyfile:118). The marketing-site host only allowlists `/v1/public/*`, but its fallback goes to `site:4174`, whose vite-preview proxy forwards `/v1` to `api:3010` anyway (apps/site/vite.config.ts preview.proxy). So `/v1/internal/caddy-ask?domain=<anything>` is reachable from the internet on every hostname the platform serves.

The handler's throttle is keyed on the *requested domain*, not the caller: `caddyask:${domain}` INCR with `max = ASK_RATE_MAX ?? 10` per `ASK_RATE_WINDOW_S ?? 60` (apps/api/src/routes/caddyAsk.ts:53-56, defaults from apps/api/src/main.ts:107-110; the apps compose sets neither var). The code comment explicitly reasons that per-domain keying avoids "one global bucket an attacker could exhaust" — but it assumed only Caddy can reach the route. Because anyone can, the per-domain bucket becomes a per-tenant denial lever: exceeding it returns 429, and Caddy treats any non-2xx ask response as "deny", refusing to mint or renew the certificate for that hostname.

Secondary: the 200-vs-403 split (caddyAsk.ts:58) is an unauthenticated oracle for `tenantDomains.isVerifiedDomain`, letting anyone enumerate which hostnames are verified tenant domains.

**failureScenario:** An attacker learns a tenant's white-label hostname `fleet.customer.lt` (visible in the tenant's own marketing, or discovered via the 200/403 oracle). They run `curl -s 'https://dash.orbetra.com/v1/internal/caddy-ask?domain=fleet.customer.lt'` at 1 request/second from a single host. After 10 requests the Redis key `caddyask:fleet.customer.lt` is above `max`, and it never drops below because the fixed window is re-filled every second. Every subsequent ask — including Caddy's own, when a real browser opens a TLS handshake for that domain or when the 90-day cert comes up for renewal — gets 429, so Caddy denies on-demand issuance. The tenant's branded domain fails TLS entirely (new domains never get a cert; existing ones stop renewing) for as long as the attacker keeps sending one request per second. Nothing is logged as an attack and no alert exists for it.

**suggestedFix:** Stop proxying the internal prefix from the edge: add `handle /v1/internal/* { respond 404 }` (or an `@internal not remote_ip <docker subnet>` guard) ahead of `handle /v1/*` in every public site block of infra/Caddyfile, and drop `/v1` from the site/web vite `preview.proxy` so the SPA containers cannot re-open the hole. Additionally require a shared secret on the ask (Caddy `ask` supports appending a query/header; compare against an env var in the handler) so a leaked path is not sufficient, and key the rate limit on `(domain, caller)` rather than domain alone so a hostile caller cannot consume Caddy's budget.

So the endpoint is internet-reachable on every hostname the platform serves — this holds independently of the already-known site-container vite-preview proxy issue, so the finding does not depend on that excluded item.\n- Defaults confirmed: app.ts:159 falls back to { max: 10, windowS: 60 }; main.ts:107-110 reads ASK_RATE_MAX/ASK_RATE_WINDOW_S; grep shows neither is set in infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml, so production runs 10/60.\n- The bucket is keyed on the attacker-supplied domain: `caddyask:${domain}` (caddyAsk.ts:54). No per-IP component at all.\n- Caddy\'s ask hook (Caddyfile:7) denies on any non-2xx, and the Caddyfile\'s own comment (lines 8-9) records that Caddy >=2.8 removed interval/burst — so the "coarse global bound" that caddyAsk.ts:23-24 and README:161-162 rely on no longer exists. The design\'s sole assumption ("only Caddy can reach this") is false.\n\nCorrection to the claim\'s mechanism (does not change the verdict): the Lua limiter (caddyAsk.ts:12-14) re-arms EXPIRE only when n == 1 or TTL < 0, so the fixed window DOES expire after windowS — it is not "re-filled every second". At the claimed 1 req/s the domain is denied ~83% of the time (10 of 60 slots open per window), not 100%. But the attacker picks the rate: at 100+ req/s the 10-request budget is consumed within ~100 ms of each 60 s window, leaving the domain denied >99.8% of the time. The claimed outcome stands; only the described request rate is under-tuned.\n\nImpact assessment: first-time cert issuance for a tenant\'s white-label hostname fails during a sustained flood (customer-visible TLS failure on the tenant\'s branded domain). certmagic also consults the ask permission on on-demand renewal, so renewal becomes a probabilistic race the attacker can dominate. Certs already in Caddy\'s in-memory cache keep serving until restart/renewal, so this is deterministic denial for new issuance and renewal starvation rather than an instant outage for live domains — availability damage to a paid white-label feature, anonymous, ~free, and completely unlogged/unalerted.\n\nAdditional angle the claim missed, which reinforces it: because the bucket is keyed solely on the attacker-chosen domain, an attacker cycling random hostnames gets a fresh 10-request budget per hostname — i.e. this route has no global bound at all from the API side. Every request past the limiter runs an unauthenticated prisma.tenantDomain.findFirst (packages/db/src/repos/tenantDomains.ts:89-92) and mints a 60 s-TTL Redis key, making the same flaw an unauthenticated DB-query and Redis-key amplifier.\n\nThe secondary 200-vs-403 oracle (caddyAsk.ts:58) is real but low value — tenant custom domains are already public via Certificate Transparency logs once issued.\n\nFix: drop /v1/internal/* at the edge in every Caddy site block (Caddy calls the api over the compose network, not through itself) and/or add a per-client-IP cap alongside the per-domain one, plus a metric on ask 429s.\n\nSeverity: "high" is slightly generous given established domains keep serving from cache and renewal denial is probabilistic; medium-high is the honest read. But the claim is accurate, reachable, unmitigated, and worth fixing before white-label domains go GA.']

### 20. [HIGH] Codec 16 packets are silently discarded and ACKed 0 — permanent device resend wedge

**Subsystem:** codec/parse · **Location:** `packages/codec/src/parse.ts:41`

`parseFrame` short-circuits codec 0x10 to `{kind:'avl', codec:16, records:[], rawFallback:true}` (parse.ts:41-44). `rawFallback` is read by NO caller anywhere in the repo (grep: only its own definition in types.ts:25 and one assertion in __tests__/wiki.spec.ts:66) — the promised "raw fallback" of PROJECT_PLAN §3.1 does not exist. The packet then flows into the normal AVL path: `persistAvlBatch` gets an empty `records` array, hits the `good.length === 0 && insane.length === 0` early return (apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:48) and returns 0, so session.ts:271 writes `encodeAck(0)`. PROJECT_PLAN §3.2 states "Count mismatch ⇒ device resends the packet" — so the device resends the identical packet forever while its records are dropped on the floor. Nothing is written to the `rejects` stream, `parseFailTotal` and `frameViolationsTotal` stay at 0, and no dedicated counter exists, so the loop is completely invisible in `/metrics`. The 8E `n1 == n2` consistency check (parse.ts:57) is also skipped for codec 16 because the switch returns before `parseAvl`. Same behaviour on the UDP channel: apps/ingest/src/udp.ts:130 only special-cases `parsed.kind !== 'avl'`, and a codec-16 packet IS `kind:'avl'`, so it falls through to persist (0 records) and `encodeUdpAck(..., 0)`. The FMB6xx family this affects is already anticipated in-tree (packages/codec/dictionaries/fmb6xx.stub.json).

**failureScenario:** Verified by execution against the real ingest server with a registered IMEI: handshake replies `01`, then a codec-16 frame (dataLen=36, valid CRC) yields reply `00000000`, the socket stays open, and msgs=1 / parseFail=0 / frameViolations=0 / sessionErrors=0. In production: an FMB640 or any device with 'Codec 16' enabled in its data-sending profile connects, uploads a buffered batch, is told 0 records were accepted, resends the identical packet, and repeats indefinitely. The customer sees a device that is 'online' with zero positions ever recorded, burns its data plan, and no alert fires because every ingest metric looks healthy.

**suggestedFix:** Do not pretend codec 16 succeeded. Either (a) implement the codec-16 record walk, or (b) make the fallback real: XADD the whole frame to the `rejects` stream with `reason:'codec16'`, ACK `bytes[9]` (NumberOfData1) so the device advances its buffer instead of looping, and add an `ingest_unsupported_codec_total{codec}` counter to prom.ts so the condition is observable. At minimum, ACK the declared record count rather than 0 and bump a counter — silently ACKing 0 forever is the worst of the three options.

Repo-wide grep hits only the producer (parse.ts:44), the type (types.ts:25), the test helper/assertion (__tests__/helpers.ts:15, __tests__/wiki.spec.ts:66-67), the fixture (__fixtures__/wiki/codec16.hex.json:11), IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md:400 and docs/adr/013-parsedpacket-contract-extension.md:13. ADR-013 explicitly specifies the intended contract as "callers read `frame.bytes` for payload" — and no caller does, so the raw payload is never captured anywhere (not the rejects stream, not a log, nothing).\n\n3. ### 21. [HIGH] GDPR device erase never deletes sms_deliveries — SIM MSISDN + full SMS body survive erasure forever and become unreachable

**Subsystem:** gdpr-erase / schema · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/jobs/gdprEraseWorker.ts:67`

runErase deletes positions, trips (`:67`), events (`:68`), commands (`:69`) and finally the devices row (`:71`), but never touches `sms_deliveries`. That table is device-scoped (`deviceId BIGINT NOT NULL`) yet has NO foreign key to devices — packages/db/prisma/migrations/20260721130000_sms_gateway/migration.sql:15-29 creates it with only a PK and two plain indexes, and the Prisma model (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:538-555) declares no `device` relation — so nothing cascades either. Its `to` column is the SIM subscriber MSISDN (E.164 phone number) and `body` is the full config-SMS text. The worker's own header comment (`:17-18`) enumerates the DELIBERATELY kept tables as exactly `usage_daily` and `audit_log`, so this is an oversight, not a documented carve-out. Contrast share_links and maintenance_items, which do carry ON DELETE CASCADE (migrations 20260713130000:25, 20260714140000:23) and are therefore correctly removed.

**failureScenario:** A TSP sends Teltonika config SMS to a customer vehicle's SIM via POST /v1/devices/:id/sms; rows land in sms_deliveries with to='+37060012345'. The customer exercises GDPR Art. 17; the admin retires the device and the erase job runs. positions/trips/events/commands and the devices row are deleted and the platform reports the erase complete — but the sms_deliveries rows persist indefinitely with the subscriber's phone number and message body. Worse, they are now unreachable: GET /v1/devices/:id/sms resolves via db.devices.get, which 404s because the device row is gone, so the retained personal data cannot even be located or purged through the product.

**suggestedFix:** Add `await pool.query('DELETE FROM sms_deliveries WHERE "deviceId" = $1', [data.deviceId])` alongside the trips/events/commands deletes (and repeat it in the post-delete late sweep), and/or add a new append-only migration giving sms_deliveries a `deviceId` FK to devices(id) ON DELETE CASCADE.

### 22. [HIGH] Geofence geometry has no complexity or count bound — an O(vertices) ray-cast runs per position record per fence on the shared worker event loop

**Subsystem:** geofences (shared validation → db → worker pipeline) · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/geofences.ts:116`

The only server-side guards on a submitted geofence are `ST_IsValid` and an AREA cap (`guardGeog`, packages/db/src/repos/geofences.ts:116-122, MAX_AREA_M2 = 10,000 km²). Neither bounds VERTEX COUNT. The zod gate (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:432-439) allows up to 50 rings × 10,000 positions each; a corridor (`geoJsonLineStringSchema`, entities.ts:449-452) allows a 10,000-point LineString that `ST_Buffer` expands server-side. There is also NO cap on how many geofences a tenant may create — `POST /v1/geofences` (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:974-991) has no count check, no entitlement gate and no rate limit, so it is reachable on a free self-serve trial plan.

The stored geometry is then (a) written verbatim into a Redis hash field (apps/api/src/routes/geofenceRegistry.ts:17), (b) HGETALL'd and JSON.parsed for the whole tenant every 30 s on the hot path (apps/worker/src/geofence/cache.ts:60-72, called from apps/worker/src/main.ts:303), and (c) evaluated by a pure-JS ray cast that iterates EVERY vertex of the outer ring — `inRing`, apps/worker/src/geofence/point.ts:15-27 — once per record per fence (apps/worker/src/geofence/engine.ts:63 → :105). All 16 shard consumers and all 13 BullMQ workers share one Node process/event loop (apps/worker/src/main.ts), so this blocking work stalls every tenant's pipeline, not just the offender's.

Verified against the running Postgres/PostGIS image: a 10,000-vertex circular polygon is a 240 KB request body (under the 1 MB `pickBodyLimit` at apps/api/src/app.ts:195-205), returns `ST_IsValid = true`, and has an area of 57 km² — 0.6% of the cap, so both existing guards pass. A 10,000-point corridor line buffered by the maximum 5,000 m yields a 5,101-vertex polygon at 100 km², also passing. Measured in Node: 200 records × 100 such fences × 10,000 vertices = 498 ms of *synchronous* event-loop blocking per batch (batch size is 200, apps/worker/src/consumer.ts:150/162).

This is also reachable accidentally: an operator importing an OSM municipality boundary routinely produces thousands of vertices.

**failureScenario:** A tenant signs up via the public self-serve trial (`POST /v1/public/signup`), registers a device, points a Codec-8 client at the open ingest port, then POSTs 200 geofences each carrying a valid, tiny-area, 10,000-vertex polygon (240 KB body each — all pass `ST_IsValid` and the 10,000 km² cap). Within 30 s the worker's GeofenceCache loads ~48 MB of JSON for that tenant and the geofence engine begins doing 200 records × 200 fences × 10,000 vertices ≈ 4×10^8 float operations synchronously per batch — roughly 1 second of blocked event loop per batch. Because the worker is a single process hosting all 16 shard consumers plus the notify/webhook/command/usage/GDPR BullMQ workers, EVERY tenant's positions stop being XACKed, pipeline_lag_ms climbs without bound, and ingest keeps XADD-ing into `raw:{shard}` until MAXLEN trimming silently drops already-ACKed records (I1 loss). Redis memory also grows unbounded under the mandated noeviction policy.

### 23. [HIGH] Tenant custom domains get a 403 from the SPA container — white-label domains are functionally dead in the deployed stack

**Subsystem:** infra/web-serving · **Location:** `apps/web/vite.config.ts:38`

`preview: { proxy, allowedHosts: ['dash.orbetra.com'] }` hard-codes the only non-IP Host the web container will serve. The Caddy tenant-custom-domain block (`infra/Caddyfile:99-124`) proxies everything except `/v1/*` to `web:5173`, and Caddy's `reverse_proxy` passes the client's Host through verbatim (the whole Host-keyed `/v1/branding` flow depends on that). Vite 7.3.6's host validator (`node_modules/.pnpm/vite@7.3.6.../vite/dist/node/chunks/config.js:20350` `isHostAllowedInternal`) allows only IPv4/IPv6 literals, `localhost`/`*.localhost`, and exact or `.suffix` matches from `allowedHosts` — everything else gets `403 Blocked request. This host (...) is not allowed.` The file's own comment (line 36) shows the authors knew domains are blocked but only enumerated one. The same trap exists for the marketing site (`apps/site/vite.config.ts:26` allows only `orbetra.com`/`www.orbetra.com`) and for any deployment that sets `ORBETRA_APP_HOST` (`infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml:16`) to something other than `dash.orbetra.com`.

**failureScenario:** A tenant verifies `track.transportas.lt` via the DNS-TXT flow; Caddy's on-demand-TLS ask succeeds and mints a cert. The browser loads `https://track.transportas.lt/` → Caddy `handle {}` → `web:5173` with `Host: track.transportas.lt` → vite preview returns `403 Blocked request`. `/v1/branding` still answers (Caddy sends it to `api:3010`), so the API and cert look healthy while every tenant on a custom domain sees a bare 403 page instead of the dashboard. E03-5 white-labeling is a V1-MUST and is silently broken by config only, so no test or CI gate catches it.

**suggestedFix:** Set `preview.allowedHosts: true` in `apps/web/vite.config.ts` (and `apps/site/vite.config.ts`) — the preview server is only reachable through Caddy on the internal Docker network and serves a static dist, so DNS-rebinding is not in scope — or drive the list from an env var populated with the verified tenant domains. Add a smoke assertion in `infra/smoke.sh` that a non-`dash.` Host returns 200 from `web:5173`.

### 24. [HIGH] Sanity-rejected records are ACKed as accepted, then written only to a capped Redis stream nobody consumes — `raw_rejects` is dead code

**Subsystem:** ingest / db (raw_rejects) · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:53`

`persistAvlBatch` partitions a packet into `good` (→ `raw:{shard}`) and `insane` (→ XADD `rejects`, MAXLEN ~100_000). The returned `persisted` count (line 82) deliberately includes the `rejects` XADDs, and the session ACKs that count, so the device is told those records were accepted and deletes them from its on-board buffer.

The `rejects` stream is described in the docblock as "the durable `rejects` stream", but it is (a) capped at ~100k entries and (b) has **no consumer anywhere in the repo**. `grep -rn "'rejects'"` over apps/, packages/, tools/ returns only this XADD and two assertions in `apps/ingest/__tests__/ingest.spec.ts:198` / `apps/ingest/__tests__/udp.spec.ts:140` — no XREAD, XREADGROUP or XAUTOCLAIM on it. The `RawReject` model that PROJECT_PLAN §3/§6.3 specifies as the destination (`packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:416`, table created in `0_init/migration.sql:103`) is never INSERTed into by any code path.

So the data path is: device hands over a record → ingest takes responsibility (ACK) → record goes into a rotating in-memory Redis stream → rotates out. `ingest_sanity_rejects_total` (prom.ts:37) shows a number, but there is no way to see *which* device or *what* payload, and no way to recover it.

**failureScenario:** An FMB1xx cold-boots after a battery change and has no GPS time sync yet; its RTC reports 2004-01-01 (below `minTsMs = Date.UTC(2020,0,1)`, apps/ingest/src/server.ts:24). The driver presses the panic button during this window. `isSaneRecord` returns false, the record is XADDed to `rejects`, counted as persisted (persist.ts:82), and ACKed — the device deletes it. The panic record never reaches `raw:{shard}`, never becomes an `events` row, never fires a notification, and never lands in `raw_rejects`. After ~100k further rejects platform-wide the only remaining copy is trimmed out of Redis. The operator sees a counter tick and nothing else; the incident is unreconstructable.

**suggestedFix:** Either (a) add a worker consumer for the `rejects` stream that inserts into `raw_rejects` (imei, reason, payload) with the existing `raw_rejects_createdAt_idx` retention story, or (b) if the table is genuinely abandoned, stop calling the stream "durable", drop the RawReject model in a new migration, and add an alert on `ingest_sanity_rejects_total` plus a per-IMEI reject sample so the loss is at least attributable.

**verifierNotes:** ['CONFIRMED: CONFIRMED — every factual leg of the claim holds up against the code, and I could not find any consumer, job, ADR, or test that closes the loop.\n\n**1. Sanity-rejected records are ACKed as accepted.**\n`apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:45-47` partitions the packet into `good` / `insane`. Insane records get `pipeline.xadd(\'rejects\', \'MAXLEN\', \'~\', 100_000, ...)` (persist.ts:53) and are *never* written to `raw:{shard}` (only the `good` loop at persist.ts:55-80 does that). Line 82 — `const persisted = results?.filter((r) => r[0] === null).length ?? 0` — counts **every** pipeline entry that returned without error, i.e. the rejects XADDs are included in the ACK count. `apps/ingest/src/session.ts:260-269` writes exactly that number back: `this.socket.write(this.codec.encodeAck(persisted))`.
