### 25. [HIGH] UDP per-IP flood guard is O(window) on its own reject path — the limiter saturates the event loop

**Subsystem:** ingest/limits · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/limits.ts:48`

`HandshakeRateLimiter.allow()` rebuilds the entire sliding window with `.filter()` on EVERY call (limits.ts:50), including the calls it is about to reject (`if (times.length >= this.maxPerMinute) { this.windows.set(ip, times); return false }`, limits.ts:51-54). On the UDP channel this limiter is constructed with `maxDatagramsPerIpPerMin` (apps/ingest/src/udp.ts:52), which main.ts:38 defaults to 6000, and it sits behind a global ceiling of `maxDatagramsPerSec` = 50_000 (main.ts:39). Once a single source IP has filled its 6000-entry window, every subsequent datagram from that IP costs a 6000-element array filter plus a fresh 6000-element array allocation — up to 50_000 times per second, all on the single Node event loop that also runs every TCP session's frame→parse→XADD→ACK. The guard designed to shed load costs more CPU than the work it sheds, and the cost scales with the attack. UDP 5027 is published to the public internet (infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml:36). The TCP path uses the same class at 600/min (server.ts:41), so it has the same shape at ~1/10 the cost.

**failureScenario:** Measured on this repo's Node v22.23.1: fill one IP's window to 6000, then time 50_000 rejected `allow()` calls = 1392 ms of pure CPU, i.e. >1.0 s of CPU burned per 1 s of traffic at the configured 50k/s global ceiling (contrast: 50_000 calls with distinct IPs = 25 ms). An attacker sending ~50 kpps of 70-byte datagrams (~30 Mbit/s) from ONE source address pegs the ingest event loop at 100%. Every TCP device session on that process stops being serviced: ACKs stop being written after XADD, `ack_latency_ms` blows past its top bucket, the 10 s handshake timer and the 40 min read-idle timer fire on real fleets, and devices mass-disconnect — all while the process is doing nothing but re-filtering a rejected attacker's timestamp array.

**suggestedFix:** Make the reject path O(1). Replace the per-call `filter` with either a fixed-window counter (`{windowStartMs, count}`, reset when `now - windowStartMs >= 60_000`) like `GlobalRateLimiter` already uses, or a ring buffer with a head index so expiry is amortised. Cheapest surgical fix: check `times.length >= maxPerMinute && times[times.length-1] > cutoff` before filtering and return false immediately without rebuilding the array.

### 26. [HIGH] Report window is built from BROWSER-local day bounds while the server buckets rows by the ACCOUNT timezone — every report has a partial first day and a spurious extra day

**Subsystem:** reports (web → API → packages/db/src/reports.ts) · **Location:** `apps/web/src/routes/app/reports.tsx:45`

`packages/db/src/reports.ts:154` buckets each row with `to_char(date_trunc('day', col AT TIME ZONE $tz), 'YYYY-MM-DD')` where `$tz` is `account.timezone` (forced server-side at `apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts:64-72`), but the RANGE predicate at `packages/db/src/reports.ts:111-116` is a raw UTC instant comparison. The window edges therefore have to be supplied already aligned to the account zone. `apps/web/src/routes/app/reports.tsx:45` calls `dayStartIso(from!)` / `dayEndIso(to!)` with NO timezone argument, so `apps/web/src/lib/playback.ts:76-79, 91-94` falls into the `timeZone === undefined` branch and uses `setHours(0,0,0,0)` / `setHours(23,59,59,999)` — i.e. the BROWSER's local zone. Every other date-filtered page passes the zone explicitly (`trips.tsx:67-68`, `events.tsx:58-59`, `playback.tsx:47-48` all pass `tz`), and `dashboard.tsx:97-100` even carries a comment about this exact hazard and fixes the lookup side — the reports page's window side was never fixed. The mismatch is near-universal because accounts are created with `timezone: 'UTC'` by default (`packages/db/src/repos/accounts.ts:59`, `packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:164`) and there is no UI anywhere in apps/web to change it (grep for 'timezone' in apps/web/src only finds display-pref and read-only uses).

**failureScenario:** A Lithuanian fleet manager (browser tz Europe/Vilnius, UTC+3 in summer) whose account row still has the default timezone 'UTC' picks 2026-07-01 → 2026-07-31 for a Mileage report. The client sends from=2026-06-30T21:00:00.000Z, to=2026-07-31T20:59:59.999Z. The server filters `t."startTime" >= 2026-06-30T21:00Z AND < 2026-07-31T20:59:59.999Z` and buckets by UTC day. Result: a spurious '2026-06-30' row containing only 21:00–24:00 UTC, and the '2026-07-31' row missing its last 3 hours (21:00–24:00 UTC) — trips driven on the evening of 31 July silently vanish from the July report, and the exported CSV/PDF the customer bills a client from is short by those kilometres. The reverse case (account tz Europe/Vilnius, manager's laptop on UTC or on US time) truncates the first day by 3–10 hours and appends a phantom trailing day.

**suggestedFix:** Pass the account timezone into the day-bound helpers, exactly as trips/events/playback already do: resolve `accounts.data?.find(a => a.id === acc)?.timezone` (the field is already returned — `apps/web/src/lib/devices.ts:22-23`) and call `dayStartIso(from!, acctTz)` / `dayEndIso(to!, acctTz)`. Defensively, `runReport` in packages/db could also derive the window edges in Postgres (`$from::date AT TIME ZONE $tz`) so a caller can pass date-only bounds and never get this wrong.

The reverse case (account `Europe/Vilnius`, browser UTC) truncates the first account-day and appends a phantom trailing day.\n\n**Refutation attempts that failed:** (a) the API does not normalize the bounds — it only rejects NaN/reversed/>366-day spans (`reports.ts:55-59`) and passes `from`/`to` through verbatim; (b) `scopeWhere` does no zone shifting (`packages/db/src/reports.ts:106-119`); (c) no test covers it — `apps/web/__tests__/reports.spec.ts` imports only `cellValue, COLUMNS, deviceLabel, pdfSafe, REPORT_TYPES, toCsv, toPdfTable, unitColumns` (CSV/PDF/column shaping), and `apps/web/__tests__/playback.spec.ts:21-45` tests `dayStartIso`/`dayEndIso` in both modes but never asserts which mode the reports page uses; (d) this is NOT the excluded known limitation — that one is the worker\'s `scheduledReporter.ts:54-58` UTC-span window, a different code path that is explicitly documented; the interactive web window is browser-zone and undocumented (the comment at `reports.tsx:25-26` asserts "account timezone still applies server-side" as if that made local-day edges safe, which is precisely the wrong assumption).\n\nFair caveat on impact: the window\'s DURATION is still a correct 31 local days, so a grand total over all returned rows is right — what is wrong is the per-day attribution, the extra leading row, and the truncated trailing row. The zone param is only pushed as `tzIndex`.\n- `packages/db/src/reports.ts:154` (`dayExpr`) — `to_char(date_trunc(\'day\', col AT TIME ZONE $tz), \'YYYY-MM-DD\')`, used by mileage/stops/engine_hours/overspeed/geofence/trips.\n\nSo the window edges are anchored in the browser zone while every `day` bucket label is anchored in the account zone. The two only agree when `browser tz == account.timezone`.\n\n**Reachability is near-universal, not theoretical:**\n- Accounts are created with `timezone: \'UTC\'` — `packages/db/src/repos/accounts.ts:59` (`data.timezone ?? \'UTC\'`) and hardcoded `\'UTC\'` on the self-serve signup path at `packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:164`.\n- `grep -rn "timezone" apps/web/src` returns only the display-pref control (`settings.tsx:291` sets `prefs.timeZone`, a render-only pref), a read-only type field, and comments — there is **no UI anywhere to set `account.timezone`**. ### 27. [HIGH] DELETE /v1/accounts/:id and /v1/tenants/:id return a raw 500 (and are permanently blocked) whenever a device row exists

**Subsystem:** schema / FK on-delete semantics · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/accounts.ts:71`

`accounts.remove` guards only users (`:75-76` AccountHasUsersError) before `prisma.account.delete` (`:77`). But `devices_accountId_fkey` is ON DELETE RESTRICT (packages/db/prisma/migrations/0_init/migration.sql:344; schema.prisma:337 declares `account Account @relation(...)` with no onDelete, i.e. Prisma's Restrict default). Prisma raises P2003, which `dbErrorHttp` (packages/db/src/errors.ts:19-27) does not handle — it only maps P2025/P2023→404 and P2002→409 — so it falls through app.onError to a bare 500. Tenants inherit this: Account.tenant is ON DELETE CASCADE (schema.prisma:228), so `tenants.remove` (repos/tenants.ts:205) cascades into accounts and trips the same RESTRICT. `tenants.remove` explicitly pre-checks commissions to convert that RESTRICT into a clean 409 (:203-204), proving the pattern was understood — the device FK was simply missed. Note the guard is on the devices ROW, so even fully retired devices block the delete.

**failureScenario:** A platform_admin offboards a churned tenant that has 40 devices (retired months ago). DELETE /v1/tenants/:id returns `500 Internal Server Error` with no actionable body; likewise DELETE /v1/accounts/:id for any account that ever held a device. There is no bulk device-erase surface, so the tenant/account is undeletable through the API and the operator has to reach for psql — while the 500 also gets logged as an unexpected server fault, masking real errors.

**suggestedFix:** Add `prisma.device.count({ where: { accountId } })` / `{ tenantId }` pre-checks throwing typed AccountHasDevicesError/TenantHasDevicesError mapped to 409 by the routes, and add `case 'P2003': return { status: 409, title: 'Conflict' }` to dbErrorHttp as the safety net.

### 28. [HIGH] POST /v1/devices/:id/sms is an unmetered SMS relay: arbitrary body text to an arbitrary, never-verified phone number, billed to the platform's Twilio account

**Subsystem:** sms gateway (api route → worker → Twilio) · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:592`

`POST /v1/devices/:id/sms` (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:592-632) accepts `smsSendRequestSchema` (packages/shared/src/sms.ts:20-23), whose `body` is `z.string().min(1).max(320)` with no charset or content restriction. When present it completely replaces the generated config SMS: `const bodyText = data.body ?? sheet.smsAuto` (crud.ts:618). The destination is `device.simMsisdn`, which is set by the same operator through `deviceCreateSchema`/`deviceUpdateSchema` and validated ONLY as a syntactic E.164 number (`/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/`, packages/shared/src/entities.ts:48 and :57) — there is no ownership/possession verification that the number is actually the device's SIM.

Critically, there is no quota or rate limit anywhere on this path. `mountRoutes` (apps/api/src/routes/registry.ts:53-76) applies only `requireRole` + `requireEntitlement`; the handler itself does no Redis throttling — unlike every other cost-bearing endpoint in this codebase, which all use the same fixed-window Lua limiter (reports.ts:41, routing.ts:53, signup.ts:79, caddyAsk.ts:55, pilotRequest.ts:53). The worker's only guard, `sms:sent:{smsDeliveryId}` (apps/worker/src/jobs/smsWorker.ts:37, :77), is a no-double-charge claim scoped to ONE delivery row; every fresh POST mints a new row (`db.smsDeliveries.create`, crud.ts:620) and therefore a new claim key and a new billable Twilio message. `enqueueSms` dedupes on `jobId: sms-${smsDeliveryId}` (apps/worker/src/jobs/smsQueue.ts) — again per row, not per caller.

The outbound send (apps/worker/src/sms/drivers.ts:57-68) posts `To`/`Body` straight to Twilio Messages using the platform's account SID and `TWILIO_FROM`, so the messages originate from the platform's own sender ID.

**failureScenario:** A tenant on any TSP plan (which grants `smsGateway`) with `account_manager` or higher — or anyone who obtains such a credential — PATCHes one of their devices to `simMsisdn: "+15551234567"` (any number worldwide passes the regex), then loops `POST /v1/devices/:id/sms {"body":"<arbitrary 320-char text>"}`. Each call is a fresh sms_deliveries row → a fresh BullMQ job → a fresh charged Twilio message from the platform's sender ID. Nothing in the API or the worker caps the rate; the sms worker runs at concurrency 4, so a single client can sustain thousands of messages per hour. Result: direct financial loss on the founder's Twilio account, plus spam/regulatory complaints and carrier filtering attributed to the platform's originating number — while the tenant looks like a normal onboarding user in the audit log (SMS sends are not audited at all here).

**suggestedFix:** Add a per-tenant (and per-device) fixed-window quota in the handler using the same Redis Lua limiter the other cost-bearing routes use — e.g. N config SMS per device per day and a tenant-wide daily ceiling — before creating the delivery row. Additionally, restrict `body` to the generated onboarding text (or a preset allow-list) until an explicit arbitrary-command feature is designed, and write an audit row for every send with the destination and the tenant.

The asymmetry is exactly as claimed.\n\n3. The worker guard is not a quota. `sms:sent:{smsDeliveryId}` (apps/worker/src/jobs/smsWorker.ts:35-37, :77-85) is an at-most-once *per delivery row* charge guard — its documented purpose (ADR-032 item 7) is preventing a double-charge of one send, not capping volume. `enqueueSms` dedupes on `jobId: sms-${smsDeliveryId}` (jobs/smsQueue.ts:38) — again per row. Every POST mints a fresh row (`db.smsDeliveries.create`, crud.ts:620 → repos/smsDeliveries.ts:54-63), hence a fresh key and a fresh billable message. Worker concurrency is 4 (smsWorker.ts:112).\n\n4. Usage metering (`apps/worker/src/jobs/usageWorker.ts`) sources billable **device-days from positions** only; grep shows zero SMS involvement in usageWorker.ts or routes/billing.ts. Notably ADR-032:48-51 justifies the tsp-only gate with "only reseller (TSP) plans, *who are already metered*, get platform-sent SMS" — that premise is false for SMS: nothing meters or re-bills a send, so the founder\'s Twilio account absorbs 100% of the cost.\n\n5. It goes live the moment creds land. `infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml:61-63,109-111` passes `TWILIO_*` straight through; `apps/api/src/main.ts:74` warns when absent. The realistic principals are: a malicious/curious paying TSP tenant, a compromised account_manager credential inside a TSP tenant, or someone who self-checks-out to a TSP price (routes/billing.ts:99-155 accepts any allowlisted priceId and billing.ts:250-255 notes the map "covers both Direct + TSP checkout"). There is no `db.audit.record` call in the handler (contrast the erase route at crud.ts:657), but `sms_deliveries` durably records tenantId/accountId/deviceId/to/body/timestamps (repos/smsDeliveries.ts:54-63). That is money and downtime, not theory.\n\nVERDICT: CONFIRMED. Severity is genuine but I\'d place it at high-minus/medium-high rather than unqualified high: it is currently latent (503 until creds), and the entitlement + role gates narrow it to a paying-or-compromised TSP principal. The fix is small and belongs before the creds land — a per-tenant fixed-window limiter reusing the same Lua pattern as reports.ts/routing.ts (e.g. N sends per device per day and per tenant per hour), plus either restricting `body` to the generated config SMS / a command allowlist, or gating free-form text behind an explicit destination-verification step.']

### 29. [HIGH] Overage for a day is reported the instant the day closes, but usage_daily keeps filling for that day for up to 48 h — every late device-day is silently never billed

**Subsystem:** usage metering / Stripe overage reporting · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageWorker.ts:33`

`createStripeUsageWorker` bills `utcDay(now - 24h)` (yesterday) on a `every: 24h` repeatable job (`stripeUsageQueue.ts:10`), which BullMQ aligns to the epoch → it fires at 00:00:00 UTC, i.e. zero settle time after the day closes. The metering pipeline that populates `usage_daily` is explicitly designed to be LATE: `runUsageSweep` windows on `server_time` with a 48 h lookback precisely so a device that buffered while offline gets its old `fix_time` days written when it reconnects (`usageWorker.ts:29,49-60`). The regression test at `apps/worker/__tests__/usage-sweep-db.spec.ts:112-121` asserts exactly this: a fix from 2026-07-06 received on 2026-07-10 inserts the `2026-07-06` device-day four days late. `reportDailyOverage` reads that day exactly once (`usageReporter.ts:87`) and nothing ever revisits it — grep shows the only caller of `reportDailyOverage` is this worker, with `day = yesterday`. There is also no missed-tick backfill: BullMQ `every` computes the next slot, so a worker that is down at 00:00 skips that day permanently. And a manual re-run is not a remedy: the Stripe idempotency `identifier` (`overage:{day}:{customer}`) only dedupes inside Stripe's 24 h window (`usageReporter.ts:21,50`), so a corrective re-run a day later would ADD the whole day again instead of the delta.

**failureScenario:** A TSP tenant is on a plan with 200 included devices. On 2026-08-03, 214 of its devices report; 5 of them are vans parked in an underground depot with no GSM from 20:00 and they flush their buffered records at 07:40 on 2026-08-04. At 00:00 UTC on 2026-08-04 the overage job reads `usage_daily` for 2026-08-03, sees 209 rows, and meters `over = 9`. At 08:00 the hourly sweep inserts the 5 late device-days (server_time is recent, fix_time buckets to 2026-08-03), so `usage_daily` now shows 214 — visible in the tenant's own /v1/usage view and in `platformSummary` — but the meter was already closed for that day and is never revisited. Five device-days of overage are lost, every day, for every buffered device. Same loss for any device whose only report of the day fell in 23:00–00:00 UTC (the sweep that covers that hour fires at 00:00 concurrently with the report — both are started from the same `recomputeConn` in `apps/worker/src/main.ts:201,209`), and for every day the worker happened to be down at 00:00.

**suggestedFix:** Give the reporter a settle delay at least as wide as the sweep lookback (bill D-3, not D-1), and/or make it idempotent in OUR database: persist the value already metered per (customer, day) and, on each run, re-scan the last N days and report only the positive DELTA under a fresh identifier. Do not rely on Stripe's 24 h identifier dedupe for correctness across days.

### 30. [HIGH] GeofenceEngine.prune() rescans the ENTIRE global pair-state map once per record, synchronously blocking the event loop

**Subsystem:** worker / geofence engine · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/geofence/engine.ts:64`

`feed()` calls `this.prune(dev, fences)` once per RECORD (engine.ts:64). `prune()` allocates a fresh `Set` of the device's fence ids and then iterates `this.state.keys()` — the global map holding one entry per (device × geofence) pair for EVERY device the worker has ever seen, not just this device's keys (engine.ts:93-99). Cost is O(records × total_pairs) per batch, per shard, and it runs synchronously inside `motionFeed.feed()` (main.ts:306), i.e. on the shard consumer's critical path between `writePositions` and the XACK. The engine is a process-wide singleton shared by all 16 shard consumers (main.ts:94), so `state` grows with the whole fleet, not with one shard.

**failureScenario:** 5 000 devices × 5 geofences = 25 000 state entries. A 200-record batch performs 200 × 25 000 = 5 000 000 `startsWith` + `slice` iterations plus 200 Set allocations, all synchronously — hundreds of milliseconds of blocked event loop per batch. With 16 shard consumers doing this back to back, the loop never yields long enough for the ShardLeaser's 10 s renew timer to run its 16 sequential Redis round trips within the 30 s lease TTL. Leases expire, `onLost` fires, shards flap — which is precisely the trigger for the duplicate-consumer and connection-leak defects above. `pipeline_lag_ms` climbs, ingest's shard-depth backpressure kicks in, and `raw:{shard}` approaches its MAXLEN 100 000 trim point.

**suggestedFix:** Keep a per-device index (`Map<deviceId, Set<geofenceId>>`) so pruning touches only that device's keys, and call prune once per device per batch (not per record) — e.g. after the record loop, using the last-seen fence set per device.

### 31. [HIGH] One ioredis connection leaked per shard-lease flap — unbounded until Redis maxclients

**Subsystem:** worker / redis connections · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/main.ts:445`

`startShardConsumer` unconditionally creates `redis.duplicate()` and pushes it into `consumerConns` (main.ts:445-446). Nothing ever disconnects it or removes it from the array outside the SIGTERM handler (main.ts:488). `onLost` (main.ts:74-80) and `onLostOwnership` (main.ts:284-288) only delete the ShardConsumer from `consumersByShard`; the dedicated connection stays connected to Redis, idle, forever. Every re-acquire of a shard therefore leaks exactly one live Redis client plus one array slot. The leak is load-correlated: the ShardLeaser renews on the SHARED main `redis` socket (main.ts:60, 70) — the same socket used by `liveState`, `tripPersister`, `geofenceCache`, `geofenceEvents`, `ruleCache`, `rulePersister` for the per-batch round trips of all 16 concurrent consumers (main.ts:303, 305, 344, 347) — so renewal EVALs queue behind hot-path traffic exactly when the system is busy. That is the same head-of-line class the code already fixed for the consumers (comment at main.ts:439-442) but left in place for the leaser.

**failureScenario:** A busy worker sees intermittent renew misses (a few shards per hour). Each miss produces onLost + a re-acquire 10 s later = one leaked connection. Over a multi-day uptime with, say, 20 flaps/hour, several thousand idle connections accumulate. Redis hits `maxclients` (default 10000); from that point `ingest` can no longer open connections either — `new Session` XADDs fail, ACKs stop, devices buffer and eventually overflow. Nothing in the metrics surfaces it (prom.ts exposes no connection-count gauge), so the first symptom is a full ingestion outage attributed to Redis.

### 32. [HIGH] Lease flap can run TWO ShardConsumers on the same shard in one process (I2 / rule-5 break)

**Subsystem:** worker / shard leasing · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/main.ts:78`

`onLost` does `void consumersByShard.get(shard)?.stop()` — fire-and-forget, NOT awaited — and then immediately `consumersByShard.delete(shard)` (main.ts:78-79). `ShardConsumer.stop()` only flips `running=false`; the loop finishes its CURRENT `process()` (writePositions + the whole `onBatch` engine pipeline) before exiting (consumer.ts:79-82, 111-137). The only duplicate guard is `if (consumersByShard.has(s)) return` (main.ts:444), which the delete has already cleared. On the leaser's next tick (leaseTtlMs/3 = 10 s later) the SAME worker re-claims the shard with SET NX (shards.ts:82) and fires `onGained` → `startShardConsumer` builds a second consumer + connection and starts it. Critically, the fencing check is `redis.get(leaseKey) === workerId` (shards.ts:15-17) — the lease is now held by the SAME workerId, so the still-draining old consumer's `ownsShard()` returns TRUE and it happily applies its batch's durable effects concurrently with the new one. Both feed the shared singleton engines (`motionFeed`, `ruleEngine`, `tripPersister`, `liveState` — main.ts:93-101), so per-device serialization is gone. The same hole exists via `onLostOwnership` (main.ts:284-288), which deletes the map entry from inside `fence()` without stopping anything else.

**failureScenario:** Single worker, 16 shards. A GC pause / the synchronous geofence prune scan (see the O(n) finding) stalls the event loop past the 30 s lease TTL. Leaser tick T: renew for shard 3 returns 0 → `owned.delete(3)`, `onLost(3)` → old consumer told to stop but is mid-`process()` on a 200-record batch whose `onBatch` is doing sequential Redis+Postgres round trips and awaited `emitWebhook` calls (main.ts:303-378) and takes >10 s. Tick T+10 s: `owned.has(3)` is false → `tryClaim(3)` SET NX succeeds (no peer) → `onGained(3)` → a second ShardConsumer for shard 3 starts, XREADGROUPs new entries and processes them. Now device X's older batch (old consumer) and newer batch (new consumer) run through `tripEngine`/`geofenceEngine`/`ruleEngine`/`liveState.applyOne` interleaved: the trip FSM sees the newer fixes first, marks them as `lastSeen`, then the older batch's records are silently dropped as 'late', and `liveState` regresses/duplicates the marker. Both consumers use the same XREADGROUP consumer name so the PENDING list is shared and XAUTOCLAIM cannot untangle it.

**suggestedFix:** Make `onLost`/`onLostOwnership` await the stop before removing the map entry, or keep the entry in `consumersByShard` (marked 'stopping') until `stop()` resolves so `startShardConsumer`'s `has()` guard still holds. Better: give each consumer generation a fencing token (e.g. lease value = `${workerId}:${epoch}` minted on every claim) so a stale consumer's `ownsShard()` fails even when the same worker re-acquires.

### 33. [HIGH] Recompute's DELETE window has no lower bound, so one device-supplied stale timestamp wipes every trip older than the 13-month positions retention

**Subsystem:** worker / trip recompute (I3 idempotency) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/trip/recompute.ts:90`

`recomputeTrips` derives its authoritative replace-window straight from the caller's `from` with no floor: `coreFrom = lo !== null && lo < from ? lo : from` (recompute.ts:90) and then `DELETE FROM trips WHERE "deviceId"=$1 AND status='closed' AND "startTime" >= $2 AND "startTime" <= $3` over `[coreFrom, coreTo]` (recompute.ts:133-136). The rebuild that is supposed to replace those rows is fed only by `SELECT ... FROM positions WHERE device_id=$1 AND fix_time >= readFrom AND fix_time <= readTo` (recompute.ts:96-100).

`from` is a raw device timestamp. `TripEngine.step` records any out-of-order record as `this.late.set(key, r.fixTime)` (trip/engine.ts:178-181), `takeLate()` hands it to main.ts:411, and main.ts:423 calls `enqueueRecompute(recomputeQueue, deviceId, from, settledTo)` with no clamp. The only floor anywhere on the path is ingest's sanity filter, `rec.tsMs < config.minTsMs` with `minTsMs: Date.UTC(2020, 0, 1)` (apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:16, apps/ingest/src/server.ts:24) — so any fix_time back to 2020-01-01 is accepted, written to `positions`, and becomes a recompute `from`.

Meanwhile `positions` is dropped at 13 months (`SELECT add_retention_policy('positions', drop_after => interval '13 months')`, packages/db/sql/001_positions.sql:26) while `trips` has no retention at all. So for any span older than 13 months the DELETE succeeds and the INSERT loop (recompute.ts:137-143) produces nothing — the rebuild is not idempotent, it is destructive. The `recomputeTrips` doc comment's claim that "running it twice over the same positions yields identical trips" silently stops holding once the source rows have been pruned.

**failureScenario:** A Teltonika unit with a flat backup battery cold-boots, its RTC falls back to a default date, and it flushes its buffer: one record carries fix_time = 2020-06-01 with satellites > 0. In `recomputeTrips` the bounds query matches essentially every closed trip the device ever had, `coreFrom = 2020-06-01`, `coreTo ~ now`. For a low-volume asset tracker (~1 fix/hour, ~45k rows over 5 years) the positions read completes fine, so the transaction runs: the DELETE removes every closed trip from 2020-06-01 onward, and the replay only regenerates the trips whose positions still exist — the last 13 months. Roughly four years of the customer's trip history, mileage and driver attribution are permanently destroyed, the job reports success, and `trip_recompute_deleted` simply increments. The same trigger is reachable over the unauthenticated UDP ingest path by anyone who knows a registered IMEI.

**suggestedFix:** Clamp the recompute window at the enqueue site and defensively inside `recomputeTrips`: `from = new Date(Math.max(from.getTime(), nowMs - MAX_RECOMPUTE_LOOKBACK_MS))` where the lookback is at most the positions retention (13 months), and short-circuit the job when `coreFrom` predates the oldest retained chunk. ### 34. [HIGH] Recompute deletes trips by time range with status re-evaluated at DELETE time, so a trip the live persister closes mid-job is deleted and never rebuilt

**Subsystem:** worker / trip recompute vs streaming trip persister (I2) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/trip/recompute.ts:133`

`recomputeTrips` establishes its rebuild data outside any transaction — the bounds query at recompute.ts:78-82 (`status='closed'` only) and the positions read at recompute.ts:96-100 — then opens a transaction at recompute.ts:121-123 and issues `DELETE FROM trips WHERE "deviceId"=$1 AND status='closed' AND "startTime" >= $2 AND "startTime" <= $3` (recompute.ts:133-136). The DELETE is keyed on a time range, not on the ids that were read, and PostgreSQL re-evaluates `status='closed'` at DELETE time under READ COMMITTED. Any trip that flips open -> closed between the bounds query and the DELETE is therefore inside the delete set but was not inside the data the rebuild saw.

The rebuild cannot replace it: `readTo = coreTo + marginMs` (recompute.ts:94) and the filter at recompute.ts:110 keeps only `close` events, with the code explicitly noting at recompute.ts:105-107 that "a trailing open snapshot is deliberately dropped". A trip whose stop is confirmed by positions written after the recompute's `pos` query never closes in the replay, so nothing is inserted for it.

The header comment at recompute.ts:75-77 ("It NEVER touches `open` rows: the live streaming persister owns those") and the RECOMPUTE_GUARD_MS note at main.ts:407-408 both assume "closed" is a stable property; it is only stable at the instant of the bounds query. The deferred branch makes it worse: main.ts:420-421 enqueues with `to = settleAt = from + 15min` plus a matching delay, so at run time `to` equals the live edge instead of `now - guard`, pushing the DELETE range right up to the present — exactly the window the guard exists to exclude.

**failureScenario:** A van has a GSM gap mid-trip and flushes buffered fixes at 10:02. `takeLate()` yields from = 09:58 which is >= settledTo, so main.ts:421 enqueues a delayed recompute with to = 10:13. At 10:13 the job runs. The van's current trip started at 09:40 and is still open, so the bounds query (recompute.ts:78) does not see it and coreTo = 10:13. The positions read (recompute.ts:96) takes ~2 s, finishing at 10:13:02 with readTo = 10:20. Meanwhile the shard consumer writes the batch containing the 10:13:05 ignition-off confirmation (consumer.ts calls writePositions before onBatch) and `TripPersister.apply` issues `closeTrip` at 10:13:06, flipping the row to status='closed' with startTime 09:40. At 10:13:07 the recompute's DELETE runs: startTime 09:40 is inside [coreFrom, 10:13] and the status is now 'closed', so the row is deleted. The replay only saw positions up to the 10:13:02 snapshot, so its engine still has the trip open at the end of the stream and drops it per recompute.ts:105-107. The completed 09:40-10:13 trip vanishes — no row, no mileage, no driver attribution — and `trip_recompute_deleted` increments as if the delete were legitimate. Because the recompute trigger (late data) and the trip close belong to the same physically-moving device, the correlation is high rather than incidental.

**suggestedFix:** Make the replace set explicit instead of range-and-status based: inside the transaction do `SELECT id FROM trips WHERE deviceId=$1 AND status='closed' AND startTime BETWEEN coreFrom AND coreTo FOR UPDATE`, then `DELETE ... WHERE id = ANY($ids)`, and run the bounds + positions reads in the same transaction (or a REPEATABLE READ snapshot) so rebuild and delete see one state. Also bound the DELETE by `"endTime" <= readTo` so a trip whose close falls outside the replayed read window can never be removed, and in the deferred branch pass `to = min(settleAt, runTime - RECOMPUTE_GUARD_MS)`.

### 35. [HIGH] A single future-dated fix (device clock up to +48 h) permanently freezes live tracking, suppresses offline alerts, and stalls the streaming trip engine — no upper clamp of fix_time against server_time anywhere

**Subsystem:** worker live-state / presence / trip engine (fix_time vs server_time) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/liveState.ts:63`

`apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:16` accepts any record with `tsMs <= nowMs + config.maxFutureMs`, and `maxFutureMs` is 48 h (`apps/ingest/src/server.ts:23`). `apps/worker/src/normalize.ts:66-67` copies the device's `tsMs` straight into `fixTime` with no clamp against `serverTime` (which it also has, right on the next line). Every downstream consumer then keys on that device-clock value and only guards the PAST direction: `apps/worker/src/liveState.ts:63` is `if (Number(stored) >= incoming) return` (max-wins, whose comment only reasons about 'buffered floods with old timestamps'); `apps/worker/src/trip/engine.ts:178` drops any record with `fixTime < lastSeen`; `apps/worker/src/rules/offline.ts:66-67` computes `offlineMs = nowMs - d.lastFixMs` (server wall clock minus device clock). Nothing rejects or clamps a fix that is ahead of server_time.

**failureScenario:** An FMB device loses GNSS lock and falls back to its RTC, which has drifted ~10 h forward after a long power-off. It emits one record stamped now+10 h (inside the 48 h sanity window, so ingest persists it), then re-acquires GNSS and returns to correct time. From that moment: (1) `liveState.applyOne` sees every subsequent correct fix as `stored >= incoming` and returns early — `device:{id}:last` and the `live:{tenantId}` WS publish freeze, so the map marker and `GET /v1/devices/last` show a 10-hour-stale position for the next 10 hours; (2) `sweepOffline` computes a negative `offlineMs`, so `isOffline` is false and a genuine 26 h outage of that vehicle raises no `device_offline` alert for ~36 h; (3) `TripEngine.step` drops every real record as out-of-order and pushes the device into `late` on every batch, so no live trips are produced for 10 h while `takeLate()` enqueues a recompute per batch. Nothing self-heals until wall-clock time passes the bogus stamp.

**suggestedFix:** Clamp in `normalize()` where both stamps are already in hand: if `p.tsMs > p.serverTimeMs + SKEW_TOLERANCE_MS` (a small value, e.g. 5 min), use `serverTimeMs` as `fixTime` (or drop the record to the rejects path) and emit a `clock_skew_total` metric. ### 36. [HIGH] `prune()` runs once per record and scans the GLOBAL cross-device/cross-shard state map, synchronously blocking the event loop

**Subsystem:** worker/geofence (hot path, backpressure) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/geofence/engine.ts:64`

`GeofenceEngine.feed` calls `this.prune(dev, fences)` inside the per-record loop (line 64), and `prune` iterates the entire `this.state` map:
```
private prune(dev: string, fences: readonly GeofenceDef[]): void {
  const live = new Set(fences.map((g) => g.id))
  const prefix = `${dev}:`
  for (const key of this.state.keys()) {                       // ALL devices × ALL fences
    if (key.startsWith(prefix) && !live.has(key.slice(prefix.length))) this.state.delete(key)
  }
}
```
`this.state` is keyed `"deviceId:geofenceId"` for every device the process has ever seen. Because `motionFeed` is a single instance shared by all 16 shard consumers (`main.ts:94`, closed over in `makeConsumer` at `main.ts:274-438`), the map holds the whole fleet, not one shard's devices. Cost per batch is O(records × devices × fences), fully synchronous.

**failureScenario:** 5 000 devices × 5 geofences = 25 000 state entries. A 200-record batch performs 200 × 25 000 = 5 000 000 `startsWith`/`slice` operations with zero awaits, and 16 shard consumers do this against the same single-threaded event loop. The loop is blocked for hundreds of ms to seconds per batch; `ShardLeaser`'s renew `setInterval` (10 s) and the consumer's own Redis I/O are starved, the 30 s lease TTL lapses, `onLost` fires for several shards, and the duplicate-consumer defect above triggers. The system degrades from 'slow' to 'I2 violated + connection leak' under nothing more than normal fleet growth.

**suggestedFix:** Only prune when the device's fence set actually changed (compare against a per-device cached id set), and index state per-device (`Map<deviceId, Map<geofenceId, PairState>>`) so pruning is O(device's fences) instead of O(global). Optionally prune once per batch rather than once per record.

### 37. [HIGH] Email notification driver has no send timeout while telegram/webpush do — a wedged SMTP socket stalls the whole alert queue for up to 10 minutes

**Subsystem:** worker/notifications · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/notify/drivers.ts:53`

`NOTIFY_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000` (line 11) is applied to telegram (`AbortSignal.timeout`, line 44) and web push (`{ timeout: NOTIFY_TIMEOUT_MS }`, line 96) but NOT to `emailDriver`, which does a bare `await transport.send(...)`. `buildEmailTransport` (`apps/worker/src/notify/emailTransport.ts:64`) constructs nodemailer with only `{host, port, secure, auth}` — no `connectionTimeout`/`greetingTimeout`/`socketTimeout` — so nodemailer's defaults apply (socketTimeout 10 min). The notify worker runs at BullMQ default concurrency 1 (`apps/worker/src/jobs/notifyWorker.ts:121` passes only `connection`), so a single stuck send blocks every other notification. The same untimed transport is shared by the auth-email worker (`apps/worker/src/main.ts:140`) and the scheduled-report worker (`main.ts:214`).

**failureScenario:** A NAT/security-group change or an SES throttle black-holes the TCP connection to `email-smtp.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com:587` (packets dropped, no RST). One notify job's `transport.send` hangs on nodemailer's 10-minute socket timeout. With concurrency 1, every subsequent panic / power_cut / geofence notification queues behind it. After 10 minutes the job throws, BullMQ retries it (attempts:5, exponential backoff), and the next attempt hangs the same way. Alerts are delayed by tens of minutes with no metric moving — `notification_failed_total` only increments after each timeout finally fires. Password-reset emails are on a separate worker but the same wedged endpoint.

**suggestedFix:** Pass explicit timeouts to `nodemailer.createTransport` in `emailTransport.ts` (`connectionTimeout: 10_000, greetingTimeout: 10_000, socketTimeout: 20_000`) and/or wrap `transport.send` in `emailDriver` with the same `NOTIFY_TIMEOUT_MS` race the other two drivers use. Raise `startNotifyWorker`/`startWebhookWorker` concurrency above 1 so one slow endpoint cannot serialize the whole fan-out.

This is an outlier: every other worker in the repo sets concurrency explicitly (smsWorker.ts:115 = 4, authEmailWorker.ts:65 = 4, scheduledReportWorker.ts:19 / usageWorker.ts:114 / offlineWorker.ts:150 / gdprExportWorker.ts:172 / stripeUsageWorker.ts:40 / dispatcher.ts:166 = 1).\n- apps/worker/src/jobs/notifyQueue.ts:46-47 — attempts: 5, backoff exponential delay 2_000.\n- Shared transport: apps/worker/src/main.ts:127 builds it once; :128 feeds the notify drivers, :140 the auth-email worker, :214 the scheduled-report worker.\n\nREACHABILITY — HIGH, no attacker required\nTrigger is an ordinary operational event against email-smtp.<region>.amazonaws.com:587: a security-group/NAT change that drops packets without RST, a stateful firewall evicting an established idle flow, an SES-side stall after DATA, or a provider partition. Email is live, not stubbed — emailTransport.ts:26 states "Email: WIRED (ADR-023, SES prod access approved 2026-07-14)" — and email is the first-listed channel in the rule editor (apps/web/src/routes/app/rules.tsx:360), so it is the common configuration.\n\nCONSEQUENCE — real, and worse than the claim states\n1. The notify queue is the delivery path for panic, power_cut, geofence and overspeed alerts — the safety-relevant core of the product. A single tenant\'s email-channel rule stalls every other tenant\'s alerts, including alerts whose only channel is telegram or webpush (which are individually timeout-guarded and would otherwise be unaffected). A per-channel outage is amplified into a total notification-pipeline outage.\n2. Intra-job blocking (not in the claim). dispatch.ts:34 iterates a rule\'s channels SEQUENTIALLY. A hung email send therefore also blocks telegram/webpush delivery within the same job, not just subsequent jobs.\n3. No recovery path (not in the claim). BullMQ 5.79.3 has no per-job timeout option, and a job awaiting a socket does not block the event loop, so the worker\'s lock-renewal timer keeps running and the job is never declared stalled — BullMQ\'s stalled-job recovery does not mitigate this. There is no SMTP_*TIMEOUT env documented anywhere in README/docs.\n4. Retry amplification. attempts: 5 with the per-channel sent-set means each retry re-attempts only the email channel and re-incurs the full nodemailer timeout, so one event can consume up to 5 x 10 min of worker time (backoff itself is in DELAYED state and does not block, but every other queued job carrying an email channel wedges identically, so the queue drains at roughly one job per 2-10 minutes).\n5. Silent to monitoring. prom.notificationFailed (main.ts:135) only increments after the timeout finally fires, so the first 2-10 minutes of a full alert outage move no metric.\n6. ### 38. [HIGH] Rule cooldown is enforced in wall-clock while events are stamped in fix_time — a buffered flush collapses hours of alerts into one event

**Subsystem:** worker/rules · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/rules/persister.ts:114`

`cooldownGate` claims `rule:cd:{ruleId}:{deviceId}` with `SET NX EX e.cooldownS` (apps/worker/src/rules/persister.ts:114). The TTL is Redis wall-clock seconds, but the event it gates carries `at: r.fixTime` (apps/worker/src/rules/engine.ts:192) — device/occurrence time, not arrival time. Default cooldown is 300 s (apps/worker/src/rules/cache.ts:81). During normal live traffic fixTime ≈ wall clock so the gate behaves as configured; on the buffered-flood path that PROJECT_PLAN §3.6 explicitly supports, an entire offline window arrives within a few wall-clock seconds, so the first event claims the key and every subsequent event for that rule+device in the whole flush is dropped. The loss is permanent: `takeLate()`/`recomputeTrips` reconcile trips only (apps/worker/src/trip/recompute.ts rebuilds `trips` rows and nothing else) — there is no recompute path that regenerates `events` rows, and the drop increments no metric. `firedLevel` already caps level kinds at one per 200-record batch (apps/worker/src/rules/engine.ts:57), so the wall-clock key is the only thing separating distinct batches, and it suppresses all of them.

**failureScenario:** A truck with an `overspeed` rule (cooldownS 300) drives 3 h through a GSM dead zone at 30 s intervals and speeds on six separate occasions. On reconnect the device flushes ~360 buffered records; the worker consumes them in ~8 batches within a couple of wall-clock seconds. Batch 1 emits one overspeed event at fixTime T1 and claims `rule:cd:{rule}:{dev}` for 300 s. Batches 2–8 emit overspeed events at T2…T6 (up to 3 h apart in fix_time) and every one gets a nil reply from `SET NX` and is discarded at persister.ts:131. The customer receives one alert instead of six, and `POST /v1/reports/overspeed` for those days reports `count: 1` with a `maxSpeedKmh` taken from the single surviving record. Nothing is logged or counted.

**suggestedFix:** Gate on event time, not TTL wall clock: store the last emitted `at` per (ruleId, deviceId) and suppress only when `e.at.getTime() - lastAt < cooldownS * 1000`, e.g. a Lua GET/compare/SET (keeping a generous EX purely for key hygiene). Keep the failure-rollback semantics by restoring the previous value instead of DELing.

### 39. [HIGH] `onLost` does not await `stop()` before removing the consumer from the map — a re-acquire creates a SECOND live consumer for the same shard in the same process

**Subsystem:** worker/shard-leasing (I2, rule 5) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/main.ts:78`

The leaser's lost-lease callback is fire-and-forget:
```
(shard) => {
  console.error(`lease lost for shard ${shard} — stopping its consumer`)
  void consumersByShard.get(shard)?.stop()   // line 78 — NOT awaited
  consumersByShard.delete(shard)             // line 79 — immediate
}
```
`ShardConsumer.stop()` (`consumer.ts:79-82`) only sets `running=false` and awaits `this.stopped`; the loop can still be parked inside `await this.process(entries)` — a full batch of `writePositions` + `onBatch` (liveState, config/geofence/rule Redis resolves, trip persist, geofence persist, per-event `await emitWebhook`), which is exactly what is slow when a lease is lost in the first place. Meanwhile the map slot is already free, so the leaser's very next tick (`shards.ts:82-84`, every 10 s) re-claims the shard, fires `onGained`, and `startShardConsumer` (`main.ts:444`) sees `consumersByShard.has(s) === false` and builds a brand-new `ShardConsumer` with a new connection. Both consumers now run against the same shard with the same `workerId`, so `ownsShardLease()` returns true for both — the fencing check cannot distinguish them.

In a single-worker deployment this is guaranteed rather than racy: the lease key expires (nobody else claims it), the same worker re-claims it 10 s later, and the old consumer's in-flight batch resumes into the shared singleton engines (`motionFeed`, `ruleEngine`, `tripPersister`, `liveState` — all created once at `main.ts:93-101` and closed over by `makeConsumer`).

**failureScenario:** A 30 s event-loop stall (GC, or the geofence `prune()` storm below) makes the renew Lua miss for 30 s. `onLost(3)` fires; consumer A is parked mid-`onBatch` for device D. 10 s later the leaser re-claims shard 3 and starts consumer B. B reads the next entries for device D and runs `motionFeed.feed()` / `ruleEngine.feed()` / `liveState.apply()` while A's continuation does the same for the older batch — interleaved async continuations on shared per-device state. Result: `TripEngine` state for D mutated by two orders (duplicate `openTrip` row, or a close applied to the wrong `openIds` entry), `RuleEngine.lastSeen` regressed, and `liveState` marker races. Direct rule-5 / I2 violation.

**suggestedFix:** Await the stop before freeing the slot, e.g. keep a `stopping: Map<number, Promise<void>>` and have `startShardConsumer` await any pending stop for that shard before constructing a new consumer; delete from `consumersByShard` only after `stop()` resolves. Also give each consumer instance a unique fencing identity (workerId + generation) so `ownsShardLease` can reject a stale generation.

The zombie\'s blocked read then returns, `ownsShard()` is now true again, and it processes a full batch concurrently with the new consumer.\n\nSame outcome, simpler trigger: any single `tick()` taking >10 s (Redis latency), or a Redis restart that loses all 16 lease keys.\n\n### Consequence — real, and the worst part is not what the claim named\n\nCorrecting the claim\'s damage list:\n- **Overstated:** `liveState` marker races are already defended by per-device promise chaining (`liveState.ts:15, 38-50`). And `RuleEngine.lastSeen` never *regresses* — `rules/engine.ts:59-61` only advances it.\n- **Understated / the actual money finding:** because both `RuleEngine` (`rules/engine.ts:60`) and `GeofenceEngine` (`geofence/engine.ts:59-61`) *silently drop* records older than `lastSeen`, if the new consumer\'s newer batch reaches `feed()` first (very plausible — the zombie sits behind `await tripPersister.apply` / `geofenceEvents.persist` Postgres writes at `main.ts:313, 325`, while a fresh consumer runs on cache hits), the zombie\'s entire older batch is discarded at both engines. `TripEngine` has a reconciliation path for this (`takeLate()` → recompute, `trip/engine.ts:178-182`, `main.ts:411-429`), but **rule events and geofence transitions have none** — `geofence/engine.ts:11-12` states outright "late reconciliation is not in scope for the stream path." So a **panic press, power_cut, or geofence enter/exit contained only in that batch is lost permanently**, silently, with no metric. For a telematics product that is a safety-alert loss, not a cosmetic race.\n- Also real: `TripPersister.openIds` (`trip/persister.ts:19, 43, 46-47`) is an unsynchronized map — a concurrent open/close pair drops the close ("no known open row"), leaving a dangling `open` trip row (recompute does reconcile this, so it is secondary).\n- Bonus leak the claim didn\'t mention: each `startShardConsumer` does `redis.duplicate()` and pushes to `consumerConns` (`main.ts:445-446`); the orphaned consumer\'s connection is never disconnected until SIGTERM, so repeated lease flapping leaks Redis connections monotonically.\n\n### Test coverage\n`apps/worker/__tests__/pipeline.spec.ts:217-232` covers only the *peer-steals-the-lease* case (`\'meNotOwner\'` vs `\'peer\'` — different ids, so the fence works). `main.ts`\'s `onLost`/`onGained` wiring has no test at all, and no test exercises same-`workerId` re-acquire, which is the exact hole.\n\nReachable via an ordinary Redis stall in the shipped single-worker topology, and the consequence is silent, unreconcilable loss of alert-class events. Confirmed.\n']

### 40. [HIGH] A successfully-sent (and charged) SMS whose local write fails is recorded as 'failed' and its 'sent' claim is destroyed

**Subsystem:** worker/sms · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/jobs/smsWorker.ts:90`

The no-double-charge design keys everything on the Redis claim value: `attempting` → `sent` → (or) `ambiguous`. `runSms` sets `CLAIM.sent` at line 89 and then calls `markSent(deps.pool, ...)` at line 90 — but both lines sit inside the SAME `try` whose `catch` (line 92) treats every non-`SmsSendError` as AMBIGUOUS.

A `pg` error from `markSent` (pool exhaustion, DB restart, statement timeout — the pool is 10 connections shared by 16 shard consumers and 13 job workers) is not an `SmsSendError`, so it falls through the `err.status >= 400` branch (line 97) straight to lines 107-108:

```ts
await deps.redis.set(key, CLAIM.ambiguous, 'EX', CLAIM_TTL_S)
await markFailed(deps.pool, smsDeliveryId, `ambiguous (not resent): ${message}`)
```

Two things go wrong at once. (1) The claim is DOWNGRADED from `sent` to `ambiguous`, deliberately overwriting the one durable piece of evidence the design created to prove the provider was charged — so the redelivery path at line 80 (`if (state === CLAIM.sent) await reconcileSent(...)`) can never reconcile the row. (2) The delivery row is marked `failed` even though Twilio accepted the message and returned a `providerMessageId`, which was then thrown away.

The method's own documented remedy for `ambiguous` is "an operator resends via a NEW delivery" — which is exactly the wrong action here: the message was definitely delivered and definitely charged.

**failureScenario:** An operator sends a Teltonika config SMS (e.g. a `setparam` server/APN change) to a tracker SIM. Twilio accepts it and returns a sid; `redis.set(key,'sent')` succeeds; `markSent` then hits a 30-second pg pool wait because the hourly usage sweep and a trip recompute are holding connections, and throws. The catch rewrites the claim to `ambiguous` and marks the row `failed: ambiguous (not resent)`. The operator sees a failed config SMS in the UI, creates a new delivery, and the tracker receives and applies the SAME config command a second time — while the customer is billed twice by Twilio. No metric distinguishes this from a genuine ambiguous outcome (`onFailed()` is fired in both).

**suggestedFix:** Split the provider call out of the local-write path: `const res = await deps.driver.send(...)` in its own try (that catch owns the 4xx/retryable/ambiguous classification), then do the claim + DB write in a separate try whose catch NEVER touches the claim (it is already `sent`) and either retries the row update or throws so BullMQ retries — the redelivery path at line 80 will then correctly `reconcileSent`.

### 41. [HIGH] Unbounded positions SELECT in trip recompute — a buffered-flood device can OOM the whole worker and halt all 16 shard consumers

**Subsystem:** worker/trip-recompute · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/trip/recompute.ts:96`

`recomputeTrips` reads the device's positions for `[readFrom, readTo]` with no `LIMIT`, no chunking and no keyset paging, then materializes `pos.rows` AND a second full array via `pos.rows.map(toRecord)` (line 101). The span is caller-controlled: `apps/worker/src/main.ts:411-423` enqueues with `from` = `TripEngine.takeLate()`'s earliest late fixTime (`apps/worker/src/trip/engine.ts:150-154`) and `to` = `now − 15 min`, and `recomputeTrips` then widens further to `coreFrom/coreTo` from overlapping closed trips (lines 90-94). Nothing bounds how old the earliest late fix can be. Every other unbounded read in the codebase is paged (`apps/worker/src/jobs/gdprExportWorker.ts:37` `PAGE = 10_000`) or capped (`packages/db/src/positions.ts:26` `MAX_PAGE = 10_000`); this one was missed. The recompute worker also runs at BullMQ default concurrency (`apps/worker/src/jobs/recomputeWorker.ts:64` passes only `connection`), so the job is retried into the same allocation.

**failureScenario:** A truck sits in a depot with no GSM for three weeks; its FMB buffers and flushes ~250k records on reconnect. The streaming engine drops all of them as out-of-order and records `late[device] = <3 weeks ago>`. `takeLate()` enqueues `recompute(device, from=3 weeks ago, to=now-15m)`. The job runs one `SELECT` over ~250k position rows and builds two full in-memory arrays (~300 MB in V8) inside the worker container. The worker OOMs. Because the worker process also owns all 16 `ShardConsumer`s, the entire ingest pipeline stops; `restart: unless-stopped` (`infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml:44`) brings it back, BullMQ re-delivers the stalled job, and it OOMs again. Meanwhile ingest keeps accepting and ACKing packets and `raw:{shard}` is trimmed at `MAXLEN ~ 100_000` — already-ACKed records are destroyed unread, which is a direct I1 break.

**suggestedFix:** Clamp the recompute window at enqueue time (e.g. `from = max(from, now − 7d)` and split older spans into multiple jobs), and page the positions read inside `recomputeTrips` by `(fix_time, rec_hash)` in 10k chunks the way `gdprExportWorker.runExport` already does, feeding the engine incrementally instead of building the whole array.

### 42. [HIGH] Open trip rows are orphaned forever on every worker restart / lease transfer — the documented recompute reconciliation does not cover them

**Subsystem:** worker/trips (durability, crash posture) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/trip/persister.ts:13`

`TripPersister`'s docstring states: "Crash posture: in-memory open ids are lost on restart, leaving `open` rows in the DB; E04-2 trip-recompute reconciles those" (lines 13-15). That reconciliation does not exist:
1. `recomputeTrips` deliberately never touches open rows — the DELETE is `status='closed'` scoped (`trip/recompute.ts:134`) and the comment at `:75-77` says "It NEVER touches `open` rows"; a trailing open snapshot is explicitly dropped (`:108-110`).
2. Recompute is only ever enqueued from `motionFeed.tripEngine.takeLate()` (the sole `enqueueRecompute` call sites are `main.ts:421` and `main.ts:423`) — i.e. only when a LATE record is observed. A clean restart produces no late signal, so no job is ever created.
3. `TripEngine` has no warm-start (unlike `GeofenceEventPersister.loadInside` and `RulePersister.loadIoState`), so the new process starts `parked` and simply opens a fresh row when movement resumes.
4. Nothing else closes stale rows: a repo-wide search for trip status writes finds only `openTrip`/`closeTrip` (`trip/writer.ts:34,47`) and the recompute DELETE. There is no sweeper and no `(deviceId, status='open')` uniqueness constraint (`schema.prisma:427-457`).
The rows are therefore permanent, and they are not inert: the reports layer aggregates trips with no status filter — `engineHours` explicitly scores an open trip as running to `LEAST(now(), $to)` (`packages/db/src/reports.ts:180-190`), and `mileage`/`stops` count them as trips (`reports.ts:156-176`).

**failureScenario:** A routine deploy (SIGTERM) with 1 000 of 5 000 devices mid-trip leaves 1 000 rows stuck at status='open' with endTime NULL. Each subsequent `engine_hours` report bills those devices for `now() - startTime` — days or weeks of phantom engine hours that grow monotonically — and `mileage` reports an extra zero-distance trip per device per deploy. The same happens on every lease transfer between workers. Customer-facing (and billing-adjacent) report data is corrupted with no operator-visible signal.

`includedFor` returns `undefined` for any price id absent from `STRIPE_INCLUDED` and the reporter treats that as "Direct plan (or unknown price)" and `continue`s (`:84-85`). The plan catalog is split across two apps with no cross-validation: the API owns `STRIPE_PRICES` / `STRIPE_PLAN_MAP` / `STRIPE_OVERAGE_MAP` (`apps/api/src/billing/stripe.ts:95-107`) while the worker independently parses `STRIPE_INCLUDED` (`usageReporter.ts:36-43`). The only observability is `prom.stripeOverageReported.inc(r.reported)` (`apps/worker/src/main.ts:207`), which counts successes — a skipped tenant is indistinguishable from a tenant with zero overage.

**failureScenario:** A new tsp_grow_annual price is added to `STRIPE_PRICES`, `STRIPE_PLAN_MAP` and `STRIPE_OVERAGE_MAP` on the API host so customers can check out; the worker host's `STRIPE_INCLUDED` is not updated (different service, different .env). Checkout attaches the metered overage line item to every subscription on that price, so the subscription is set up to bill overage, but the daily job skips those tenants forever. Every annual TSP customer runs uncapped at the flat base price and no alert fires — the leak is only discovered by manually reconciling `usage_daily` against Stripe invoices.

### 44. [MEDIUM] The monotonic webhook guard keys on `event.created` in whole SECONDS, so two distinct subscription events in the same second collapse — the later one is silently dropped forever

**Subsystem:** Stripe webhook / subscription state · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:250`

`applySubscriptionEvent` only writes when `lastBillingEventAt < eventAt`, where `eventAt = new Date(event.created * 1000)` (`apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:256`). Stripe's `created` has one-second granularity and carries no uniqueness guarantee, and there is no processed-event-id ledger anywhere in the repo (grep: no table or Redis key stores `event.id`), so equality is the ONLY replay defence — `apps/api/__tests__/billing.spec.ts:206-208` explicitly relies on this ("a replay of the canceled event (same t=200) is a no-op"). That means the code cannot distinguish a redelivery of event X from a genuinely different event Y emitted in the same second, and Stripe does not guarantee delivery order within a second. Whichever of the two is processed first wins permanently: there is no reconciliation job that re-reads the subscription from Stripe, so `subscriptionStatus`, `subscriptionPriceId`, `plan` and `currentPeriodEnd` can stay stale indefinitely.

**failureScenario:** A tsp_scale tenant downgrades to tsp_start in the Customer Portal. Stripe emits two `customer.subscription.updated` events in the same second (the item swap, then the state after the proration invoice settles), both with `created = 1786000000`. The one carrying the OLD tsp_scale price is delivered first: it writes `subscriptionPriceId = price_tsp_scale`, `plan = tsp_scale`, `lastBillingEventAt = 1786000000`. The second event, carrying the new tsp_start price, hits `lastBillingEventAt < eventAt` = false and is dropped with a 200. The tenant now pays for tsp_start but keeps tsp_scale entitlements (SSO, data residency, SLA) and — because `reportDailyOverage` looks `included` up from the stale `subscriptionPriceId` (`usageReporter.ts:84`) — is measured against tsp_scale's much larger included allowance, so their overage is systematically under-billed until the next subscription event (potentially a full billing period later).

**suggestedFix:** Store the processed Stripe `event.id` (unique index) and use that for replay dedupe, keeping the timestamp comparison as `<=`-tolerant ordering; or order on a sub-second key from the object itself. At minimum, add a periodic reconciliation that re-reads each subscribed tenant's subscription from Stripe and repairs status/price/plan drift.

**Subsystem:** affiliate commissions · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/packages/db/src/repos/affiliates.ts:171`

The docstring (`affiliates.ts:88-92`, `:166-170`) states the window runs `commissionMonths` from "the tenant's FIRST PAYMENT". The implementation derives the anchor from the earliest existing `Commission` row for that (affiliate, tenant) pair and, when there is none, falls back to `invoice.paidAt` — the payment being processed right now (`:171-176`). Commissions are not created for payments made while the affiliate is not `active` (`:165`), for $0/coupon invoices (`apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:221`), or when the computed amount floors to 0 (`:182`). Every such early payment leaves the anchor unset, so the window silently restarts at the first payment that happens to accrue. The existing test (`packages/db/__tests__/affiliates.spec.ts:188-199`) only covers the case where the first payment DOES accrue.

**failureScenario:** Affiliate ACME (`commissionMonths = 12`, active) refers a tenant on 2026-01-01. On 2026-01-15 an admin suspends ACME pending a compliance check. The tenant converts and pays on 2026-02-01, 2026-03-01 and 2026-04-01 — no commission rows are written because `affiliate.status !== 'active'`. On 2026-04-20 the check clears and ACME is reactivated. The 2026-05-01 invoice arrives: `first` is null, so `anchor = 2026-05-01` and the window now runs to 2027-05-01 instead of the contractual 2027-02-01. ACME is paid three extra months of recurring commission on that tenant, and the same drift applies to every tenant referred during the suspension.

**suggestedFix:** Anchor on the tenant's first payment, not on the first accrued commission: persist the earliest observed `paidAt` per (affiliate, tenant) — e.g. a `commission_windows` row or a `firstPaidAt` column on Tenant — written on the first `invoice.payment_succeeded` regardless of whether a commission was actually accrued, and read that as the anchor.

The window test at `:177` uses `affiliate.commissionMonths` read live from the affiliate row, while only `commissionPct` is snapshotted onto the Commission (`:180,191`; schema `packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:188-189` has `ratePct` but no months column). **failureScenario:** Affiliate PARTNER1 signed 40 tenants under 12-month terms; the windows for the 2025 cohort closed months ago and those tenants stopped generating commission. `POST /v1/devices` guards its count-then-create with a per-tenant Redis lock `device:create:{tenantId}` (crud.ts:373-378, released in `finally` at 399-400) precisely because a plain count-then-insert races. **failureScenario:** Tenant on `direct_10` with 5 active devices. The same overshoot occurs between a running import and a concurrent `POST /v1/devices`, or between a platform admin's quarantine claim and either of those, because none of them contend for `device:create:{tenantId}`.

**suggestedFix:** Acquire the same `device:create:{tenantId}` lock (or a Postgres transaction-scoped advisory lock on the tenant id, mirroring `createSelfServeSignup`) around the count-then-create in the import and claim paths as well.

### 48. [MEDIUM] Signup honeypot branch runs argon2 BEFORE the rate limiter — unauthenticated saturation of the shared 8-slot hashing semaphore

**Subsystem:** api / public signup · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/api/src/routes/signup.ts:65`

The honeypot branch calls `await hashPassword(body.password)` and returns at signup.ts:65-68; the per-IP + global fail-closed rate limiter is only reached at signup.ts:77-86, i.e. AFTER that return. `hashPassword` goes through a process-wide semaphore of `ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT` (default 8) 64 MB argon2id operations (passwords.ts:26-45) that is SHARED with `verifyPassword` — used by login, password change and partner login. The route's own comment at signup.ts:76 states the global bucket exists 'to protect the shared argon2 semaphore'; the honeypot path escapes it. The route is registered at app.ts:171, before any other throttle, and its own 64 KB body cap is the only other gate.

**failureScenario:** An unauthenticated attacker POSTs `/v1/public/signup` with `{"hp_field":"x", "password":"...", ...}` at ~20 rps from a handful of IPs. Every request consumes an argon2 slot (~200 ms, 64 MB) and none of them is counted by `signup:rl:{ip}` or `signup:rl:global`. All 8 slots stay pinned and `waiters` grows without bound; every legitimate `POST /v1/auth/login` and password change queues behind them, and RSS climbs to 8 × 64 MB of concurrent hashing plus the queue. Login latency goes from ~200 ms to seconds/minutes across the whole platform, from a completely unauthenticated endpoint.

**suggestedFix:** Move the per-IP + global rate-limit block above the honeypot check, then run the timing-equalizing hash. Also bound `waiters` in `withSlot` (reject with 503 past a queue depth) instead of letting it grow unbounded.

### 49. [MEDIUM] Revocation routes are gated behind the very entitlement they revoke — a lapsed/downgraded tenant keeps webhook egress and a live custom domain it can no longer see or delete

**Subsystem:** api — entitlement gating vs. revocation · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:1038`

`requireEntitlement` is chained onto every method of a gated route, including DELETE (apps/api/src/routes/registry.ts:63-70). `DELETE /v1/webhooks/:id` and `GET /v1/webhooks` both carry `entitlement: 'webhooks'` (crud.ts:1015, 1038), and `DELETE /v1/tenant/domains/:id` carries `entitlement: 'customDomains'` (crud.ts:1173). When a subscription lapses, `db.tenants.getEntitlements` returns `FLOOR_ENTITLEMENTS` (packages/shared/src/plans.ts:67-79, `webhooks:false`, `customDomains:false`), so every one of those routes 403s. Nothing on the delivery side re-checks the plan: the worker's `loadWebhooks` (apps/worker/src/jobs/webhookWorker.ts:33-40) selects purely on `tenantId`/`accountId`/`enabled`, and `tenantDomains.isVerifiedDomain`/`tenantIdForDomain` (packages/db/src/repos/tenantDomains.ts:89-96) select purely on `verified`. So the paid feature keeps running while the management plane — including the OFF switch — is locked out.

**failureScenario:** A `tsp_grow` tenant cancels; Stripe sends `customer.subscription.deleted`; `subscriptionStatus` becomes `canceled` and entitlements floor. The worker keeps HMAC-POSTing every geofence/overspeed/panic event with device ids and coordinates to the tenant's configured endpoint indefinitely (that endpoint may be an ex-integrator's server, which is exactly when a customer wants it off). The ex-tenant's admin opens Settings → Webhooks and gets 403 `plan_upgrade_required` on both the list and the delete, so there is no way to stop the egress without a platform_admin editing the DB. Identically, their verified custom domain keeps resolving, keeps getting certs via `/v1/internal/caddy-ask`, and keeps serving their branding from `/v1/branding` — and `DELETE /v1/tenant/domains/:id` 403s.

**suggestedFix:** Exempt destructive/read methods from the plan gate (apply `requireEntitlement` only to `post`/`patch` in `mountRoutes`, or add an explicit `entitlementMethods` field to `RouteDef`), and independently enforce the entitlement where the feature actually runs: have `loadWebhooks` join the tenant's effective entitlements (or have the webhook enqueue path skip tenants without `webhooks`), and have `isVerifiedDomain`/`tenantIdForDomain` require the tenant to still hold `customDomains`.

### 50. [MEDIUM] Retiring a device does not revoke its public share links — the unauthenticated /v1/public/share/:token endpoint keeps publishing the decommissioned vehicle's last known position for up to 30 days

**Subsystem:** api — public share links · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:417`

`DELETE /v1/devices/:id` (crud.ts:417-428) tears down the Redis registry and soft-deletes the row (`retiredAt`), but never touches `share_links`. The public resolver's existence check is `db.devices.get({ tenantId: resolved.tenantId }, resolved.deviceId.toString())` (apps/api/src/routes/caddyAsk.ts:101) and `devices.get` applies no `retiredAt` filter (packages/db/src/repos/devices.ts:82-86), so a retired device still resolves. `readLatestValidPosition` (packages/db/src/positions.ts:118) then returns the device's last valid fix. The code comment at caddyAsk.ts:99-100 asserts "if the device was reassigned/erased since minting, this 404s rather than leaking anything" — retire, the normal decommission path an operator reaches from the UI's delete button, is not covered. Share TTL is up to 720 h (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:648). The only cleanup is the `ShareLink.device` `onDelete: Cascade` (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:365), which requires a full GDPR erase — itself refused until the device has been retired for 60 minutes and only reachable by TENANT_ADMINS (crud.ts:643-661).

**failureScenario:** An operator mints a 30-day share link for a customer's van, then the lease ends and they "delete" the device in the UI (retire). They reasonably believe all access stopped — the device is gone from every list and ingest rejects it. Anyone still holding the share URL (the ex-customer, anyone the link was forwarded to) keeps getting 200 with `{lat, lon, fixTime, speedKph}` for the vehicle's final parked location — commonly a driver's home address — for the remainder of the 30-day TTL, with no login and no audit trail beyond the rate-limit counter.

**suggestedFix:** In the retire handler, revoke the device's share links in the same operation (`UPDATE share_links SET "revokedAt" = now() WHERE "deviceId" = $1 AND "revokedAt" IS NULL`, exposed as a scoped repo method), and additionally make the public resolver fail closed by filtering `retiredAt IS NULL` on the device lookup at caddyAsk.ts:101 so the documented behaviour matches the code.

### 51. [MEDIUM] An account-scoped tsp_admin reads the whole tenant's audit trail — audit.list ignores scope.accountId

**Subsystem:** api/db audit · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/audit.ts:57`

`audit.list` (and `audit.get`) filter on `tenantId` only — `where: { tenantId: scope.tenantId, … }` (`audit.ts:57-70`, `:73`) — deliberately, because `audit_log` has no accountId column (`schema.prisma:707-721`). The route's only compensating control is the role gate: `READ_POLICY.audit = TENANT_ADMINS` (`apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:117`), which assumes every tenant admin is tenant-WIDE (the assumption is written into `packages/db/src/scope.ts:10`: "undefined ⇒ tenant-wide (tsp_admin / platform_admin)").

That assumption is not enforced. `POST /v1/users` (`crud.ts:254-274`) accepts `{role:'tsp_admin', accountId:<uuid>}` from a tenant-wide tsp_admin: `canGrantRole('tsp_admin','tsp_admin')` is true (`packages/shared/src/roles.ts:28-31`, tier 2 >= 2), and the accountId is only checked for in-scope-ness. `scopeOf` then pins that user to the account (`routes/registry.ts:79-83`), and every other repo honours it via `scopedWhere` — but audit silently does not.

The isolation suite covers the role dimension only (`tests/isolation/suite.spec.ts:207-219` asserts viewer/account_manager → 403, tsp_admin → 200) and never exercises an account-scoped admin, so the gap is untested.

**failureScenario:** A white-label TSP runs three unrelated customers as accounts A1/A2/A3 in one tenant and gives each customer's IT lead a `tsp_admin` pinned to their own account (accepted by POST /v1/users). The A1 lead calls `GET /v1/audit` and receives the entire tenant's audit log: A2's and A3's device creates with full before/after row snapshots (IMEI, plate, name, SIM MSISDN — `repos/devices.ts:113`), their user creates/updates with email addresses and role changes (`repos/users.ts:57`, `:68`), their geofence and share-link activity. Every other surface correctly 404s or filters for that same token, so the leak is not visible from the UI's device/user lists — only the audit page exposes it. `GET /v1/usage` has the identical shape (`repos/usage.ts:57` scopes on tenantId only).

**suggestedFix:** Two options: (a) enforce the invariant — reject creating/patching a user with `role: 'tsp_admin' | 'platform_admin'` together with a non-null accountId in `POST/PATCH /v1/users`, so the scope.accountId-undefined assumption the audit repo relies on is actually guaranteed; or (b) add a nullable `accountId` column to `audit_log`, stamp it from `scope.accountId` in `audit.record`, and filter with `scopedWhere(scope, { nullableAccount: true })`. Either way add an account-scoped-admin case to the isolation suite so the assumption is pinned.

### 52. [MEDIUM] GET /v1/devices/last does a platform-wide HGETALL plus one Redis round-trip per device, unrate-limited, on the shared API connection

**Subsystem:** api/hot-path · **Location:** `apps/api/src/app.ts:226`

The handler calls `deps.redis.hgetall('device:tenant')` — the registry hash for EVERY device of EVERY tenant, not just the caller's — pulls it entirely into API memory, filters in JS, then issues `Promise.all(deviceIds.map((id) => deps.redis.hget(...)))`, i.e. one command per in-scope device (classic N+1). It is registered right after `authMiddleware`, so it is reachable by every authenticated role AND by read-only API keys (which `authMiddleware` maps to `role:'viewer'`). There is no rate limiter on it (unlike reports/routing/share, which all have one), and it sits inside the isolation-suite exemption regex (`tests/isolation/suite.spec.ts:262`). `deps.redis` is the same single ioredis connection used by the WS ticket issuance, the caddy-ask/share/report/signup rate-limit scripts and the live-fanout subscriber setup, so its command queue is shared.

**failureScenario:** A TSP customer wires a naive integration that polls `GET /v1/devices/last` from an API key at its full 600 req/min allowance. At 5 000 platform devices with 500 in their tenant, each request transfers a 10 000-field hash to the API and issues 501 Redis commands. That is ~5 000 commands/sec and ~1 GB/min of hash payload through one ioredis socket. Every other API call that touches Redis — login rate-limit checks, `GET /v1/ws-ticket`, `/v1/internal/caddy-ask` (Caddy's on-demand-TLS gate, which denies on failure) — queues behind it. Certificate issuance for new tenant domains starts failing and logins slow to seconds, from one authenticated read-only key.

**suggestedFix:** Replace the `HGETALL device:tenant` scan with a per-tenant index (`SADD device:tenant:{tenantId}`) written by `deviceRegistry.activateDevice`/`rehydrate.ts`, fetch the snapshots with a single pipeline/`MGET`, and add the same fixed-window per-user rate limiter used by `mountReports`.

### 53. [MEDIUM] Partner login is permanently impossible for any affiliate whose email was created with uppercase characters

**Subsystem:** api/partner auth · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/affiliates.ts:206`

`affiliates.create` stores `email` exactly as submitted (`affiliates.ts:130-137`) — `affiliateCreateSchema` (`packages/shared/src/entities.ts:252-258`) only validates `z.string().email()`, it does not normalise case, and `Affiliate.email` is a plain case-sensitive `@unique` (`schema.prisma:128`).

The login handler lowercases before lookup: `const email = parsed.data.email.trim().toLowerCase()` (`apps/api/src/routes/partner.ts:76`) then `findByEmailForAuth(email)` → `prisma.affiliate.findUnique({ where: { email } })` (`affiliates.ts:206-207`), which is an exact, case-sensitive equality on the unique index.

Note the contrast: the tenant user path DOES normalise on write (`repos/users.ts:50`, `email: data.email.trim().toLowerCase()`), and the referral-code lookup was already hardened to `lower(code) = lower($1)` (`affiliates.ts:120-126`). The affiliate email path was missed on both sides.

**failureScenario:** A platform_admin creates a partner via `POST /v1/affiliates` with `{"email": "Jonas@Partner.lt"}` (the natural form pasted from a contract or email signature) and issues a set-password link via `POST /v1/affiliates/:id/set-password-token`. The partner successfully sets a password — `set-password` resolves by token, not email (`partner.ts:107-111`), so that step works and gives false confidence. Every subsequent `POST /v1/partner/login` lowercases to `jonas@partner.lt`, `findUnique` misses, `partner === null`, the code burns a DUMMY_HASH verify and returns 401 `invalid credentials` (`partner.ts:84-92`) — while also incrementing the per-IP+email lockout counter, so the partner eventually 429s themselves out. The partner can never reach `/v1/partner/commissions`, and support sees only 'invalid credentials'. ### 54. [MEDIUM] Daily report aggregates have no row cap while the trips report does — a 366-day fleet report materializes six-figure row counts in API memory

**Subsystem:** api/reports · **Location:** `packages/db/src/reports.ts:161`

`mileage` (line 161), `stops` (172), `engineHours` (188), `overspeed` (200) and `geofence` (213) all end in `GROUP BY 1,2,3,4 ORDER BY 1,2` with no `LIMIT`, returning one row per (day × device). The `trips` list query on line 233 does carry `LIMIT ${TRIP_LIST_CAP}` (5 000, defined line 82), showing the cap was a deliberate control that the five aggregate reports were left out of. `apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts:19` caps the span at 366 days and rate-limits to 60 requests/min per user (line 30), so a single authenticated user can drive this repeatedly.

**failureScenario:** An account with 500 devices requests `POST /v1/reports/mileage` with a full 366-day range. Postgres returns ~183 000 rows; `mileage()` maps every one into a JS object and Hono serializes the whole array into a single JSON response held entirely in memory (~40-60 MB per request). A user (or a dashboard that retries on timeout) issues these at the allowed 60/min and the API process — which also serves the WS gateway and every other tenant's traffic — spends its heap on report arrays and GCs hard. There is no streaming, no pagination cursor and no row cap to fall back on.

**suggestedFix:** Apply the same `LIMIT` discipline as `trips`: add a row cap (e.g. 20 000) to each aggregate with a `truncated: true` flag in `ReportResult`, or add keyset pagination on `(day, deviceId)`. Tighten the default max span for the aggregate types, and lower the per-user report rate limit.
