### 55. [MEDIUM] WS fanout has no send backpressure and no heartbeat — one stalled subscriber buffers the tenant's whole live feed in API memory

**Subsystem:** api/websocket · **Location:** `apps/api/src/ws.ts:156`

The pmessage fanout (lines 151-160) does `if (ws.readyState === ws.OPEN) ws.send(message)` for every live position of the tenant, for every subscribed socket. There is no `ws.bufferedAmount` check, no drop/coalesce policy, and no close-on-slow-consumer rule. The `ws` library queues everything the peer has not read into the process heap; Node's socket write buffer is unbounded.

Compounding it, `attachWsGateway` installs no ping/pong heartbeat — there is no `ws.ping(...)` anywhere in `apps/api/src`, and `WebSocketServer` does not send one by itself. A half-open TCP connection (laptop lid closed, mobile handover, NAT timeout) therefore keeps `readyState === OPEN` and stays in `subscribers` until the OS TCP keepalive fires, which on Linux defaults to ~2 hours. The only other reaper is the revocation sweep (line 104), which closes a socket only when a revocation marker exists.

So the API will happily write a fleet's entire position stream into a socket whose peer vanished 90 minutes ago, holding every one of those buffers resident.

**failureScenario:** A dispatcher on a 1000-vehicle tenant has the live map open on a laptop; the laptop suspends on a train. `LiveState.apply` publishes roughly one ~200-byte message per device per batch — a few hundred messages/second for that tenant. The socket never closes (no ping, no keepalive for ~2 h), `readyState` stays OPEN, and every message is appended to that socket's buffer: ~40 MB after 10 minutes, hundreds of MB before TCP keepalive reaps it. A handful of such clients — or one abusive client that connects, holds a valid ticket, and simply never reads — exhausts the API container's heap and takes down REST + auth for every tenant.

**suggestedFix:** Before `ws.send`, check `ws.bufferedAmount` against a cap (e.g. 1 MB) and on breach close the socket with a policy code (the client already reconnects with a fresh ticket) or drop the message and count it in a metric. Add the standard ws heartbeat: `setInterval` → for each socket, terminate if `isAlive === false`, else `isAlive = false; ws.ping()`, with `ws.on('pong', () => isAlive = true)`.

The `ws` library sends no ping by itself, and a browser client cannot ping from JS (apps/web/src/lib/ws.ts has no app-level keepalive either). ### 56. [MEDIUM] A ws-ticket minted before a logout but redeemed after it produces a socket the revocation sweep can never close

**Subsystem:** api/ws gateway · **Location:** `apps/api/src/ws.ts:124`

Revocation is checked at ticket ISSUANCE (`app.ts:214` → `revokedAfter(redis, userId, tokenIssuedAtS)`), but the socket's `establishedAt` is stamped at REDEMPTION (`ws.ts:183`, `Date.now()`), and the sweep closes a socket only when `revokedAt >= establishedAt` (`ws.ts:124`). The upgrade path (`ws.ts:166-193`) does a bare `GETDEL` on the ticket and performs no revocation check of its own.

So any ticket fetched before the revoke instant and redeemed after it yields `establishedAt > revokedAt` — the sweep's predicate is false forever, and since sockets have no TTL or re-auth, the stream survives for the socket's whole lifetime. The window is the ticket TTL (default 30 s, `app.ts:217`).

**failureScenario:** An attacker holding a stolen (still-unexpired, ≤15 min) access token calls `GET /v1/ws-ticket` at T−5 s. The victim notices and logs out at T; `logout` calls `markSessionsRevoked` (`auth/login.ts:251`) writing `ws:revoke:{uid} = T` and revokes the refresh family, so all HTTP access dies. At T+2 s the attacker redeems the still-valid ticket: `establishedAt = T+2000ms`, `revokedAt = T`. `t >= e.establishedAt` is false on every subsequent 15 s tick, so the socket is never closed and continues receiving the user's full `live:{tenantId}` fanout indefinitely. The same applies to an admin-driven password reset, role demotion, or user delete.

**suggestedFix:** Re-check the revocation marker at redemption, not just issuance: in the `server.on('upgrade')` handler after `GETDEL`, call `revokedAfter`-style logic against `ws:revoke:{ctx.userId}` and refuse the upgrade if a marker newer than the ticket's mint time exists. Cheapest fix: store the ticket's issuance timestamp inside the ticket payload and set `establishedAt = ticketIssuedAtMs` instead of `Date.now()`, which makes the existing sweep predicate correct with no extra Redis round-trip.

### 57. [MEDIUM] GET /v1/driver-scores passes from/to straight through with no maximum span and no rate limit, unlike the equivalent reports route

**Subsystem:** apps/api + packages/db — driver scores query bounds · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/driverScores.ts:24`

`GET /v1/driver-scores` forwards the raw `from`/`to` query params to `readDriverScores` (driverScores.ts:20-25) with no validation beyond what the repo does. In packages/db/src/driverScores.ts:36-37 the bounds are only run through `pgSafeDate`, which accepts anything Postgres can store — the floor is `PG_MIN_MS` = 0001-01-01 (packages/db/src/dateGuard.ts:9). There is no maximum span and no `LIMIT` on the query (driverScores.ts:42-64), which does a LEFT JOIN over `trips` plus a correlated `count(DISTINCT e.id)` subquery over `events` per driver.

The route is also registered with no rate limiter (mountDriverScores at app.ts:270 takes only `{db, pool}`) and no `requireRole`, so every authenticated principal reaches it — including read-only `X-Api-Key` integrations, which authenticate as role `viewer` (apps/api/src/auth/apiKey.ts:56).

This is inconsistent with the sibling aggregate route: `POST /v1/reports/:type` rejects a range over 366 days (reports.ts:18, :59) AND enforces a per-user 60/min Redis fixed window (reports.ts:39-46) precisely because 'a report is a full GROUP BY over trips/events'. driver-scores runs a heavier query with neither guard.

**failureScenario:** A holder of a read-only API key (or any viewer) loops `GET /v1/driver-scores?from=0001-01-01T00:00:00Z` at a few requests per second. Each request makes Postgres aggregate the tenant's entire trips history and run one full-history correlated overspeed subquery per driver, with no row cap and nothing to throttle repeats. The shared connection pool saturates and every other tenant's API reads (positions history, reports, live snapshot) stall behind it.

**suggestedFix:** Mirror the reports route in driverScores.ts: parse `from`/`to`, reject NaN / reversed / >366-day spans with 400, and add the same per-user Redis fixed-window limiter (`mountDriverScores` already receives no redis — thread `deps.redis` in from app.ts:270). Optionally clamp the default window server-side in packages/db/src/driverScores.ts:36-37 as defense in depth.

### 59. [MEDIUM] Public signup returns a distinct 409 email_in_use, giving an unauthenticated platform-wide account-existence oracle

**Subsystem:** auth/enumeration · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/signup.ts:111`

`POST /v1/public/signup` maps `SignupEmailInUseError` to `409 {"error":"email_in_use"}` (signup.ts:111). The underlying check is **platform-wide**, not tenant-scoped: `createSelfServeSignup` runs `prisma.user.findFirst({ where: { email: data.email } })` with no tenant predicate (packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:149-150, repeated inside the advisory-locked transaction at :153).

This directly contradicts the anti-enumeration posture the rest of the unauthenticated auth surface is explicitly built around: login burns a dummy argon2 verify so "response timing must not reveal email existence" (login.ts:176-181, passwords.ts:47-50), and forgot-password "ALWAYS answers 200 with the same body — existence of the email is never revealed" including a fabricated DB write on the miss path (login.ts:315-343). The signup route re-opens the oracle over the same identity space, with a response that requires no timing analysis at all.

Signup is registered at app.ts:171, before `authMiddleware`, and is reachable on every host Caddy serves.

**failureScenario:** An attacker wants to know whether `ceo@bigcorp.com` is an Orbetra user (worth knowing before a spear-phish, and worth knowing in bulk to size a customer list). They POST `{name:'x',email:'ceo@bigcorp.com',password:'aaaaaaaa'}` to `/v1/public/signup`: a 409 means the address has an account somewhere on the platform, a 201 means it does not (and they can simply abandon the created trial tenant). The per-IP limit is 5/hour (signup.ts:52) with a global ceiling of `max*40`, so a cheap rotating-proxy pool enumerates a target list at scale, and a single targeted check costs one request. Neither the 409 nor the resulting throwaway tenants raise any alert.

**suggestedFix:** Return the same opaque success shape for an in-use email that the honeypot branch already returns (`{ ok: true, id: randomUUID() }`, signup.ts:67) and deliver the real "this address already has an account, sign in or reset your password" message out-of-band by email — the standard non-enumerating signup pattern, and the one this codebase already applies to forgot-password. If a synchronous 409 is required for UX, gate it behind a much tighter per-email (not per-IP) budget and emit a metric so bulk probing is visible.

### 60. [MEDIUM] Login lockout is keyed on (IP, email) only — no per-IP or per-account counter, so one host gets unlimited argon2 verifies and distributed stuffing is unbounded

**Subsystem:** auth/lockout · **Location:** `apps/api/src/auth/login.ts:168`

The only throttle in front of `POST /v1/auth/login` is `auth:fail:${ip}:${sha256(email).slice(0,16)}` (login.ts:168-174), incremented only on failure (login.ts:190) and reset on success (login.ts:200). There is no counter on `ip` alone and none on the email alone. The route is not covered by any other limiter: infra/Caddyfile has no rate limiting for `/v1/*` on the app host, and app.ts registers no limiter before the auth sub-app.

Two consequences follow directly from the key shape:
1. A single IP can send unlimited attempts as long as each uses a fresh email — the lockout key is different every time, so the gate at login.ts:170 never trips. Every such request still burns one full argon2id verify (login.ts:181, `DUMMY_HASH_PROMISE`), holding one of the 8 slots in the shared semaphore at passwords.ts:23.
2. Conversely, credential stuffing against one real account gets `maxFails` (default 5) free attempts per source IP with no account-level ceiling, so N IPs yield 5N attempts against that account.

The existing test `apps/api/__tests__/auth.spec.ts:363` ("lockout is per identity: a different email from the same IP is unaffected") pins this behaviour as intended, which is why the gap has no coverage.

**failureScenario:** (a) DoS: an attacker POSTs `/v1/auth/login` with `{"email":"<random>@x.co","password":"x"}` at 50 rps from one host. Every request reaches login.ts:181 and consumes an argon2id slot, saturating all 8 and queueing every legitimate login and password-change behind it — the same outcome as the signup-honeypot path, via a different door. (b) Stuffing: a botnet of 2000 IPs gets 10 000 password guesses against one known admin address without ever tripping a lockout, and nothing in the system emits a signal that a single account is under attack.

**suggestedFix:** Add a second, coarser bucket alongside the existing one: a per-IP failure counter (`auth:fail:ip:{ip}`, e.g. 20/15 min) checked before the argon2 work, and a per-email counter (`auth:fail:email:{hash}`) so an account under distributed attack degrades globally (with a longer window and an unlock path). Both can reuse `LOCKOUT_SCRIPT`. Emit a metric on lockout trips so distributed stuffing is observable.

The semaphore is only a partial mitigation, and by its own admission.** `passwords.ts:17-22` explicitly anticipates this attack ("a burst across many emails/IPs could otherwise run unbounded 64 MB ops and OOM the process") and solves only the memory half: "excess requests queue." The queue is `const waiters: (() => void)[]` (passwords.ts:25) with an uncapped `waiters.push(r)` (:28) and FIFO `waiters.shift()?.()` (:34) — no cap, no timeout, no load shedding, and the queued work still executes for clients that already disconnected. Availability only; no data loss or privesc. Medium is the right severity.\n\n**6. Not already known or accepted.** The accepted-gaps list at `security-pass-2026-07.md:41-48` covers only the API-key pre-lookup flood and the refresh throttle — different endpoints. Line 34 of that same doc asserts the login lockout *is* an "attacker CPU cap ✅", which this finding disproves for the fresh-email shape: the doc is wrong, so the gap is undocumented rather than accepted. It is also absent from the task\'s do-not-report list.\n\n**7. The codebase\'s own reasoning corroborates the premise.** `signup.ts:74-76` adds a GLOBAL rate-limit bucket behind the per-IP one specifically because it "also protects the shared argon2 semaphore (hashPassword) that login depends on." Login itself never received the equivalent guard.\n\n**8. ### 61. [MEDIUM] A partner password reset does not invalidate outstanding partner JWTs

**Subsystem:** auth/partner · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/partner.ts:100`

`POST /v1/partner/set-password` (partner.ts:100-114) consumes the one-time token, sets the new hash, and burns sibling tokens — but it never invalidates already-issued partner access tokens. Partner JWTs carry only `{sub, typ, iss, iat, exp}` (auth/partnerJwt.ts:28) with no `jti` and no token-version claim, and `partnerAuth` (partner.ts:50-62) validates the signature and then only re-loads the affiliate to check `status === 'active'` (partner.ts:58). There is no per-affiliate revocation marker anywhere (the `ws:revoke:` mechanism is user-only).

Default TTL is 8 h (partner.ts:37), and there is no refresh flow to rotate against, so "reset my password" — the standard user response to a suspected compromise — has no effect on an already-stolen token.

**failureScenario:** A partner's laptop is compromised and the attacker exfiltrates the `Bearer` partner token from browser storage. The partner is told to reset, redeems a fresh admin-issued set-password link and picks a new password. The attacker's token keeps returning 200 on `GET /v1/partner/me` and `GET /v1/partner/commissions` — exposing the partner's email, referral code, commission rate, and the full per-invoice commission ledger (amounts, currencies, `sourceInvoiceId`) — for the remainder of the 8 h TTL. The only way to actually cut it off is for a platform_admin to notice and flip `status` to `suspended`.

**suggestedFix:** Add a `tokenVersion Int @default(0)` (or `passwordChangedAt`) column to `Affiliate`, bump it in `affiliates.setPassword`, embed it as a claim in `mintPartnerToken`, and reject a mismatch in `partnerAuth` alongside the existing `status` check — the affiliate row is already loaded there, so this costs nothing extra. Add a partner.spec case: login → set-password → old token must 401.

### 62. [MEDIUM] GET/POST/PATCH /v1/affiliates return every partner's argon2id passwordHash in the JSON response

**Subsystem:** auth/secrets-handling · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/affiliates.ts:112`

`affiliates.list` (affiliates.ts:112) and `affiliates.get` (:113) call `prisma.affiliate.findMany/findUnique` with **no `select`**, so they return the full `Affiliate` model — which includes `passwordHash` (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:138, the argon2id hash for partner self-service login). `create` (:126) and `update` (:145) likewise return the raw model.

All four are piped straight to the client with no redaction: routes/crud.ts:1258 (`json(c, await db.affiliates.list())`), :1261 (`db.affiliates.get(id(c))`), :1271 (create) and :1289 (patch). The `json()` helper (crud.ts:177-180) only stringifies BigInt/Date — it strips nothing.

This is inconsistent with the codebase's own established pattern for exactly this problem: `packages/db/src/repos/webhooks.ts:28-29` sets `readRedact: ['secret']` so the HMAC secret "never RETURNs over the API (list/get) — rule 12", and `apps/api/src/routes/partner.ts:120-125` hand-picks fields with the comment "never leak the hash". The affiliate repo is the one that forgot. Note these are `scopeClass: 'platform'` routes so only `platform_admin` reaches them — but the partners are third parties, not staff.

**failureScenario:** A platform_admin opens the partners page in the admin SPA. `GET /v1/affiliates` returns a JSON array containing the argon2id `passwordHash` of every partner on the platform, in bulk. That credential material now sits in the admin's browser memory/devtools, in any HAR the admin captures for support, in any front-end error-reporting breadcrumb that attaches response bodies, and in any proxy/APM that samples response payloads. A single compromised or malicious admin session — or one leaked HAR — hands an attacker the offline-crackable hashes of every partner account, which they can then use against `POST /v1/partner/login`. `PATCH /v1/affiliates/:id` leaks the same hash on every routine name/status edit.

**suggestedFix:** Add an explicit `select` to `affiliates.list`/`get`/`create`/`update` that omits `passwordHash` (mirroring `VIEW` in repos/users.ts:32 and `toView` in repos/apiKeys.ts), keeping `findByEmailForAuth` (:206) as the only method that returns it. Add a repo-level test asserting `'passwordHash' in row === false` for the four API-facing methods.

### 63. [MEDIUM] A subscription webhook that matches no tenant is silently acked 200 — a paying Stripe customer can stay permanently unprovisioned with zero signal

**Subsystem:** billing / Stripe webhook · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:256`

`applySubscriptionEvent` returns `result.count > 0` (packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:278) precisely so the caller can tell "applied" from "matched no row". The webhook discards it: `await deps.db.tenants.applySubscriptionEvent(mapped.customerId, ...)` (apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:256) with no check, no log, and no metric; `mapped === null` (billing.ts:248) is likewise dropped. The handler then returns `c.text('ok', 200)` (billing.ts:280), so Stripe considers the event delivered and never retries.

The mismatch is reachable. `POST /v1/billing/checkout` creates the Stripe customer and persists it in two separate steps (billing.ts:143-144), and the per-tenant serialization lock around them is best-effort: `catch { /* Redis blip — fall through */ }` (billing.ts:138-140) proceeds WITHOUT the lock. Two concurrent checkouts during a Redis outage both see `stripeCustomerId === null`, both call `ensureCustomer` (which is not idempotency-keyed — apps/api/src/billing/stripe.ts `ensureCustomer` calls `stripe.customers.create` directly), producing customers A and B; `setStripeCustomer` last-write-wins leaves B in the DB while the checkout URL the browser actually follows belongs to A.

**failureScenario:** Redis blips while a tenant admin double-clicks "Subscribe". Customer A and customer B are both created in Stripe; the DB ends up with B, the browser is redirected to the session for A. The admin pays. Stripe emits `customer.subscription.created` for customer A; `prisma.tenant.updateMany({ where: { stripeCustomerId: 'cus_A', ... } })` matches zero rows, returns `count: 0`, and the webhook answers 200. The tenant is charged monthly by Stripe forever while: `subscriptionStatus` stays `trialing`, `getEntitlements` floors them at trial expiry (packages/shared/src/plans.ts:116), `listActiveSubscribers` never returns them so no overage is ever metered, and `GET /v1/billing` reports `canSubscribe: true` — inviting a second subscription and a genuine double-charge. Nothing in the logs or metrics records that a paid subscription event was dropped.

**suggestedFix:** Check the boolean: when `applySubscriptionEvent` returns false for a `customer.subscription.created`/`updated` event, log the customer id at error level and increment a counter (an alertable `stripe_webhook_unmatched_total`); same for `mapped === null`. Separately, make the checkout customer binding safe: persist `stripeCustomerId` with a conditional update (`updateMany where stripeCustomerId IS NULL`) and re-read it, or pass `client_reference_id`/`subscription_data.metadata.tenantId` (already set, billing.ts:147) through a `checkout.session.completed` consumer as a fallback tenant resolver.

The `Promise<boolean>` return is discarded. No `if`, no log, no metric.\n- `apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:248` — `if (mapped !== null)`: a subscription event with an empty/absent `customer` is silently dropped too.\n- `apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:280` — `return c.text(\'ok\', 200)` on every path that isn\'t a signature failure or an affiliate-accrual fault. ### 64. [MEDIUM] Hourly usage sweep and daily overage report both fire at 00:00 UTC — the day's last hour of device-days can be missed and is never re-billed

**Subsystem:** billing / usage metering · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageQueue.ts:22`

Both repeatable jobs use BullMQ `every` with no offset, which is epoch-aligned: `USAGE_SWEEP_EVERY_MS = 3_600_000` (usageQueue.ts:11,23) and `STRIPE_USAGE_EVERY_MS = 86_400_000` (stripeUsageQueue.ts:10,22). Both therefore tick at exactly 00:00:00 UTC. `createStripeUsageWorker` bills `utcDay(now - 24h)` = yesterday and reads `db.usage.tenantSummary(...{from: dayIso, to: dayIso})`, i.e. the count of `usage_daily` rows for yesterday (usageReporter.ts:87-92; usage.ts:54-63). But the rows for yesterday's 23:00–00:00 UTC slice are only written by the sweep that runs AT 00:00 (usageWorker.ts:62-72) — the two run concurrently with no ordering or lock. There is no re-run: the next daily tick computes a different `dayIso`, and the Stripe idempotency `identifier` is `overage:{day}:{customer}`, so even a manual re-fire within 24 h is a Stripe-side no-op that cannot correct the number.

**failureScenario:** A tenant on a TSP plan with 100 included devices runs 130 devices. Eight vehicles start a night shift and first report between 23:10 and 23:55 UTC; their `usage_daily` rows for that day are inserted only by the 00:00 sweep. At 00:00 the overage reporter races it and reads 122 device-days → reports `over = 22` instead of `30`. Eight device-days of overage are lost permanently, every single day the pattern repeats. Nothing detects it — `reportDailyOverage` returns success and increments `stripeOverageReported`.

**suggestedFix:** Offset the daily reporter (e.g. run at 01:00 UTC, or use a cron pattern instead of `every`), and/or have the overage job run a targeted `runUsageSweep` for the billed day before reading `usage_daily`.

### 65. [MEDIUM] Hourly usage sweep and daily Stripe overage report both fire at exactly 00:00:00.000 UTC — the overage read races the sweep that writes the day's final device-days, and the day is never re-reported

**Subsystem:** billing — usage metering vs Stripe overage reporting · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageQueue.ts:10`

BullMQ computes `every`-based repeats as `Math.floor(millis/every)*every + every` (node_modules/.pnpm/bullmq@5.79.3/.../classes/repeat.js:183-185), i.e. epoch-aligned. `STRIPE_USAGE_EVERY_MS = 24 * 3_600_000` (`apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageQueue.ts:10`) therefore fires at exactly 00:00:00.000 UTC, and `USAGE_SWEEP_EVERY_MS = 60 * 60_000` (`apps/worker/src/jobs/usageQueue.ts:11`) fires at the same instant. Both workers are started in the same process (`apps/worker/src/main.ts:195-209`) with no ordering between them. `runUsageSweep` (`apps/worker/src/jobs/usageWorker.ts:56-72`) windows on `server_time >= now-48h`, so positions received during 23:00–00:00 UTC of day D-1 are first inserted into `usage_daily` by the 00:00 sweep. `reportDailyOverage` (`apps/worker/src/billing/usageReporter.ts:87`) reads `usage_daily` for D-1 at that same instant via `tenantSummary({from: dayIso, to: dayIso})`. The sweep is an `INSERT…SELECT DISTINCT` over 48 h of `positions` (seconds to minutes at fleet scale); the overage read is a tiny groupBy, so the reader usually wins. An undercount does not throw, so `attempts: 5` never retries it, and the next tick computes a new `day` (`apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageWorker.ts:33`) — the day is never re-reported.

**failureScenario:** A TSP tenant on a plan with 50 included devices runs 53 active devices on 2026-08-03. Three of them (night-shift vehicles) send their first position of that UTC day between 23:00 and 00:00 UTC. At 00:00:00.000 UTC on 08-04 the Stripe job reads `usage_daily` for 2026-08-03 before the concurrently-firing sweep commits those three rows, gets `active = 50`, computes `over = max(0, 50-50) = 0`, and skips the tenant entirely (usageReporter.ts:90 `if (over <= 0) continue`). The 01:00 sweep inserts the missing rows, but no job ever revisits 2026-08-03 — three device-days of overage are permanently unbilled, silently, with no error and no metric.

**suggestedFix:** Decouple the two schedules: give the Stripe job a cron pattern offset from the hour (e.g. `pattern: '30 1 * * *'`, reporting the previous UTC day at 01:30) so it always runs after at least one full sweep has covered the day's final hour. Alternatively have the stripe worker `await runUsageSweep(pool, Date.now())` (idempotent by PK + ON CONFLICT) as its first step before reading `usage_daily`.

### 66. [MEDIUM] Signed AVL parameters are decoded and surfaced as unsigned — sub-zero temperatures read as ~250 °C

**Subsystem:** codec/dictionaries · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/normalize.ts:52`

The codec decodes every fixed-size IO value as unsigned: the vendored parser converts the hex slice with `parseInt(x, 16)` and `normalizeIoValue` (packages/codec/src/parse.ts:143-159) passes that straight through as a bigint. The AVL dictionaries DO carry the signedness — packages/codec/dictionaries/fmb1xx.json declares id 32 'Coolant Temperature' as `bytes:1, type:'Signed', units:'°C'`, ids 72-75 'Dallas Temperature 1-4' as `bytes:4, type:'Signed', multiplier:'0.1'`, ids 17-19 'Axis X/Y/Z' as `bytes:2, type:'Signed'`, ids 25-27 'BLE Temperature' as `bytes:2, type:'Signed'` — but nothing in the repo ever reads `entry.type`. `apps/worker/src/normalize.ts:47` fetches `dict.get(id)` solely to pick the attribute KEY, then line 52 stores the raw unsigned number. `packages/db/src/can.ts:42` reads `COALESCE(attrs->>'io_32', attrs->>'Coolant Temperature')` and returns it verbatim as `coolantC`, which `apps/web/src/routes/app/devices/can.tsx:32` renders with a ' °C' suffix. Grep confirms `BigInt.asIntN` appears exactly once in the whole codebase (normalize.ts:76, for rec_hash) and never for IO values.

**failureScenario:** Winter cold start in Vilnius: the vehicle's CAN bus reports coolant temperature −7 °C. The FMB120 encodes AVL id 32 as the single signed byte 0xF9. The codec yields 249n, normalize stores `attrs['Coolant Temperature'] = 249`, `readCanLatest` returns `coolantC: 249`, and the device CAN panel displays '249 °C' — an engine that appears to be boiling. Dallas probes (ids 72-75, 4-byte signed ×0.1) are worse: −5.0 °C on the wire is 0xFFFFFFCE, which surfaces as 4294967246, i.e. 429496724.6 °C once the ×0.1 multiplier is applied. Any future refrigerated-cargo temperature rule or report built on these ids will never fire below 0 °C, and will fire constantly above it.

**suggestedFix:** Apply signedness where the dictionary entry is already in hand. In apps/worker/src/normalize.ts, when `dict.get(id)` has `type === 'Signed'`, reinterpret with `BigInt.asIntN(Number(entry.bytes) * 8, v)` before writing to `attrs` (do the same for the promoted columns if any signed id is ever promoted). Alternatively push it into the codec so both transports and any future consumer inherit it. Add a golden fixture pinning a negative AVL 32 and a negative AVL 72 so the direction cannot regress.

### 67. [MEDIUM] parseCommandFrame reads past the buffer on short codec 12/13/14 frames — RangeError escapes the ACK-0 contract

**Subsystem:** codec/parse · **Location:** `packages/codec/src/parse.ts:163`

`parseCommandFrame` reads `bytes[10]` (the type byte) and `bytes.readUInt32BE(11)` (the size field) with no bounds check (parse.ts:163-164). The only length validation that ran beforehand is `bytes.length !== 8 + dataLen + 4` (parse.ts:25), which happily accepts `dataLen = 1` (13-byte frame) or `dataLen = 2` (14-byte frame). CRC is computed over `bytes[8..8+dataLen]`, so a one-byte data field `[0x0C]` with its matching CRC passes the CRC gate (parse.ts:32) and reaches the command branch. `readUInt32BE(11)` then throws a **RangeError**, not `FrameError`. `session.ts:224` catches only `CrcError | FrameError`, so the RangeError is rethrown, escapes to the constructor's chunk catch (session.ts:76-84), increments `sessionErrorsTotal` and calls `destroy()`. This breaks CLAUDE.md hard rule 4 / PROJECT_PLAN §3.2 ("on parse/CRC failure send count of good records actually persisted — 0 if whole packet bad"): the device gets no ACK at all and its socket is dropped. It is also invisible: `sessionErrorsTotal` is never `reflect()`ed in prom.ts:30-43, and neither `parseFailTotal` nor `frameViolationsTotal` is incremented. The UDP listener has the same hole — udp.ts:119-125 catches `FrameError`/`CrcError` and rethrows anything else, so the datagram takes the generic `.catch` at udp.ts:71 and no ACK is sent.

**failureScenario:** Verified by execution against the real ingest server: after a successful handshake for a registered IMEI, sending the 13-byte frame `00000000 00000001 0C <crc16(0x0C)>` produced `RangeError: The value of "offset" is out of range. It must be >= 0 and <= 9. Received 11`, no ACK was written, the socket was destroyed, and metrics read msgs=1 parseFail=0 frameViolations=0 sessErr=1. Realistically triggered by a device firmware that truncates a Codec 12 response frame, or by any peer that knows one registered IMEI: 13 bytes per session kill, no per-frame rate limit, and the ops dashboard shows nothing at all.

**suggestedFix:** Bounds-check before reading: at the top of `parseCommandFrame`, `if (dataLen < 8) throw new FrameError(\`command frame data length ${dataLen} too short\`, bytes)` (codec 12/13/14 need at least codec+quantity1+type+4B size+quantity2 = 8 bytes). Additionally harden the seams: in session.ts:224 and udp.ts:119, treat `RangeError` as a parse failure (ACK 0) rather than letting it escape, and add `sessionErrorsTotal` to the prom.ts reflect list so this class of bug is not silent.

### 68. [MEDIUM] The entire affiliate + commission money ledger writes zero audit rows — payout rates and paid/void marks are mutable with no trace

The routes that reach these are platform-only but fully exposed: `PATCH /v1/affiliates/:id` (crud.ts:1285, accepts `commissionPct`, `commissionMonths`, `status`) and `PATCH /v1/commissions/:id` (crud.ts:1305, sets `pending|paid|void`). `AuditLog.tenantId` is nullable (schema.prisma:709), so platform-scope audit rows are already supported — the capability exists and simply is not used here.

They then mark a batch of commissions `paid` via `PATCH /v1/commissions/:id`. `GET /v1/audit` shows nothing — the tenant/device/user trail is intact but the money trail has no entries at all. There is no way to establish who changed the rate, when, or who authorized the payouts; the only surviving evidence is the snapshotted `ratePct` on rows that happen to have accrued inside the window, and the `status` field's current value.

Stamp `tenantId: null` (platform scope) as the tenants repo does for its own platform actions.

`runErase` deletes positions (`erasePositions`, line 66), trips (67), events (68), commands (69), Redis state (70) and finally the `devices` row (71), plus a final resurrection sweep (75-79). It never touches `export_jobs`.

`POST /v1/accounts/:id/export` (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:664) produces a full NDJSON.gz dump of the account containing every device row (incl. IMEI), every trip, every event and **every position row per device** (apps/worker/src/jobs/gdprExportWorker.ts:93-125). The job row carries a 7-day `expiresAt` (`packages/db/src/repos/exports.ts` `EXPIRY_MS = 7 * 24 * 3_600_000`), the file sits in `EXPORT_DIR`, and `GET /v1/exports/:id/download` (crud.ts:695) serves it to any tenant admin until then; `runExportSweep` only unlinks at `expiresAt`.

The erase cascade is documented as exhaustive apart from `usage_daily` and `audit_log` ("DELIBERATELY KEPT" header comment). The export dump is neither documented as kept nor cleaned up — it is simply missed, so an Art. 17 erasure is not actually complete on disk or over the API.

**failureScenario:** Monday: a tsp_admin runs an account export; the worker writes `<EXPORT_DIR>/<uuid>.ndjson.gz` containing device 1234's full 13-month position history, trips and events, and marks the job `done` with `expiresAt = Monday+7d`. Tuesday: the customer exercises Art. 17 for that vehicle; the operator retires device 1234 and calls `POST /v1/devices/1234/erase`. `runErase` wipes positions/trips/events/device row. Through the following Sunday, `GET /v1/exports/<uuid>/download` still returns the complete location history of the "erased" device, and the plaintext file remains on the server filesystem (and in any filesystem backup) the whole time.

**suggestedFix:** In `runErase`, after the device row delete, mark every non-expired `export_jobs` row for that device's account as `expired` and unlink its file (reuse `runExportSweep`'s unlink path), so an erase invalidates dumps that predate it. Alternatively refuse an erase while a `done` export exists for the account and force the admin to expire it first.

### 70. [MEDIUM] GDPR account export omits the `drivers` table (name, licence no, phone, notes) and every trip's driverId

**Subsystem:** db / GDPR export completeness · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/jobs/gdprExportWorker.ts:94`

`runExport` exports account, users, devices, trips, events, commands, geofences, rules, webhooks (lines 91-103). It does **not** export `drivers`, even though `Driver` (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:375-392) is account-scoped (`tenantId` + `accountId` both NOT NULL, so a one-line `scoped('driver', …)` would work) and holds the most obviously personal data in the schema: `name`, `licenseNo`, `phone`, `notes`, `ibutton`.

Worse, the trips projection at line 94-95 is `id, "deviceId", status, "startTime", "endTime", "startLat", "startLon", "endLat", "endLon", "distanceM", "distanceSource", "maxSpeed", "idleS"` — `driverId` is omitted, so the who-drove-what linkage is absent from the dump entirely.

Also missing: `maintenance_items`, `share_links`, `scheduled_reports` (recipient e-mail addresses), `sms_deliveries` (SIM MSISDN + full SMS body), `push_subscriptions`. The file header comment asserts the export covers the account's data and enumerates only `users.passwordHash`, `webhooks.secret` and api_keys/refresh_tokens as deliberate omissions — driver PII is not on that list, so this is an oversight rather than a documented decision.

**failureScenario:** A driver files a GDPR Art. 15 subject-access request against a fleet operator running Orbetra. The operator runs `POST /v1/accounts/:id/export` and hands over the dump. The dump contains the vehicles and every trip, but nothing that identifies the driver (no `drivers` row with his name/licence/phone, and no `driverId` on any trip), so the operator cannot show what personal data is held about him nor which trips are attributed to him. The response is incomplete and the controller believes it is complete because the tool reported success.

**suggestedFix:** Add `await scoped('driver', 'SELECT id, name, "licenseNo", ibutton, phone, notes, active, "createdAt" FROM drivers WHERE "tenantId" = $1 AND "accountId" = $2')` (and the same for `maintenance_items`, `scheduled_reports`, `sms_deliveries`, `share_links`), and add `"driverId"` to the trips column list at line 95.

### 71. [MEDIUM] Events are ordered by insertion id, not occurrence time — a device flushing buffered data evicts genuinely recent events from the "recent events" views

**Subsystem:** db/api (events) · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/events.ts:39`

`EventRepo.list` uses `orderBy: { id: 'desc' }` with `take` capped at 1000 (packages/db/src/repos/events.ts:39-41); the cursor is also the id. `events.id` is an insertion sequence, and rule/geofence events are written at consume time (apps/worker/src/rules/writer.ts, apps/worker/src/geofence/writer.ts) while their `at` column is `r.fixTime` (apps/worker/src/rules/engine.ts:192, apps/worker/src/geofence/engine.ts:122). A buffered flush therefore mints the *highest* ids for the *oldest* occurrence times. Neither consumer re-sorts: the dashboard takes `rows24.slice(0, 6)` as "Recent" (apps/web/src/routes/app/dashboard.tsx:88, rendered under `dash.recent` at line 300) and the events table renders `query.data.pages.flat()` in server order with an `at` column (apps/web/src/routes/app/events.tsx:76, 146).

**failureScenario:** A van reconnects at 15:00 after 6 h offline and its flush produces 400 ignition/din_change/overspeed events with `at` between 09:00 and 15:00. They get the newest ids in the table. The dashboard's `listEvents({ from: dayAgo, limit: 300 })` returns 300 rows that are all from that one van, so the "Recent events" card shows six 09:00 entries and a panic event that fired on another vehicle two minutes ago is not in the response at all. On the events page, paging by id cursor walks that van's backlog before ever reaching the newer events of other devices.

**suggestedFix:** Order by `[{ at: 'desc' }, { id: 'desc' }]` and use a composite (at, id) keyset cursor instead of the bare id cursor, so the list is ordered by occurrence and pagination stays stable.

### 72. [MEDIUM] Self-serve signup hard-codes the account timezone to UTC and no UI can change it — every Direct-plan tenant's reports are bucketed in the wrong day

**Subsystem:** db/api (signup) · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:165`

`createSelfServeSignup` creates the tenant's only account with `timezone: 'UTC'` literal (packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:165). `signupSchema` collects name/email/password/company/ref only — no timezone or country (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:274-281) — and `createSignupRoute` never supplies one (apps/api/src/routes/signup.ts:100-108). That value is the sole basis for report day bucketing: `POST /v1/reports/:type` forces `timezone: account.timezone` (apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts:72) into `date_trunc('day', col AT TIME ZONE $tz)` (packages/db/src/reports.ts:154), and `POST /v1/scheduled-reports` snapshots `data.timezone ?? account.timezone` at creation (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:871). The web SPA has no accounts page at all (apps/web/src/routes/app/ contains no accounts.tsx; settings.tsx only reads `listAccounts` for the export picker), so the only way to correct it is a hand-crafted `PATCH /v1/accounts/:id`.

**failureScenario:** A Vilnius fleet signs up self-serve (plan direct_10). Their account is Europe/Vilnius in reality but stored as 'UTC'. In summer (UTC+3) every trip that starts between 00:00 and 03:00 local — night shifts, early deliveries — is bucketed by Postgres into the *previous* calendar day in the mileage, stops, engine-hours, overspeed and geofence reports, and in the emailed scheduled report which snapshotted 'UTC' at creation. The dashboard's "today km" tile (apps/web/src/routes/app/dashboard.tsx:100-102 keys on `acctTz`) reads 0 km for the first three hours of every local day. The customer has no screen anywhere in the product to fix it.

**suggestedFix:** Accept an IANA timezone in `signupSchema` (defaulting from the browser's `Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone` on the signup form) and thread it into `createSelfServeSignup`; independently, expose account timezone in the web settings page so an existing tenant can correct it.

### 73. [MEDIUM] pg pool of 10 shared by 16 shard consumers and 13 job workers, with no acquire timeout and no statement_timeout

**Subsystem:** db/connection-pool · **Location:** `packages/db/src/pool.ts:8`

`createPool` defaults to `max = 10` and both callers use the default (`apps/worker/src/main.ts:61`, `apps/api/src/main.ts:33`). In the worker that single pool serves 16 concurrent `ShardConsumer`s (each doing `writePositions` plus trip/geofence/rule persister queries per batch) AND 13 BullMQ workers, one of which (`trip/recompute.ts:121`) holds a dedicated `PoolClient` for an entire `BEGIN … COMMIT` that issues one `INSERT` round-trip per recomputed trip (lines 137-153). No `connectionTimeoutMillis` is set, so `pg.Pool` queues acquisitions forever with no error and no metric; no `statement_timeout` is set on the connection string or session, so a single pathological query runs unbounded. `grep` confirms no `statement_timeout`, `connectionTimeoutMillis`, `idleTimeoutMillis` or Prisma `connection_limit` anywhere in the repo.

**failureScenario:** A late-batch recompute over a multi-week span (see the unbounded-SELECT finding) holds one pool client for 90 s while it streams positions and then loops hundreds of per-trip INSERTs inside a transaction. Concurrently the hourly usage sweep, the daily retention prune and a GDPR export each hold a client. Only ~6 remain for 16 shard consumers, so `writePositions` calls start queueing inside `pg.Pool` with no timeout and no visibility. `pipeline_lag_ms` and `stream_depth` climb; ingest's `pauseAboveDepth` backpressure kicks in and devices start being throttled — and the operator has no signal that the cause is pool starvation rather than DB slowness, because a queued acquire produces no log, no error and no metric.

**suggestedFix:** Size the worker pool from the concurrency it actually serves (e.g. `createPool(databaseUrl, Number(process.env.PG_POOL_MAX ?? 24))`), set `connectionTimeoutMillis` (fail fast + a counter) and `statement_timeout` via `options=-c statement_timeout=…` on the connection string or a `pool.on('connect')` `SET statement_timeout`, and export a `pg_pool_waiting` gauge from `pool.waitingCount`.

### 74. [MEDIUM] CSV import skips deviceCreateSchema entirely, and any non-duplicate-IMEI DB error aborts the batch mid-loop and discards the created-count report the code claims to protect

**Subsystem:** device CSV import (api) · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/deviceImport.ts:195`

The CSV path never applies `deviceCreateSchema`. `rowsToImport` (apps/api/src/routes/deviceImport.ts:104-115) copies `name`, `plate` and `groupName` straight out of the parsed CSV, and `dryRun` (:130-148) only checks `name !== ''` plus the IMEI/profile/account/SIM rules — so unlike `POST /v1/devices` (which enforces `name` max 120, `plate` max 32, `groupName` max 64 at packages/shared/src/entities.ts:43-45) these fields have no length and no charset validation on this route, up to the 2,000,000-char `csv` cap (entities.ts:65) under the dedicated 3 MB body limit (apps/api/src/app.ts:196).

`applyImport` (:175-199) then creates rows one at a time and its catch handles ONLY `DuplicateImeiError`; everything else re-throws (`:197`). The comment immediately above (:171-174) states the per-row try/catch exists specifically so a failure is "NOT a 500 that aborts the batch and loses the report of what was already created" — but that promise only holds for the one error class it catches. Every earlier row has already been committed via `db.devices.create` AND activated in Redis via `activateDevice` (:190-193, which writes `registry:imei`, `device:tenant`, `device:account`, `device:config`), so the abort leaves real, live devices behind with no response telling the operator which ones.

A trivially reachable trigger for the unhandled class: a NUL byte in `name`. JSON permits `␀` in the `csv` string and nothing strips it. Verified against the project's Postgres image through the pg driver: inserting a text parameter containing 0x00 raises SQLSTATE 22021, `invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00`. That code is not P2002/P2023/P2025, so `dbErrorHttp` (packages/db/src/errors.ts:17-28) returns null and `app.onError` (apps/api/src/app.ts:133) emits a bare 500. The same abort happens for any other unmapped fault — e.g. a P2003 FK violation if the target account or profile is deleted concurrently mid-import.

**failureScenario:** An operator imports a 900-row CSV exported from a legacy system where row 400's `name` carries a stray NUL byte (or the account referenced by the file is deleted by a colleague while the import runs). Rows 1–399 are created in Postgres and activated in Redis; row 400 raises SQLSTATE 22021, `applyImport` re-throws, and the request returns a bare 500 with no body. The operator sees only "error", retries the same file, and every one of the first 399 IMEIs now comes back as `IMEI already registered` — while 399 devices are silently live, counting against the plan device cap and being billed as device-days by the usage sweep. Nothing in the response or the audit trail tells them where the import stopped.

**suggestedFix:** Validate the imported fields with the same constraints as the manual path (reuse the `deviceCreateSchema` field rules inside `dryRun` — length caps plus a rejection of control characters/NUL), and widen the `applyImport` catch to record ANY per-row failure as a `RowError` and continue, so the request always returns the accurate `{ created, errors }` report instead of a 500 that hides partially-applied state.

### 75. [MEDIUM] The zero-entitlement floor's `deviceLimit: 0` is enforced only at device CREATE, so a lapsed subscription or an expired trial never actually stops the billable product

**Subsystem:** entitlements / plan enforcement · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/packages/shared/src/plans.ts:78`

`FLOOR_ENTITLEMENTS` claims to stop "a non-paying tenant keeping billable features like smsGateway, or an uncapped device count" (`:81-86`). `deviceLimit` is read in exactly three places, all creation paths: `POST /v1/devices` (`apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:372,378`), import preview (`:735`) and import apply (`:755`). No read/live route carries an `entitlement:` — the grep of `entitlement:` in crud.ts yields only accounts, sms, webhooks, branding and domains — so device lists, `/v1/devices/last`, positions, trips, reports, WS live tracking and the whole ingest path are ungated by billing status. Nothing revokes or deactivates existing devices when a subscription lapses (`activateDevice`/`deactivateDevice` are only called from the device CRUD routes), and there is no sweep that acts on `LAPSED_SUBSCRIPTION_STATUSES`.

**failureScenario:** A self-serve tenant signs up (`routes/signup.ts:42-43`: `direct_10`, `trialing`, 30 days), registers 10 devices in week one, and never subscribes. On day 31 `effectiveEntitlementsAt` floors them to `deviceLimit: 0` — which only means `POST /v1/devices` now 403s. All 10 trackers keep connecting to ingest, positions keep being written and charged to our storage, and the customer keeps full live tracking, history, trips and reports indefinitely for free. The identical outcome applies to a paying tenant whose subscription goes to `canceled`.

**suggestedFix:** Make lapse actionable: either add a suspension step that tears down the ingest registry entries for a tenant whose subscription is in `LAPSED_SUBSCRIPTION_STATUSES` (with a grace period and an explicit un-suspend on re-subscribe), or gate the core read/live routes on a `serviceActive` entitlement so a lapsed tenant is visibly blocked rather than silently free.

### 77. [MEDIUM] ingest_paused_sockets gauge leaks permanently: a backpressure-paused socket closed by the peer never decrements it

**Subsystem:** ingest · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/session.ts:93`

`metrics.pausedSockets` is incremented in `maybeBackpressure()` (apps/ingest/src/session.ts:287-290) and decremented in exactly two places: `Session.destroy()` (session.ts:101-108) and the `pollForDrain()` resume branch (session.ts:303-306). The socket lifecycle handlers are `socket.on('error', () => this.destroy())` and `socket.on('close', () => this.clearTimer())` (session.ts:92-93) — the close handler does **not** touch the paused accounting and does not call `destroy()`.

A normal peer-initiated disconnect (device sends FIN → 'end' → net.Server's default `allowHalfOpen:false` auto-ends the socket → 'close') emits no 'error' event, so `Session.destroy()` never runs. `pollForDrain()`'s tick also returns early on `this.socket.destroyed` (session.ts:302) without decrementing. The counter is therefore leaked by +1 for every paused socket whose peer disconnects gracefully — the ordinary way a GPRS device drops a session.

`pausedSockets` is not internal bookkeeping: it is exported as the Prometheus gauge `ingest_paused_sockets` (apps/ingest/src/prom.ts:40), logged every 60 s (apps/ingest/src/main.ts:64), and is the sole expression of the `BackpressureSustained` alert (infra/prometheus/alerts.yml:61, `max(ingest_paused_sockets) > 0 for 10m`).

**failureScenario:** A worker restart causes a genuine 3-minute shard backlog; 400 sockets pause. The backlog clears, but 250 of those devices had already been dropped by their carrier NAT and closed gracefully while paused, so only 150 sessions reach the `pollForDrain` resume path. `ingest_paused_sockets` reports 250 forever, `BackpressureSustained` fires 10 minutes later and never clears, and the number ratchets upward with every subsequent backpressure episode. The one alert that is supposed to say "a shard is not draining" becomes a permanently-firing counter of historical pauses, so the next real stall is indistinguishable from the noise.

**suggestedFix:** Route the close path through the same accounting: change session.ts:93 to `socket.on('close', () => { this.clearTimer(); if (this.paused) { this.paused = false; this.deps.metrics.pausedSockets-- } })`, or have the close handler call a `releasePaused()` helper that both `destroy()` and `close` share (make it idempotent so a destroy-then-close pair cannot double-decrement). Add a unit test that pauses a session, ends the socket from the peer side, and asserts `metrics.pausedSockets === 0`.

### 78. [MEDIUM] drainPending LPOPs before recording in-flight — a command can end up in neither queue, and the JSDoc claims the opposite

**Subsystem:** ingest / command transport · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/ingest/src/session.ts:186`

`drainPending` LPOPs the command off `cmd:pending:{deviceId}` first (session.ts:186) and only records it in `cmd:inflight:{deviceId}` after the write, via a MULTI at session.ts:205-211. Between those two points the entry exists nowhere in Redis. If `socket.write(encodeCodec12(...))` throws, the handler does `continue` (session.ts:199-203) — the command is now gone from `cmd:pending` and was never added to `cmd:inflight`. The same hole covers a process crash or a Redis error on the MULTI. The dispatcher's reconciliation only ever looks at those two lists (dispatcher.ts:70-74), so it can never recover the entry; the DB row stays `queued` until the blanket 24 h expiry sweep (dispatcher.ts:135) flips it to `expired`. The method's own JSDoc at session.ts:178-180 asserts 'a send failure leaves the command in-flight; the dispatcher times it out and re-queues it', which the code does not do.

**failureScenario:** Redis returns an error (failover/READONLY/OOM) on the MULTI at session.ts:205 after the Codec-12 frame was already written to the socket. The device RECEIVES and EXECUTES the command (e.g. `setdigout 1`), the `await ... .exec()` rejects, the session's chained catch logs and destroys the socket (session.ts:76-84). The command is in no Redis list, so the dispatcher never marks it `sent` or `acked`; 24 hours later the operator sees status `expired` for a command the vehicle actually performed. Conversely, on the `socket.write` throw path the operator sees `expired` for a command that never left the server, with no automatic retry — for both cases the UI reports a state that contradicts reality.

**suggestedFix:** Move the entry to in-flight atomically before writing to the socket — e.g. `LMOVE cmd:pending:{id} cmd:inflight:{id} LEFT RIGHT` (then rewrite the moved value with `sentAtMs`), or claim with a Lua script — so a failure anywhere after the pop still leaves a recoverable in-flight record. Fix the JSDoc to match whichever semantics are chosen.

### 79. [MEDIUM] `pollForDrain` bypasses the shard-depth cache with `force=true` every 500 ms per paused socket — backpressure amplifies load on the exact Redis connection that is already the bottleneck

**Subsystem:** ingest/backpressure · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/session.ts:298`

`getCachedShardDepth` exists precisely to bound XLEN traffic: it memoises the depth per shard for `depthCacheMs` (session.ts:318-329), and the post-ACK check honours the cache (`force=false`, session.ts:280-286). But the drain poller calls it with `force = true` (session.ts:298), which skips the cache unconditionally, and re-arms itself every 500 ms per paused socket (session.ts:308, 311). There is no per-shard coordination — each paused session runs its own independent timer.

All of these XLENs go through `this.deps.redis`, the single ioredis connection created in apps/ingest/src/main.ts:14 and shared by every TCP session's XADD/HGET/MULTI and by the UDP listener. Sockets are paused exactly when `raw:{shard}` is above `pauseAboveDepth` — i.e. when the worker is behind and Redis is already the constrained resource — so the mechanism that is supposed to shed load instead injects O(paused sockets) extra round-trips per second onto the contended connection, ahead of the ACK-path commands in the same pipeline queue.

**failureScenario:** A worker deploy or lease flap stalls the shard consumers; `raw:{shard}` climbs past `pauseAboveDepth` (50k). With a 5,000-device fleet, roughly 5,000 sessions hit `maybeBackpressure()` and pause. Each now issues an uncached `XLEN` every 500 ms → ~10,000 extra Redis commands/second, all serialized on the same connection as the XADDs and registry HGETs of the still-unpaused devices and of every UDP datagram. ACK latency rises past the 250 ms SLA (AckLatencyHigh fires), which lengthens each session's processing chain, which keeps more sockets paused — a self-reinforcing loop that persists after the worker recovers, because the depth only drains while the poller floods. The `depthCache` is never populated usefully during this window since every poll forces a refresh.

**suggestedFix:** Drop `force` from the poller (`getCachedShardDepth(this.deps.redis, this.shard, this.now(), false, this.deps.config.depthCacheMs)`) so all paused sockets on a shard share one XLEN per cache window, or better: run a single per-shard drain poller that resumes all paused sessions for that shard, instead of one timer per socket. Add jitter to the 500 ms interval, and export a metric for the poll rate so the amplification is visible.

**Subsystem:** ingest/observability · **Location:** `apps/ingest/src/prom.ts:43`

`IngestMetrics` defines `sessionErrorsTotal` (`apps/ingest/src/metrics.ts:13`, incremented at `session.ts:78` and `udp.ts:73`) and `udpInflightDropsTotal` (`metrics.ts:17`, incremented at `udp.ts:66`), but `startIngestProm` only `reflect()`s ten gauges — neither of those two is among them. `udpInflightDropsTotal` is specifically the OOM guard that fires when Redis is slow or unavailable: `udp.ts:60-68` drops the datagram BEFORE the `handle()` path, so the exported `ingest_udp_backpressure_drops_total` (which is only incremented by the downstream shard-depth check, itself a Redis call) stays flat. `apps/ingest/src/prom.spec.ts` asserts only a handful of names, so the gap is not test-caught.

There is no metric or alert that says 'ingest is shedding traffic', so the operator sees only a vague drop in ACK rate and no cause. ### 81. [MEDIUM] No `up` alert for the exporters every infra rule depends on, and no `probe_success` alert — a total customer-facing outage produces zero alerts

**Subsystem:** observability/alerting · **Location:** `infra/prometheus/alerts.yml:92`

`TargetDown` is scoped to `up{job=~"ingest|worker|api"} == 0` (alerts.yml:92). The scrape config defines four more jobs — `node`, `postgres`, `blackbox-tls`, `prometheus` (infra/prometheus/prometheus.yml / prometheus.staging.yml) — and none of them is covered.

That matters because the remaining rules are built entirely on those uncovered exporters: `DiskFillingUp`/`DiskCritical` read `node_filesystem_avail_bytes` (node-exporter, alerts.yml:96-105), and `WalArchiveFailing`/`WalDirGrowing` read `pg_stat_archiver_*` (postgres-exporter, alerts.yml:70-84). A Prometheus rule whose series disappears simply stops evaluating — it does not fire. So if either exporter container dies or crash-loops, the disk-full and WAL-archive safety nets go silent with no indication.

Separately, `probe_success` is never referenced anywhere in alerts.yml (verified by grep). The only blackbox rule is `CertExpiringSoon`, which was deliberately guarded with `probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry > 0` (alerts.yml:132-133) so it would *not* fire during an outage — a correct fix that removed the last incidental outage signal without adding a replacement.

**failureScenario:** Caddy fails to renew the cert for `dash.orbetra.com` (rate-limited by Let's Encrypt, or the on-demand ask is being throttled), or the caddy container crash-loops on a bad Caddyfile edit. Every customer gets a TLS error; the product is 100% down. Prometheus scrapes `ingest:9101`, `worker:9102` and `api:3010` over the internal compose network, all of which are unaffected, so `up{job=~"ingest|worker|api"}` stays 1 and `TargetDown` never fires. `probe_success{instance="https://dash.orbetra.com"}` drops to 0 but no rule reads it, and `CertExpiringSoon` is explicitly suppressed because `probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry` is 0. Alertmanager sends nothing. The same holds for the slower variant: node-exporter OOMs, `DiskFillingUp` stops evaluating, and the positions hypertable fills the root filesystem until Postgres refuses writes.

**suggestedFix:** Widen the rule to `up{job!="blackbox-tls"} == 0` (or add a second `ExporterDown` rule for `job=~"node|postgres|prometheus"`), and add `- alert: EndpointDown / expr: probe_success == 0 / for: 5m` over the blackbox targets. Also add the real staging/prod hostnames to the blackbox target list — it currently probes only `https://orbetra.com` and `https://dash.orbetra.com`, which do not resolve on the staging deployment.

### 82. [MEDIUM] The API exports exactly one metric (`ws_clients`) — a fully-failing API keeps `up == 1` and fires no alert

**Subsystem:** observability/api · **Location:** `apps/api/src/app.ts:97`

`createApiProm()` registers a single `Gauge` named `ws_clients` and nothing else (apps/api/src/app.ts:97-101). `collectDefaultMetrics()` is never called anywhere in the repo (verified by grep), so there is not even process RSS / event-loop-lag / heap. There is no request counter, no status-code counter, no latency histogram, no auth-failure counter, no pg-pool-saturation gauge. The `onError` handler logs `unhandled API error` to stdout (app.ts:133) and increments nothing.

Prometheus scrapes `api:3010/metrics` (infra/prometheus/prometheus.staging.yml) and the only alert covering it is `TargetDown: up{job=~"ingest|worker|api"} == 0` (infra/prometheus/alerts.yml:92). Serving `ws_clients` is enough to keep `up == 1`, so the alert only catches a dead process/port — never a process that is alive and answering every request with a 500.

**failureScenario:** The pg pool (max 10, no acquire timeout — packages/db/src/pool.ts:11) saturates because a long report query and the 16-shard worker load coincide, or Postgres restarts and Prisma's pool is stale. Every `/v1/*` request now hangs or falls through to `problem(c, 500, 'Internal Server Error')`. The `/metrics` endpoint still returns `ws_clients 0` because it touches neither pg nor prisma, so `up` stays 1, `TargetDown` never fires, and no other rule references any api-side series. The founders' Telegram stays silent; the outage is discovered when a customer calls. The same blindness applies to a credential-stuffing wave (no auth-failure counter) and to Stripe webhook rejections (no counter).

**suggestedFix:** Call `collectDefaultMetrics({ register: registry })` in `createApiProm`, add a Hono middleware that increments `http_requests_total{method,route,status}` and observes `http_request_duration_ms`, and add counters in `app.onError` for mapped-vs-unhandled errors. Then add alert rules for `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])` and event-loop lag alongside the existing `TargetDown` in infra/prometheus/alerts.yml.

### 83. [MEDIUM] pushSubscriptions.subscribe upserts on a global unique key with NO tenant predicate — cross-tenant re-homing of a push subscription

**Subsystem:** packages/db repos · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/pushSubscriptions.ts:34`

`subscribe()` takes a `Scope` but never applies it to the lookup: `prisma.pushSubscription.upsert({ where: { endpoint }, … })` (`pushSubscriptions.ts:34-38`). `endpoint` is globally `@unique` across all tenants (`schema.prisma:624`), and the `update` branch rewrites `tenantId`, `accountId` and `userId` to the CALLER's values. There is no `tenantId` guard anywhere in the statement.

This is the one mutation in the repo layer that can cross the tenant boundary, and it is invisible to the isolation suite: `push` sits in the manifest EXEMPT regex (`tests/isolation/suite.spec.ts:262`) and `apps/api/__tests__/push.spec.ts` seeds only a single tenant (`P1`), so no cross-tenant case exists anywhere.

The route (`routes/push.ts:32-43`) is reachable by any `account_manager`/`tsp_admin`/`platform_admin` in any tenant with a JWT.

**failureScenario:** Tenant B's account_manager POSTs `/v1/push/subscribe` with tenant A's push endpoint URL (obtained from a shared/kiosk browser, a support-ticket paste of a PushSubscription JSON, or a browser-extension/log leak). The upsert takes the `update` branch and rewrites the row to `{tenantId: B, accountId: B1, userId: attacker}`. Two consequences: (1) tenant A's user silently stops receiving their own alerts — `listByAccount(A, A1)` (`pushSubscriptions.ts:46`) no longer returns the row, so a panic/geofence alert never reaches them; (2) tenant B's `webpush` rule channel now fans out to tenant A's browser, delivering B's device names, geofence names and speeds as OS-level notifications on A's machine. Neither tenant has any API surface that would reveal the re-homing.

**suggestedFix:** Replace the blind upsert with a scoped write: `updateMany({ where: { endpoint, tenantId: scope.tenantId }, data: {…} })` and, when `count === 0`, `create(...)` inside a try/catch that maps a P2002 on `endpoint` to a 409 ("endpoint already registered elsewhere") rather than silently stealing it. If genuine cross-tenant re-homing is required for multi-tenant users on one browser, make it an explicit, separately-audited path — not a side effect of subscribe. Add a two-tenant case to push.spec.ts.

### 84. [MEDIUM] scheduled_reports has no FK to tenants/accounts — rows outlive tenant deletion and the worker keeps emailing reports forever

**Subsystem:** packages/db schema + scheduled reports · **Location:** `packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:593`

`model ScheduledReport` declares `tenantId`/`accountId` as bare uuid columns with no `@relation` (`schema.prisma:593-616`), and the migration `20260715030000_scheduled_reports/migration.sql` creates no foreign key (only a PK and an `enabled` index). Every other tenant-owned model either cascades from Tenant or is explicitly guarded.

`tenants.remove` (`packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:198-208`) only blocks on commissions and then hard-deletes the tenant; nothing deletes the schedules. `accounts.remove` (`repos/accounts.ts:71-80`) only blocks on users. `db.scheduledReports.listEnabled()` (`repos/scheduledReports.ts:43`) is UNSCOPED by design and is the worker cron's entry point (`apps/worker/src/reports/scheduledReporter.ts:153`), which then runs the report and emails every recipient (`scheduledReporter.ts:167-173`). `resolveBranding` (`scheduledReporter.ts:127-131`) explicitly falls back to `'Orbetra'` when the tenant row is gone, so a missing tenant does not even abort the send.

After tenant deletion the row is also unreachable by ANY API caller — `GET/DELETE /v1/scheduled-reports` scope on `tenantId` (`repos/generic.ts:61-64`), and no tenant with that id exists — so there is no way to stop it short of manual SQL.

**failureScenario:** A tenant churns; platform_admin calls `DELETE /v1/tenants/:id`. Trips/events/devices cascade away, but the tenant's `scheduled_reports` rows survive with `enabled = true`. Every hour the worker's cron picks them up via `listEnabled()`, `isDue` fires at the configured `hourUtc`, `claimRun` succeeds, `runReport` returns zero rows, and the formatter emails an empty report — now branded 'Orbetra' instead of the tenant's white-label name — to up to 20 recipient addresses of the ex-customer, daily or weekly, indefinitely. This is unsolicited mail to ex-customers from the platform's own SES identity (a bounce/complaint-reputation risk given the existing SES guard work) and a GDPR data-lifecycle violation (recipient email addresses retained and processed after the controller relationship ended). The same happens per-account for `DELETE /v1/accounts/:id`, though there a surviving tenant admin can still see and delete the row.

**suggestedFix:** Add `tenant Tenant @relation(fields:[tenantId], references:[id], onDelete: Cascade)` and `account Account @relation(fields:[accountId], references:[id], onDelete: Cascade)` to ScheduledReport (and the same to PushSubscription, which has the identical missing-FK shape at schema.prisma:618-630), with a new append-only migration adding the FK constraints after a one-off cleanup of existing orphans. Belt-and-braces: have `runDueSchedules` skip (and disable) a schedule whose tenant row no longer resolves, instead of falling back to the 'Orbetra' brand.

### 85. [MEDIUM] Expanded-year ISO timestamps pass the 366-day range guard and are then silently DROPPED by the repo, turning a bounded report into a full-history aggregate scan

**Subsystem:** reports API range guard · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts:57`

`apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts:55-59` validates the window with `Date.parse`, whose range is ±273,790 years, and rejects only NaN, reversed, or >366-day spans. `packages/db/src/reports.ts:111-116` then re-checks each bound with `isPgSafeDate`, which only accepts 0001-01-01 … 9999-12-31 (`packages/db/src/dateGuard.ts:9-19`), and SILENTLY OMITS the predicate when it fails. The two validators disagree on the accepted range, so a pair of bounds that is JS-valid, ordered, and less than 366 days apart but outside Postgres range clears the route guard and produces a query with no time predicate at all — exactly the unbounded scan the `MAX_REPORT_RANGE_MS` comment (line 17-18, 'audit MED') was added to prevent. Verified by execution: `Date.parse('+020000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z') = 568971820800000`, span to `+020000-01-02` is exactly 1 day, and both fail `isPgSafeDate`.

**failureScenario:** Any authenticated user (including a read-only `viewer` and, where reachable, an API key) POSTs `/v1/reports/mileage` with `{"from":"+020000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","to":"+020000-01-02T00:00:00.000Z","accountId":"…"}`. The route sees a valid, ordered, 1-day span and passes it through. `scopeWhere` drops both bounds, so the query becomes `SELECT … FROM trips t WHERE t."tenantId"=$1 AND t."accountId"=$2 GROUP BY …` over the account's ENTIRE history. The per-user limiter allows 60/min (`apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts:30`) and fails open on any Redis error (lines 43-45), so a single caller can hold 60 full-history GROUP BYs per minute open against the same pool the live pipeline uses.

**suggestedFix:** Use one shared validator. In `apps/api/src/routes/reports.ts`, replace `Date.parse` with `pgSafeDate` from `@orbetra/db` and 400 when either bound is not pg-safe. Additionally make `scopeWhere` fail closed — reject the request rather than dropping a bound the caller explicitly supplied.

### 87. [MEDIUM] refresh_tokens and password_reset_tokens are never deleted — unbounded growth on the hot auth path

**Subsystem:** retention / auth tables · **Location:** `packages/db/src/auth.ts:144`

`buildAuthMethods` only ever inserts or flags rows: refreshTokens.create (auth.ts:144), claimForRotation stamps rotatedAt (`:147-151`), revokeFamily/revokeAllForUser stamp revokedAt (`:160`, `:163`); passwordResetTokens.create (`:168`), consume stamps usedAt (`:171-175`), invalidateAllForUser (`:179`). There is no delete path anywhere for either table, and the retention worker prunes only webhook_deliveries (jobs/retentionWorker.ts:26). Each table carries a unique index on tokenHash plus btrees on userId (and familyId for refresh_tokens) — three indexes that grow with every row. Access tokens are 15 minutes (per the auth surface table), so every active session mints a new refresh_tokens row four times an hour, forever.

**failureScenario:** A 500-seat TSP with users active 8h/day generates ~500 × 32 = 16k refresh_tokens rows/day ≈ 6M rows/year, none of which is ever removed even though every one of them expired long ago. `revokeAllForUser` (an UPDATE ... WHERE userId AND revokedAt IS NULL, run on every password change, scope change and user delete) and the per-refresh `findUnique(tokenHash)` keep walking indexes that only ever grow; autovacuum churn and index bloat climb on the login/refresh critical path with no ceiling, and the table permanently retains a per-user session timeline (createdAt/rotatedAt) far beyond any stated retention.

**suggestedFix:** Extend the existing daily retention sweep with batched deletes: `DELETE FROM refresh_tokens WHERE "expiresAt" < now() - interval '30 days'` and `DELETE FROM password_reset_tokens WHERE "expiresAt" < now() - interval '30 days'` (same LIMIT-batched pattern as webhookDeliveries.pruneOlderThan:65-71), plus the equivalent for affiliate_password_tokens.

### 88. [MEDIUM] Rule `scope.deviceIds` is an unvalidated arbitrary JSON array that is re-materialised with map(String) for every device in every batch

**Subsystem:** rules engine (shared schema → worker rule cache) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/rules/cache.ts:93`

`ruleCreateSchema.scope` is `z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:173) — no shape, no element type, no size bound. The whole object is persisted and then synced verbatim into Redis (`apps/api/src/routes/ruleRegistry.ts:30-36`), reloaded by `RuleCache.load` every 30 s (apps/worker/src/rules/cache.ts:67-89), and consumed on the hot path by `inScope` (apps/worker/src/rules/cache.ts:93-97):

    const list = scope['deviceIds']
    if (!Array.isArray(list) || list.length === 0) return true
    return list.map(String).includes(deviceId)

`inScope` is called from `resolveBatch` (cache.ts:56) once per unique device × per tenant rule, and it allocates a brand-new N-element string array on every call before doing a linear `includes`. Nothing validates that `deviceIds` is small, or even that its elements are device ids. The 1 MB `pickBodyLimit` (apps/api/src/app.ts:195-205) is the only bound: at ~21 bytes per quoted numeric id that permits roughly 45,000 entries in a single rule. Batches are 200 records (apps/worker/src/consumer.ts:150/162), so up to 200 unique devices per batch. This work is synchronous and sits directly in front of the XACK, in the same single-process event loop shared by all 16 shard consumers.

**failureScenario:** An account_manager creates ten enabled rules on one tenant, each with `scope: {"deviceIds": [ ...45,000 strings... ]}` (a ~950 KB body, accepted — `z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())` inspects nothing). Once the rules land in `rule:tenant:{id}` and a batch of that tenant's positions arrives with 200 distinct devices, `resolveBatch` performs 200 × 10 × 45,000 ≈ 9×10^7 String() allocations plus the same number of comparisons synchronously per batch, plus a ~10 MB HGETALL + JSON.parse of the rule hash every 30 s. Rule evaluation, trip closing and geofence transitions for every other tenant on the process stall behind it, and the GC pressure from the throwaway arrays compounds the pause.

**suggestedFix:** Give `scope` a real schema (e.g. `z.object({ deviceIds: z.array(z.string().regex(/^\d+$/)).max(500).optional() }).strict()`) instead of `z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())`, and in `RuleCache.load` precompute a `Set<string>` of the normalised ids once per cache load so `inScope` is an O(1) `set.has(deviceId)` instead of an O(N) `map(String).includes(...)` per device per batch.

### 89. [MEDIUM] push_subscriptions has no FK or cleanup on user delete — a removed user's browser keeps receiving the account's alerts

**Subsystem:** schema / FK on-delete semantics · **Location:** `packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:623`

PushSubscription.userId is a bare `String @db.Uuid` with no relation (schema.prisma:623), and migration 20260716120000_push_subscriptions/migration.sql:2-14 creates the table with zero foreign keys. `users.remove` (packages/db/src/repos/users.ts:69-75) deletes the user row and the route additionally revokes WS sessions (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:349) and refresh-token families — but nothing deletes the user's push subscriptions. The web-push driver fans out purely by account: `subscriptions.listByAccount(ctx.tenantId, ctx.accountId)` (apps/worker/src/notify/drivers.ts:88) never consults userId or checks that the user still exists. Rows are only ever removed by an explicit browser unsubscribe (pushSubscriptions.ts:44) or a 404/410 from the push service (`:52`).

**failureScenario:** An employee is terminated; the tenant admin deletes their user account. Their access token, refresh family and live WS socket are all correctly killed — but their browser's push subscription row survives. Every subsequent `panic`, `geofence`, `overspeed` or `power_cut` alert for that account is still pushed to the ex-employee's machine, complete with device name, timestamp and message body, indefinitely (a Chrome/Firefox push endpoint stays valid for months and never returns 410 while the profile lives). The same stale-scope bug fires when a user is moved between accounts via PATCH /v1/users/:id — accountId on the subscription row is never updated, so they keep getting the OLD account's alerts.

**suggestedFix:** New migration adding `push_subscriptions.userId` FK → users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE (and tenantId/accountId FKs), plus an explicit `pushSubscriptions.deleteByUser(userId)` called from users.remove and on any accountId change.

### 90. [MEDIUM] Deleting an account orphans its scheduled_reports, which keep firing hourly and emailing external recipients forever

**Subsystem:** schema / orphan rows · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/scheduledReports.ts:43`

scheduled_reports carries tenantId/accountId as plain UUID columns with NO foreign keys (schema.prisma:593-614; migration 20260715030000). `accounts.remove` (repos/accounts.ts:71-80) deletes only the account row — it does not touch scheduled_reports, rules, drivers, api_keys, webhooks, geofences or export_jobs, all of which are accountId-keyed without FKs. The worker's hourly cron then selects `prisma.scheduledReport.findMany({ where: { enabled: true } })` (repos/scheduledReports.ts:43) with no existence check on the account/tenant, and apps/worker/src/reports/scheduledReporter.ts:164-168 runs the report for `{tenantId, accountId}` and mails every address in `s.recipients`.

**failureScenario:** A TSP offboards a sub-account that had a daily mileage report going to fleet@ex-customer.com. The admin deletes the account (succeeds, since users and devices were moved first). The scheduled_reports row is orphaned but still `enabled`, so at its configured UTC hour every single day the worker runs the report against a dead scope and emails an empty report to the ex-customer indefinitely — unsolicited mail the platform has no UI to stop (the account it hangs off no longer exists to be listed). Given the repo's existing SES bounce-reputation guard (commit 5211219), a growing set of these to stale addresses is a direct sending-reputation risk. Secondary orphans from the same missing-FK class: `drivers` rows keep employee name/licenseNo/phone forever, and account-scoped `api_keys` rows keep authenticating.

**suggestedFix:** Add FKs (tenantId → tenants, accountId → accounts, ON DELETE CASCADE) for scheduled_reports, drivers, rules, geofences, api_keys, webhooks and export_jobs in a new migration; short term, have accounts.remove delete the account's scheduled_reports and api_keys, and make listEnabled join accounts so an orphan can never dispatch.

**Subsystem:** schema / unique constraints · **Location:** `packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:325`

`imei String @unique` (schema.prisma:325) is a TOTAL unique index — it ignores `retiredAt`. `devices.retire` (packages/db/src/repos/devices.ts:129-136) is a pure soft delete that only stamps `retiredAt`, leaving the IMEI row in place. The claim path therefore always collides: `db.devices.create` catches P2002 and throws DuplicateImeiError (devices.ts:116), which apps/api/src/routes/quarantine.ts:83 turns into `409 IMEI already registered`. This directly contradicts the billing model documented in apps/worker/src/jobs/usageWorker.ts:25-27 ("a physical tracker re-claimed cross-tenant mid-day is a NEW device row, so both tenants are billed their own device-day"), which the schema makes impossible. Meanwhile `listAllForRegistry` filters `retiredAt: null` (devices.ts:93), so the retired tracker is unknown to ingest and lands in the quarantine list — offering the admin a Claim button that can only ever 409.

**failureScenario:** Tenant A's lease ends and the reseller retires device IMEI 350424061234567. The physical unit is re-fitted for tenant B and starts dialing in; ingest quarantines it and it shows up in the platform quarantine list. The platform_admin clicks Claim into tenant B → 409 "IMEI already registered", with no hint of why (the API deliberately does not leak the other tenant's row). The only unblock is running the GDPR erase job on tenant A's device, which destroys tenant A's entire trip/event/position history and its audit-visible device row — data tenant A may still be contractually owed.

**suggestedFix:** New append-only migration: drop `devices_imei_key` and create `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX devices_imei_active_key ON devices (imei) WHERE "retiredAt" IS NULL` (mirroring the tenant_domains partial-unique pattern in 20260708000000), keeping the Prisma model in sync via an @@index + documented raw index. Alternatively add an explicit "release IMEI" step to retire.
