### 92. [MEDIUM] account.timezone accepts any string with no IANA validation, and every consumer silently falls back to UTC — a typo permanently shifts all reports with a 200 OK

**Subsystem:** shared/db (reports) · **Location:** `packages/shared/src/entities.ts:11`

`accountCreateSchema.timezone` is `z.string().min(1).max(64).optional()` and `accountUpdateSchema` is its `.partial()` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:9-13); `PATCH /v1/accounts/:id` (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:227-233) writes it through unvalidated. Every reader then swallows an unresolvable zone: `safeTz` in packages/db/src/reports.ts:93-100 returns 'UTC' on an `Intl.DateTimeFormat` throw, and `safeZone` in apps/worker/src/format/localize.ts:20-27 does the same for scheduled-report tables and alert emails. I verified with the repo's Node 22.23.1 that `Intl.DateTimeFormat` rejects `'GMT+3'` and `'Europe/Vilnus'` (a plausible typo for Europe/Vilnius) while accepting `'+03:00'` — so a bad value is either silently downgraded to UTC or handed to Postgres `AT TIME ZONE` as an offset string, and the account row keeps displaying the wrong value the admin typed.

**failureScenario:** A TSP admin sets a sub-account's timezone to `Europe/Vilnus` (missing 'i') via the API. The PATCH returns 200 and `GET /v1/accounts/:id` echoes `Europe/Vilnus`, so the setting looks applied. `safeTz` cannot resolve it and returns 'UTC', so from that moment every mileage/stops/overspeed report and every emailed scheduled report for that account is day-bucketed 3 hours off, and the email footer prints "All times shown in Europe/Vilnus" (scheduledReporter.ts:95) while the timestamps are actually UTC. No error, no log line, no metric.

**suggestedFix:** Validate the zone at the API boundary with a `.refine()` that constructs `Intl.DateTimeFormat` (or checks `Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone')`) and reject with 400 otherwise; keep `safeTz`/`safeZone` as a last-resort guard but log a warning when they fire so an already-stored bad value is visible.

### 93. [MEDIUM] There is no record of which days have been overage-reported, so a daily job that exhausts its 5 retries loses the whole platform's overage revenue for that day, permanently

**Subsystem:** usage metering / overage billing · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/billing/usageReporter.ts:73`

The daily overage job computes its target day purely from the wall clock — `const day = utcDay(nowMs - 24 * 3_600_000)` (apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageWorker.ts:33) — and nothing persists which days have been successfully reported. The only durability is BullMQ retries: `attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 30_000 }` (apps/worker/src/jobs/stripeUsageQueue.ts:30-31), i.e. roughly 30s + 60s + 120s + 240s ≈ 7.5 minutes of total retry window, with `removeOnFail: 100`. The next tick 24 h later computes a NEW day and never revisits the failed one.

Critically, the first await in the job is `const subs = await deps.db.tenants.listActiveSubscribers()` (usageReporter.ts:73) — a Postgres read. A failure there aborts before any tenant is processed, so the whole platform's day is lost, not one tenant's. ### 94. [MEDIUM] XAUTOCLAIM's deleted-message list is discarded, so records ACKed to the device and then trimmed out of the stream vanish with no counter, log or dead-letter

**Subsystem:** worker · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/consumer.ts:153`

`ShardConsumer.autoclaim()` (apps/worker/src/consumer.ts:139-153) issues XAUTOCLAIM and types the reply correctly as `[Buffer, [Buffer, Buffer[]][], Buffer[]]` — the third element is Redis 7's list of pending message IDs that no longer exist in the stream. Line 153 returns only `res[1]` and drops `res[2]` on the floor.

Those IDs are precisely the entries that were XADDed, delivered to a consumer that died before XACK, and then removed by `MAXLEN ~ 100_000` trimming (apps/ingest/src/persist.ts:56-60) before the surviving consumer could reclaim them. Redis purges them from the PEL and reports them in `res[2]`; the code neither counts nor logs them. There is no `deadLettered` increment (that path only covers cbor/normalize failures, consumer.ts:186-199), no `raw:dead` entry, and no metric in apps/worker/src/prom.ts. Ingest already told the device those records were persisted (`encodeAck(persisted)`, apps/ingest/src/session.ts:263-271), so the device deleted them from its own buffer — I1 ("ACK count == records durably in stream") is violated after the fact, silently and unrecoverably.

**failureScenario:** Worker process A does XREADGROUP on raw:7, gets 200 entries into the PEL, and is OOM-killed (or loses its shard lease and is fenced at consumer.ts:105-108) before XACK. Ingest keeps writing to raw:7. Once 100 000 newer entries have been added — the exact burst the 100k MAXLEN is sized to absorb per PROJECT_PLAN §5 R8-4 — those 200 PEL ids are trimmed away. Thirty seconds later worker B's XAUTOCLAIM returns them in the third array; `autoclaim()` returns an empty `res[1]`, the loop treats the shard as clean, and 200 positions that the devices were told were durable are gone. `stats.deadLettered`, `raw:dead`, and every Prometheus counter stay at zero, so the loss is invisible in both metrics and logs.

**suggestedFix:** Read `res[2]` in apps/worker/src/consumer.ts:153: increment a dedicated counter (e.g. `stream_entries_lost_total{shard}`, exported from apps/worker/src/prom.ts alongside `stream_depth`), log the id range at error level, and add an alert rule in infra/prometheus/alerts.yml so post-ACK loss is never silent. Pair it with a bounded backlog guard (see the XLEN/backpressure finding) so trimming cannot outrun an unhealthy consumer in the first place.

### 95. [MEDIUM] `events` has no idempotency constraint and the rule-event replay guard is skipped entirely when a rule's cooldownS is 0

**Subsystem:** worker / db schema (events idempotency) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/rules/persister.ts:110`

`events` (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:495-515) has no unique index — the only replay protection for rule events is the Redis cooldown claim. `RulePersister`'s docblock states this explicitly: "Applies the per-rule cooldown as an atomic `SET NX EX` … so event emission is idempotent under the ACK-replay window (onBatch runs before XACK; a replayed batch re-emits, but the cooldown key already exists ⇒ no duplicate row)".

But `cooldownGate` filters with `const needsGate = events.filter((e) => !e.bypassCooldown && e.cooldownS > 0)` (line 110). A rule whose `cooldownS` is **0** therefore claims no key at all, and `persist()` inserts its events unconditionally. `cooldownS: 0` is explicitly accepted by the API (`packages/shared/src/entities.ts:175` — `z.number().int().min(0).max(86_400)`) and preserved by the cache (`apps/worker/src/rules/cache.ts:81` only defaults to 300 when the value is not a number). Contrast the geofence path, which claims a dedup key unconditionally with a fixed 24 h TTL (`apps/worker/src/geofence/persister.ts:16,72`).

Note the state-rewind does not save this either: `saveIoState` runs only after a successful persist, so a crash *after* persist and *before* XACK leaves the durable IO state advanced — but the replayed batch re-feeds records r1..r4 first, which resets the engine's `prev` back below the edge, so record r5 produces the same rising edge again.

**failureScenario:** An operator creates a `din_change` (or `ignition`) rule with cooldown 0 to capture every door-open edge. Worker shard 3 processes a batch: `writePositions` commits, `ruleEngine.feed` detects the edge, `writeRuleEvents` inserts the event row, notify/webhook are enqueued, `saveIoState` commits — then the worker is SIGKILLed (OOM, deploy) before `XACK`. Another worker's `XAUTOCLAIM` (60 s idle) redelivers the identical batch; the engine re-feeds the same records, re-detects the same edge, `cooldownGate` claims nothing because `cooldownS === 0`, and `writeRuleEvents` inserts a second `events` row for the same physical edge — with a second notification and a second webhook POST to the customer's endpoint. Nothing in the DB can dedupe it afterwards.

**suggestedFix:** Claim a dedup key for every rule event regardless of cooldown — e.g. always `SET NX EX` on `rule:evt:{ruleId}:{deviceId}:{at.getTime()}` with a fixed TTL (the geofence persister's pattern), and keep the cooldown key as a separate, additional gate. Longer term, give `events` a natural idempotency key (e.g. a unique index on `(deviceId, ruleId, kind, at)`) so replay safety does not depend on Redis surviving.

### 96. [MEDIUM] Hour-bucketed recompute jobId silently discards a later, wider reconciliation request — BullMQ keeps the first job's window and drops the new payload

**Subsystem:** worker / trip recompute enqueue (E04-2 late-data reconciliation) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/jobs/queue.ts:61`

`enqueueRecompute` derives `jobId: recompute-${deviceId}-${bucket}` where `bucket = from.toISOString().slice(0, 13)` — the hour of `from` (queue.ts:47, 61). BullMQ's `addStandardJob` Lua does `if rcall("EXISTS", jobIdKey) == 1 then return handleDuplicatedJob(...)` (verified in node_modules/.pnpm/bullmq@5.79.3/node_modules/bullmq/dist/cjs/scripts/addStandardJob-9.js:521-524): the second `add` is a no-op and the existing job keeps its original from/to data. The new, possibly much earlier `from` is thrown away.

The comment at queue.ts:55-57 assumes `removeOnComplete: true` frees the id fast enough that this only collapses "concurrent WAITING bursts". That does not hold for the deferred branch: main.ts:420-421 enqueues with `delayMs = settleAt - now`, up to the full RECOMPUTE_GUARD_MS of 15 minutes, so the jobId sits in the delayed set for that whole period. Any subsequent late signal for the same device whose `from` lands in the same hour is silently dropped — and `TripEngine.takeLate()` has already cleared the late map (trip/engine.ts:150-153), so the signal exists nowhere else. There is no error, no metric and no retry: `queue.add` resolves successfully.

The two windows are not interchangeable. The discarded request typically has the earlier `from`, and `recomputeTrips` only expands `coreFrom` to trips overlapping `[from, to]` (recompute.ts:78-82, 90), so a trip that ended before the surviving job's `from` is never in the bounds result and its region is never rebuilt.

**failureScenario:** At 10:02 a device sends a re-transmitted event record with fix_time 09:58 (older than the previous periodic fix). `takeLate()` yields from = 09:58; settledTo = 09:47, so 09:58 >= settledTo and main.ts:421 enqueues a delayed job with jobId `recompute-1234-2026-08-04T09`, data {from: 09:58, to: 10:13}, delay ~11 min. At 10:05 the same device reconnects after a real 30-minute GSM outage and flushes its buffer: records from 09:20 onward, all older than lastSeen, so the streaming trip engine drops every one of them (trip/engine.ts:178-182) and `takeLate()` yields from = 09:20. settledTo is now 09:50, so 09:20 < 09:50 and main.ts:423 calls `enqueueRecompute(..., 09:20, 09:50)` — same hour bucket "2026-08-04T09", same jobId, job already exists in the delayed set, so BullMQ returns the existing job and discards {from: 09:20}. Eleven minutes later the original job runs over [09:58, 10:13] only. The 09:20-09:58 buffered region — the exact data the streaming engine refused to process — is never reconciled: the customer's trip list keeps a 38-minute hole in mileage and trip segmentation that no later job will repair, because the late-map signal was consumed at 10:05.

**suggestedFix:** Stop relying on jobId collision to coalesce a window. Either (a) make the jobId unique per signal and coalesce inside the worker against a per-device `recompute:pending:{deviceId}` key holding min(from)/max(to), or (b) after `queue.add`, read back the existing job and, when its `from` is later than the requested one, update its data or enqueue a distinct job for the uncovered `[newFrom, existingFrom]` sub-range. At minimum, detect the duplicated return value and increment a metric so silently-dropped reconciliation signals are observable.

### 97. [MEDIUM] Orphaned GDPR export `.tmp` files are never swept — every deploy landing during an export leaves a full personal-data dump on the shared volume forever

**Subsystem:** worker/gdpr-export · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/jobs/gdprExportWorker.ts:53`

`runExport` writes the NDJSON.gz to `${finalPath}.${randomUUID()}.tmp` (gdprExportWorker.ts:53) and only renames it into place on success (:139). The `catch` block unlinks the temp file (:135), but that path is reached only for a thrown JS error. Any non-exception termination — SIGKILL, container OOM, or the worker's own hard `process.exit(1)` — skips it.

That is not hypothetical: the worker's SIGTERM handler awaits ~20 sequential shutdown steps (apps/worker/src/main.ts:457-492) including `await gdprExportWorker.close()`, behind a `setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 5_000)` (main.ts:493). An export of a real account streams every position row through gzip; it will not finish in 5 s, so the process force-exits mid-write on every deploy that overlaps an export. BullMQ's stalled-job recovery then re-runs the job, which allocates a *new* UUID temp path — so each interrupted attempt leaves one more orphan.

Nothing ever removes them. `runExportSweep` (:149-158) selects only `status = 'done' AND expiresAt < now()` and unlinks the recorded `row.path` — the final name. It never lists the directory, so `*.tmp` files are invisible to it. The api's lazy expiry unlink (apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts) likewise only knows `info.path`.

**failureScenario:** A tenant admin requests a GDPR export for a 300-device account; the job starts streaming ~40 GB of positions into gzip. Ninety seconds later a release is deployed (`docker compose up -d`), the worker gets SIGTERM, the 5 s budget expires and it `process.exit(1)`s with a multi-GB `<id>.ndjson.gz.<uuid>.tmp` on the `exports` named volume. BullMQ recovers the stalled job and re-runs it with a fresh UUID; the first orphan stays. Two consequences: (1) the volume — which shares the root filesystem with the Postgres data directory — fills with partial personal-data dumps that no sweep removes, and `DiskFillingUp` is the first thing anyone hears about it; (2) the orphan is raw personal data (lat/lon histories, user emails) that outlives the 7-day `expiresAt` retention the export flow promises, indefinitely.

**suggestedFix:** Have `runExportSweep` also `readdir(exportDir)` and unlink any `*.tmp` whose mtime is older than a safe threshold (e.g. 6 h, comfortably longer than the longest export), in addition to the row-driven unlink. Separately, raise the worker's SIGTERM budget or move `gdprExportWorker.close()` ahead of the long chain in apps/worker/src/main.ts:483 so a normal deploy does not routinely kill exports mid-write.

### 98. [MEDIUM] pipeline_lag_ms measures device clock skew, not pipeline lag — buffered devices page a false critical and a fast device clock silently zeroes the gauge

**Subsystem:** worker/observability · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/main.ts:292`

`onBatch` sets the SLO gauge as `prom.setLagMs(Math.max(0, Date.now() - newestMs))` where `newestMs = records[records.length-1].fixTime.getTime()` (apps/worker/src/main.ts:291-292). Two mismatches with what the metric is documented and alerted as: (1) it uses **fix_time** (device clock) although `NormalizedRecord.serverTime` — the ingest receive instant, written to `positions.server_time` — is available on every record (apps/worker/src/normalize.ts:64-65); (2) it uses the **newest** record while infra/prometheus/alerts.yml describes it as "age of the oldest unprocessed record" and both alert descriptions read "Oldest unprocessed record is >30s old". The gauge is a single unlabelled global (apps/worker/src/prom.ts:64-68) shared by all 16 shard consumers, so the last batch processed anywhere wins. Ingest's sanity filter accepts fix_time up to now+48 h (apps/ingest/src/persist.ts `isSaneRecord`), so a future-dated device produces a negative value that `Math.max(0, …)` clamps to 0.

**failureScenario:** (a) One fleet vehicle returns from a 6 h coverage gap and flushes its buffer. The last batch's newest fixTime is ~6 h old, so `pipeline_lag_ms` jumps to ~21,600,000 and stays above 120,000 for the duration of the flush → `PipelineLagCritical` pages the founders with the instruction "do NOT run GDPR erase", while the pipeline is in fact healthy. (b) Inversely, a single tracker whose RTC is 2 h fast reports every 30 s; every batch it lands in sets the gauge to 0 via the clamp. Prometheus scrapes 0 even while a genuine shard stall has the worker minutes behind, so `PipelineLagHigh`/`Critical` never fire and the real backlog is invisible.

**suggestedFix:** Compute lag from `server_time`, not `fix_time`, and from the oldest record in the batch: `prom.setLagMs(Math.max(0, Date.now() - records[0].serverTime.getTime()))`. Label the gauge by shard so one healthy shard cannot mask another, and update the `help` string plus the alerts.yml comments to match.

### 99. [MEDIUM] A trip-persist DB error loses the close event AND skips the takeLate()/recompute enqueue that is supposed to compensate for it

**Subsystem:** worker/pipeline (durability) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/main.ts:313`

`await tripPersister.apply(tripEvents)` (line 313) sits inside the big try whose catch is at lines 430-436. A throw there means:
- the `TripEngine` has already consumed the close (`engine.ts:320-322` sets `phase='parked'`, `trip=null`), so the close event is gone from memory and will never be re-emitted;
- the DB row for that trip is still `status='open'` (or, if `openTrip` was the failing call, there is no row while the engine believes a trip is open, so the eventual close silently `continue`s at `persister.ts:47`);
- the `takeLate()` drain and `enqueueRecompute` loop at lines 411-429 are skipped entirely, so even if the batch DID contain late records, their reconciliation signal is not enqueued this pass.
The only trace is `prom.tripPersistErrors.inc()`, whose help text claims "advisory; E04-2 recompute reconciles" (`prom.ts:81`) — but as established above, recompute is never triggered for this case.

**failureScenario:** A 5-second Postgres failover during a batch containing device D's trip close. `closeTrip` throws, control jumps to the outer catch. D's trip row remains open forever (see the orphaned-open-trips finding), the closed trip and its distance/idle figures are never written, and no recompute job is created to rebuild them from the durable positions that ARE present. Mileage and engine-hours for D are permanently wrong for that day even though the raw data is intact.

**suggestedFix:** Wrap the trip block in its own try (as the geofence and rule blocks already are), and on failure enqueue a recompute for `[trip.startTime, now - RECOMPUTE_GUARD_MS]` for the affected device so the durable positions are replayed authoritatively. Move the `takeLate()`/enqueue loop into a `finally` so it always runs.

**Subsystem:** worker/pipeline (durability) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/main.ts:421`

The realistic rejections are (a) a command in flight when the socket resets — Redis restart/failover, and (b) `OOM command not allowed` under `maxmemory-policy noeviction` (which `queue.ts:7-9` explicitly requires). (b) is precisely correlated with a buffered flood: `LPUSH`/`HSET` behind `queue.add` are denyoom while `XACK` is not, so the enqueue fails while the batch is still ACKed and never redelivered — permanent loss, no replay rescue.\n- Blast radius is usually smaller than "3 days". `consumer.ts:206` fixTime-sorts each batch, so late-ness is a cross-batch property, and each subsequent batch of the same backlog re-registers a fresh signal. With LIFO device sorting the successive `from` values move *earlier*, so a later job\'s window subsumes the failed one (self-healing). With FIFO/live-then-backlog ordering the successive `from` values move *later*, so a single failure permanently loses roughly one batch\'s worth of window (batchSize 200, `consumer.ts:158`) — minutes to a couple of hours of trips for that device. The full multi-day hole requires the failure to persist across the whole flush, which is exactly what a sustained OOM/failover does.\n\nWHY IT STILL LANDS: silent-by-default (only the generic `tripPersistErrors` counter moves, shared with the outer trip-persist swallow at main.ts:434), zero automatic reconciliation, permanent wrong customer-facing mileage data, and a trivial fix — have the catch re-register the signal on the engine (an `addLate(deviceId, from)` that keeps the earliest time, mirroring engine.ts:180-181) so the next batch retries, instead of dropping it. Severity medium is fair.']

### 101. [MEDIUM] Redis connections leak one per shard re-acquire — `consumerConns` is append-only and never disconnected outside SIGTERM

**Subsystem:** worker/shard-leasing (resource exhaustion) · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/main.ts:446`

`startShardConsumer` creates a dedicated connection per consumer and records it:
```
const conn = redis.duplicate()
consumerConns.push(conn)   // line 446
```
Nothing ever removes or disconnects an entry: the leaser's `onLost` (lines 74-80) calls `stop()` and deletes from `consumersByShard` only; `onLostOwnership` (lines 284-288) only deletes from the map; `ShardConsumer.fence()` (`consumer.ts:105-109`) does not touch the connection. The array is only drained in the SIGTERM handler (`main.ts:488`). Every lease flap therefore permanently leaks one ioredis connection (plus its socket, buffers and reconnect timers), and the leaked consumer's stopped loop leaves it idle but open.

**failureScenario:** A worker under load flaps shards a few times per hour (each 30 s lease lapse costs one connection per affected shard — up to 16 per flap). Over a multi-day uptime the process accumulates hundreds of idle Redis connections and eventually hits Redis `maxclients`. New connections are refused — which takes down ingest (which shares the same Redis) and every BullMQ worker, not just this process. The failure looks like a Redis outage with no Redis-side cause.

**suggestedFix:** Track the connection alongside the consumer (`Map<number, {consumer, conn}>`) and call `conn.disconnect()` in `onLost`/`onLostOwnership` after `stop()` resolves; drop the append-only `consumerConns` array.

Because the map entry was deleted, the `has(s)` guard at line 444 does not short-circuit, so a fresh `redis.duplicate()` is created. `apps/worker/__tests__/shards.spec.ts:34-51` and `:68-76` prove both callbacks fire in exactly this lose→regain sequence. ### 102. [MEDIUM] Recompute deletes closed trips by startTime, so a trip closed by the streaming persister mid-job is erased and never re-inserted

**Subsystem:** worker/trips · **Location:** `apps/worker/src/trip/recompute.ts:134`

`recomputeTrips` reads `bounds` (line 78) and `positions` (line 96) on the POOL, outside any transaction, replays the engine, and only then opens the transaction (line 123) that runs

```sql
DELETE FROM trips WHERE "deviceId"=$1 AND status='closed' AND "startTime" >= $2 AND "startTime" <= $3   -- [coreFrom, coreTo]
```

The safety argument (header comment lines 76-77 and main.ts's `RECOMPUTE_GUARD_MS`) is "recompute only rebuilds CLOSED trips, so it never races the live open trip." That guard is applied to the WINDOW END (`to = now − 15 min`), but the DELETE predicate is on `startTime`, not `endTime` — and a row's `status` can flip from `open` to `closed` between the read and the DELETE (`closeTrip`, apps/worker/src/trip/writer.ts, is a plain `UPDATE trips SET status='closed' … WHERE id=$1 AND status='open'`).

A trip that started before `to` and is still open when `positions` is read is dropped from the recomputed set on purpose (line 106-110 keeps only `close` events, and its close confirmation lies beyond `readTo = coreTo + margin`). If the streaming persister closes it before the transaction runs, it now matches the DELETE predicate (`status='closed'`, `startTime ∈ [coreFrom, coreTo]`) and is removed — with no replacement row, because the engine never produced a close event for it. Nothing re-creates it: `TripPersister.openIds` already dropped the device entry, and recompute only re-runs when new late data arrives.

**failureScenario:** A van has been driving for 40 minutes (open trip, startTime = T−40 min). A buffered flush arrives, `takeLate()` fires, and a recompute is enqueued with `to = settledTo = T−15 min`; `coreTo` is therefore ≥ T−15 min, well after the trip's startTime. The job reads several hours of positions (no LIMIT), taking a few seconds; during that read the van parks and the streaming pipeline closes the trip. The transaction then DELETEs the just-closed trip and inserts only the older trips the replay produced. The completed 40-minute trip disappears from the device's trip list, from the trips report and from the driver's distance totals, with no error logged anywhere — `deleted` simply exceeds `created` by one.

**suggestedFix:** Take a per-device serialization point that also covers the streaming close (e.g. `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(deviceId)` at the top of the transaction, taken by both `recomputeTrips` and `TripPersister.apply`), and move the bounds + positions read INSIDE that transaction so the replayed set and the deleted set come from the same snapshot. Alternatively, restrict the DELETE to rows whose `endTime <= readTo` (or `createdAt <` the job's read instant) so a trip closed after the read is never deleted.

The reads are on the POOL, outside the transaction.** `bounds` at recompute.ts:78-82 (and it only sees `status=\'closed\'`, so a live open trip is invisible to it), `positions` at recompute.ts:96-100. The transaction does not begin until recompute.ts:123. Nothing re-reads `bounds` or re-checks status inside the transaction. No `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, and `grep -rn "advisory"` over the repo shows the only advisory lock in the codebase is in `packages/db/src/repos/tenants.ts:152` (signup), nothing in the trip path.\n\n**3. ### 103. [LOW] PATCH /v1/devices/:id does not validate profileId, and Prisma P2003 is unmapped — an unknown profile uuid returns a raw 500

**Subsystem:** api / db error mapping · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:403`

`deviceUpdateSchema` (packages/shared/src/entities.ts:59) accepts `profileId: z.string().uuid()`, and the PATCH handler passes the body straight to `db.devices.update` → `prisma.device.update({ where: { id: before.id }, data })` (packages/db/src/repos/devices.ts:120). `devices.profileId` has an FK to `device_profiles` (`0_init` — `devices_profileId_fkey`), so a well-formed but non-existent uuid raises Prisma P2003.

`dbErrorHttp` (packages/db/src/errors.ts:19-27) maps only P2025/P2023 → 404 and P2002 → 409; P2003 falls through to `null`, so `app.onError` returns an untyped 500. The POST handler was explicitly hardened against exactly this (crud.ts:382-383: "validate the (global) profile — a bad uuid would else be a P2003 500 (review MED)"); the PATCH path was missed.

The same gap makes the `commissions` RESTRICT FK comment in `20260804090000_commission_ledger_integrity/migration.sql` inaccurate — it claims "the API turns the resulting FK violation into a 409", which is only true because `tenants.remove` added an explicit pre-count guard, not because P2003 is mapped.

**failureScenario:** An integrator syncing device profiles via the API PATCHes `/v1/devices/42` with `{"profileId":"3f2a…"}` copied from a stale/other-environment profile list. Instead of a 400 "unknown profileId" (what POST returns), the API answers 500 with no problem detail; the client's retry loop hammers the same 500 and the operator has no signal that the profile id is simply wrong.

**suggestedFix:** Mirror the POST guard in the PATCH handler (`if (data.profileId !== undefined && (await db.profiles.get(data.profileId)) === null) return problem(c, 400, 'Bad Request', 'unknown profileId')`), and add `case 'P2003': return { status: 409, title: 'Conflict' }` to `dbErrorHttp` so any remaining FK violation degrades to a typed 409 rather than a 500.

**verifierNotes:** ['CONFIRMED: CONFIRMED — I reproduced the exact Prisma error against a real migrated database.\n\nCode chain (all read, no speculation):\n\n1. `packages/shared/src/entities.ts:52-61` — `deviceUpdateSchema` is `z.object({... profileId: z.string().uuid() ...}).partial()`, so a well-formed but unknown uuid passes validation.\n2. `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:403-408` — the PATCH handler validates only against the zod schema and passes `data` straight through: `const row = await db.devices.update(scopeOf(auth(c)), { userId: auth(c).userId }, id(c), data)`. ### 104. [LOW] A Redis failure during CSV import aborts the batch mid-loop, leaving already-created devices invisible to ingest with no report to the caller

**Subsystem:** api/devices · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/deviceImport.ts:190`

`applyImport` loops over `dr.create` and, per row, does `db.devices.create(...)` then `await activateDevice(redis, ...)` (line 190). The per-row `catch` (line 195-197) only converts `DuplicateImeiError` into a row error and RETHROWS everything else, so a Redis failure inside `activateDevice` aborts the whole loop.

Two consequences follow from the abort. First, every device inserted by an earlier iteration is committed in Postgres but never written to `registry:imei` / `device:tenant` / `device:account` / `device:config` — ingest rejects those IMEIs on handshake and quarantines them, silently discarding their data. Second, the exception propagates as a 500, so the caller loses the `{created, errors}` report entirely and has no way to learn which rows were applied; re-uploading the same CSV yields `IMEI already registered` for exactly those rows.

The registry entries do self-heal, but only on the next API process start (`rehydrateRegistries`, apps/api/src/rehydrate.ts:24-31) — potentially weeks later. Note that every other Redis sync in the device/geofence/rule/driver CRUD path is deliberately routed through `bestEffortSync` (routes/crud.ts:66-72) for exactly this reason; the import path is not.

**failureScenario:** An installer imports a 400-row CSV for a new customer. Redis stalls (failover, `MISCONF`, connection reset) at row 137. Rows 1-136 are in `devices` but absent from `registry:imei`. The API returns 500; the installer sees a generic failure and re-uploads, and now 136 rows come back as `IMEI already registered` while the trackers he installs on those 136 vehicles hand-shake, are rejected as unknown, and pile into `quarantine:imei` — the fleet appears completely dead for those vehicles until someone restarts the API pod.

**suggestedFix:** Route `activateDevice` through the same `bestEffortSync` wrapper used by the rest of the device CRUD (routes/crud.ts:66), or catch its error per row, push it into `errors` as `registry sync failed (retry)`, and keep going — so the caller always receives the `{created, errors}` report.

### 105. [LOW] Device retire tears down the Redis registry before the DB write, so a failed retire leaves a live, billable device that ingest silently quarantines

**Subsystem:** api/devices · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/crud.ts:425`

`DELETE /v1/devices/:id` does `await deactivateDevice(deps.redis, ...)` (line 425) and only then `await db.devices.retire(...)` (line 426). The in-code rationale (lines 419-421) reasons about one direction only — "Registry FIRST so a Redis failure leaves the device consistently active-in-both" — and never considers the other: if the Redis MULTI succeeds and the DB write fails, the device is de-registered from ingest while `retiredAt` stays NULL.

In that state the device is simultaneously (a) rejected on every handshake by `registry.lookup` and dumped into `quarantine:imei`, with every position it sends discarded, and (b) fully live in Postgres — counted by `db.devices.countActive` against the tenant's plan cap, swept into `usage_daily` only if positions arrive (they no longer do), and shown as an active device in the UI. Nothing reconciles it until an API process restarts and `rehydrateRegistries` (apps/api/src/rehydrate.ts:24-31) re-adds it from the DB.

**failureScenario:** An admin retires a vehicle that has just been sold. `deactivateDevice` succeeds; `db.devices.retire` then hits a pg pool timeout and 500s. The admin sees an error, assumes nothing happened, and moves on without retrying. The device now reports into `quarantine:imei` forever: the fleet manager sees a vehicle that stopped reporting weeks ago with no alert (its `device_offline` rule cannot fire either — `runOfflineSweep` iterates `device:tenant`, from which it has been removed), while the tenant keeps paying for a device slot that produces nothing. A platform admin reviewing quarantine sees an unknown IMEI and may re-claim it into the wrong tenant.

**suggestedFix:** Do the DB soft-delete FIRST and the registry teardown second (a device flagged retired but still in the registry is the safe direction — ingest's per-frame re-check plus the next rehydrate converge), or make the Redis teardown best-effort with a reconcile marker so a partial retire is retried rather than silently stranded.

Note that the file *has* a swallow-errors helper for exactly this class of dual-write (`bestEffortSync`, crud.ts:66-72), and it is deliberately NOT used here — line 425 is a bare `await`, so a Redis failure 500s before the DB write (the direction the comment reasons about), and a DB failure at 426 throws after the Redis MULTI has already committed (the direction it does not).\n\n`deactivateDevice` (apps/api/src/routes/deviceRegistry.ts:40-50) is a MULTI that removes `registry:imei`, `device:tenant`, `device:account`, `device:config` and `device:{id}:last`. `retire` (packages/db/src/repos/devices.ts:129-136) does `scopedById` → `prisma.device.update` → `audit.record`, not wrapped in a transaction. ### 106. [LOW] API graceful shutdown is dead code whenever a WebSocket client is connected — the process hard-exits at 5 s without draining Redis/pg/Prisma

**Subsystem:** api/shutdown · **Location:** `apps/api/src/main.ts:132`

`httpServer.close(cb)` only invokes its callback when the server's connection count reaches zero. `attachWsGateway` registers `server.on('upgrade', …)` on the same `httpServer` (`apps/api/src/ws.ts:166`) and upgraded sockets remain counted in `net.Server._connections` until destroyed, so with any dashboard tab open the callback never fires and the `redis.quit() → redisSub.quit() → gdprEraseQueue.close() → … → pool.end() → db.$disconnect() → process.exit(0)` chain never runs. The only thing that terminates the process is `setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 5_000)` on line 143. Nothing calls `wss.close()` or `httpServer.closeAllConnections()`, so WS clients are never told to reconnect. `infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml` sets no `stop_grace_period`, so Docker's 10 s default never gets a chance to matter.

**failureScenario:** A deploy restarts the api while a fleet manager is mid-`POST /v1/devices/import` (3 MB CSV, up to a few seconds of Prisma writes) and three dashboards hold WS streams. `httpServer.close()` stops accepting new connections but its callback is never reached; 5 s later `process.exit(0)` kills the process mid-transaction. The pg pool and Prisma client are never drained, so their backends are torn down by TCP reset rather than a clean `Terminate`, and the WS clients see an abrupt socket close instead of a normal-closure frame.

**suggestedFix:** On SIGTERM: call `wss.close()` and `httpServer.closeAllConnections()` (or `closeIdleConnections()` then a short grace before `closeAllConnections()`), run the resource-teardown chain unconditionally rather than inside the `close` callback, and set an explicit `stop_grace_period` in the compose file that exceeds the internal timer.

### 107. [LOW] caddy-ask's rate-limit eval is unguarded, so a Redis blip 500s the on-demand-TLS gate and blocks every white-label certificate

**Subsystem:** api/tls · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/caddyAsk.ts:55`

`GET /v1/internal/caddy-ask` runs `await deps.redis.eval(RL_SCRIPT, …)` (line 55) with no try/catch. A Redis error therefore propagates to `app.onError` and returns 500. Caddy's `on_demand_tls ask` mints/renews a certificate only on a 2xx, so a 500 is a hard deny.

The asymmetry is the point: the two sibling PUBLIC limiters in this very file and its neighbour explicitly fail OPEN with a documented rationale — `/v1/public/share/:token` (caddyAsk.ts:88-94, "fail OPEN on a Redis blip — a public read is low-value; availability wins") and `/v1/routing/optimize` (routes/routing.ts:52-57). The one endpoint whose denial has a multi-day, self-inflicted consequence (a cert that cannot be issued or renewed) is the one with no catch at all.

**failureScenario:** Redis is unavailable for 20 minutes during maintenance. A tenant's custom domain `fleet.customer.lt` has a certificate expiring that day; Caddy's renewal ask returns 500 instead of 200, so ACME renewal is refused. Caddy backs off and, on a domain whose cert lapses in that window, the tenant's white-label dashboard serves a browser TLS error — a full outage for that tenant caused by a rate limiter, not by the domain being unverified. New tenant onboarding (first-time issuance) is blocked for the whole outage window too.

**suggestedFix:** Wrap the eval in try/catch and, on a Redis error, skip the throttle and fall through to the authoritative `isVerifiedDomain` check (fail open on the LIMITER, never on the verification), matching the documented posture of the share and routing limiters in the same codebase.

### 108. [LOW] Password reset consumes the single-use token and writes the new password before revoking sessions — a failure in between leaves old sessions live and the reset link burned

**Subsystem:** auth/session-revocation · **Location:** `apps/api/src/auth/login.ts:391`

`POST /v1/auth/reset-password` executes five independent awaits with no transaction and no compensating action: `passwordResetTokens.consume` (login.ts:387, atomically single-use), `users.setPassword` (:391), `passwordResetTokens.invalidateAllForUser` (:392), `revokeAllUserSessions` (:394) and `markSessionsRevoked` (:395). The security-relevant half — evicting existing sessions — runs last, so any throw at :392 or :394 propagates to `app.onError` (app.ts:125-135) as a 500 *after* the token has been consumed and the password already changed.

`POST /v1/auth/password` has the same ordering (setPassword at :297, revoke at :306, markSessionsRevoked at :309).

All of these share the same Prisma pool, so a pool-timeout (`P2024`) or a transient DB fault under load is the realistic trigger — and `dbErrorHttp` does not map it, so it surfaces as an opaque 500.

**failureScenario:** A user whose account was compromised clicks their reset link. `consume` burns the token, `setPassword` writes the new hash, then `revokeAllUserSessions` hits a Prisma connection-pool timeout under load and throws. The handler 500s. From the user's perspective the reset "failed", but their password has in fact changed and their one-time link is now dead, so retrying the link returns `400 invalid or expired token`. Meanwhile the attacker's refresh families were never revoked and no `ws:revoke` marker was written, so the attacker's session and any live WebSocket stream survive the reset entirely — the exact outcome the flow exists to prevent.

**suggestedFix:** Invert the order so the eviction is durable before the credential change is observable: revoke refresh families and write the `ws:revoke` marker first, then `setPassword`. Better, wrap `consume` + `setPassword` + `invalidateAllForUser` + `revokeAllForUser` in a single `prisma.$transaction` so a failure rolls the token back to unused, and treat `markSessionsRevoked` as the only best-effort step (it already swallows its own errors, ws.ts:43-47).

And the natural user response to the 500 — request a fresh link and redeem it — runs the full revoke path successfully and closes the exposure. Absent a compromise, the residual harm is a confusing state (password silently changed while the UI says it failed, dead link, and on `/password` a retry that now answers "current password is wrong") — a support incident, not data loss or money.\n\nReal defect, correctly located, worth the cheap reorder; but the consequential version of it depends on an infrastructure fault coinciding with an active compromise and has a plausible recovery path. Low severity is right; PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED.']

### 109. [LOW] The self-referral guard compares raw email domains, so a partner on a free-mail address silently loses commission on every referral who also uses that provider

**Subsystem:** commissions / referral attribution · **Location:** `apps/api/src/routes/signup.ts:95`

`signup.ts:94-97` drops referral attribution whenever the signing-up user's email domain equals the affiliate's:

```
const domainOf = (e: string) => e.slice(e.lastIndexOf('@') + 1).toLowerCase()
const selfReferral = candidate !== null && domainOf(candidate.email) === domainOf(email)
```

The check has no notion of free-mail / shared-domain providers, and `Affiliate.email` is a plain string with no domain policy (schema.prisma:128) — `POST /v1/affiliates` (crud.ts:1264) accepts any address. When the affiliate is registered as `jonas@gmail.com`, every referred customer signing up with a `@gmail.com` address is classified as a self-referral. The tenant is created normally and `referredByAffiliateId` is set to null, so `accrueForPaidInvoice` returns at `tenant.referredByAffiliateId === null` (packages/db/src/repos/affiliates.ts:163) forever after. The only trace is `console.warn('signup: self-referral attribution dropped', candidate.code)` (signup.ts:96) — the partner sees nothing, and the tenant row carries no marker, so it cannot be reconciled later.

**failureScenario:** A partner is onboarded with the address they gave the founder, `jonas@gmail.com`. They promote `?ref=JONAS12`. Small-fleet owners — the exact Direct/`direct_10` self-serve segment this signup path targets — overwhelmingly sign up with gmail/outlook addresses. Every one of those signups is silently classified as a self-referral: attribution dropped, no commission ever accrues, no row records that a referral was attempted. The partner reports "my link doesn't work", but `/v1/partner/commissions` is legitimately empty and the tenant rows show `referredByAffiliateId = null`, so there is no evidence to reconstruct the lost payouts. A minority of referrals (those on corporate domains) do work, which makes the bug look like weak conversion rather than a defect.

**suggestedFix:** Exempt public free-mail domains from the heuristic (a small denylist of gmail/outlook/yahoo/proton/icloud/… means "same domain proves nothing"), or anchor the self-referral test on something the partner actually controls — compare the signup email to the affiliate's exact email, or require affiliates to register a corporate domain and apply the domain rule only then. Either way, persist the dropped-attribution decision (e.g. a nullable `attributionBlockedReason` on the tenant) so a partner dispute is reconcilable instead of living only in a log line.

### 110. [LOW] The documented staging/prod compose stack publishes Caddy on 8088/8449 in addition to 80/443, past the UFW policy; `ports: []` for pg/redis is a silent no-op

**Subsystem:** infra/compose-exposure · **Location:** `infra/compose/docker-compose.yml:167`

Compose concatenates the `ports` sequence across override files rather than replacing it. The base file publishes caddy on `${CADDY_HTTP_PORT:-8088}:80` and `${CADDY_HTTPS_PORT:-8449}:443` with no host-IP prefix, i.e. 0.0.0.0 (docker-compose.yml:167-168), and docker-compose.staging.yml:28-31 *adds* `80:80` and `443:443`. Verified with `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.apps.yml -f docker-compose.staging.yml config` (the exact three-file invocation documented in docker-compose.staging.yml:5): caddy resolves to four published ports — 8088→80, 8449→443, 80→80, 443→443, all unbound.

The ansible UFW role opens only 22/80/443/5027 (infra/ansible/roles/ufw/tasks/main.yml), and the base compose's own header warns that "Docker publishes ports by inserting iptables rules that BYPASS UFW, so every internal service binds 127.0.0.1". Caddy is the one service with no bind address, so 8088 and 8449 are reachable from the internet even though UFW's deny-default says otherwise.

The same merge semantics make the staging overrides `pg: ports: []` (staging.yml:8) and `redis: ports: []` (:11) no-ops — the merged config still shows `127.0.0.1:5432` and `127.0.0.1:6379`. Harmless today only because the base already loopback-pins them, but the comment "not exposed publicly on staging" documents a removal that does not happen.

**failureScenario:** A prod host is provisioned with the ansible playbook (UFW allows 22/80/443/5027 only) and brought up with the documented three-file compose invocation, but `/opt/orbetra/.env` omits `CADDY_HTTP_PORT`/`CADDY_HTTPS_PORT` (they are only mentioned in the staging runbook's one-time-prep list, not enforced anywhere). Docker inserts DNAT rules for 0.0.0.0:8088 and 0.0.0.0:8449 that UFW never sees. The operator's port scan of the firewall config says only 22/80/443/5027 are open; an external scan finds the full application — including the whole `/v1` API surface — served over plain HTTP on 8088, outside any HSTS/redirect assumption made for port 80, and not covered by the blackbox TLS probe.

**suggestedFix:** Give the base caddy publish an explicit intent: either bind it to `127.0.0.1` like every other service and let the staging/prod overlay be the only file that publishes 0.0.0.0:80/443, or drop the `CADDY_HTTP_PORT`/`CADDY_HTTPS_PORT` defaults from the base and require them. Replace the `ports: []` lines in docker-compose.staging.yml with a comment stating that the base already loopback-binds pg/redis, since the empty list removes nothing.

The merged caddy service resolves to FOUR published ports, all with host_ip null (0.0.0.0): 8088→80, 8449→443, 80→80, 443→443. Compose appends the `ports` sequence across override files; it does not replace it. ### 111. [LOW] events/audit/webhookDeliveries coerce cursors and deviceId with bare BigInt() instead of toInt8OrNull, so an oversize numeric query param returns 500 instead of a clean response

**Subsystem:** packages/db — bigint id/cursor coercion · **Location:** `packages/db/src/repos/events.ts:42`

packages/db/src/bigid.ts:5-11 documents the house rule verbatim: "BigInt('999…') never throws — it happily makes a value larger than int8, which then explodes as 'bigint out of range' when bound as a query param (a 500). Every `:id`/deviceId coercion must go through this so an oversize id becomes a clean 404, not a 500." Three read repos bypass it, gating only on the digit regex and then calling `BigInt()` directly:
- packages/db/src/repos/events.ts:37 (`deviceId`), :42 (`cursor`), :45 (`get` by id)
- packages/db/src/repos/audit.ts:68 (`cursor`), :72 (`get` by id)
- packages/db/src/repos/webhookDeliveries.ts:61 (`cursor`)

By contrast trips.ts:48,57 and positions.ts:33 correctly use `toInt8OrNull`, and crud.ts:899 uses `toDeviceId` with the comment 'toDeviceId range-guards int8 (a huge-but-numeric id must not 500)'. The route-level guard at crud.ts:1133 (`/^\d+$/`) is the same insufficient check. The resulting Prisma error (P2033 / bigint-out-of-range) is not in `dbErrorHttp`'s switch (packages/db/src/errors.ts:19-27), so app.onError falls through to `console.error('unhandled API error')` + a raw 500 (app.ts:133-134).

**failureScenario:** Any authenticated caller — including a read-only API key — requests `GET /v1/events?cursor=99999999999999999999` (or `?deviceId=99999999999999999999`, `GET /v1/audit?cursor=…`, `GET /v1/audit/99999999999999999999`, `GET /v1/webhook-deliveries?cursor=…`). The regex passes, `BigInt()` produces a value beyond int8, Prisma rejects it, and the client gets a 500 with an 'unhandled API error' stack in the logs instead of an empty page / 404. Repeated calls pollute error logs and any 5xx-based alerting with attacker-controlled noise.

**suggestedFix:** Replace the local `numeric()`/`/^\d+$/` + `BigInt()` pairs in events.ts:37,42,45, audit.ts:68,72 and webhookDeliveries.ts:61 with `toInt8OrNull` from packages/db/src/bigid.ts, treating null as 'no cursor / no filter / not found' — exactly the pattern trips.ts:48,57 already uses. Optionally also map P2033 in packages/db/src/errors.ts:19-27 as a safety net.

### 112. [LOW] 7-day event sparklines are built from a truncated 300-row page with no truncation guard, so older days silently render as zero

**Subsystem:** web/dashboard · **Location:** `apps/web/src/routes/app/dashboard.tsx:84`

`events7` fetches `listEvents({ from: weekAgo, limit: EVENTS_CAP })` with `EVENTS_CAP = 300` (apps/web/src/routes/app/dashboard.tsx:47, 25) and the repo returns them newest-first (packages/db/src/repos/events.ts:39). The page computes `trunc7 = rows7.length >= EVENTS_CAP` (line 75) and correctly surfaces it on the donut and the hourly histogram via the `dash.sampled` note (lines 218, 229, 252). `eventsSpark` and `criticalSpark` — the per-day series rendered on the StatCards (lines 84-85, consumed at 148 and 157) — use the same truncated `rows7` with no guard, and `dailyCounts` returns 0 for any day key it finds no events for (apps/web/src/lib/dashboard.ts:148-154).

**failureScenario:** A 60-device fleet with ignition rules enabled generates well over 300 events per week. The 300 newest all fall in the last ~day, so `dailyCounts(rows7, 7, now, dayOfTz)` yields something like [0,0,0,0,0,0,300]: the sparkline under "Events (24 h)" draws a flat line that explodes on the final day, reading as an incident spike when event volume has actually been constant all week. Unlike the donut and hourly chart next to it, nothing marks the series as sampled.

**suggestedFix:** Either suppress the sparks when `trunc7` is true (same pattern as the existing `spark:` conditional spreads), or drive the daily series from a server-side aggregate rather than a capped row page.

**verifierNotes:** ['CONFIRMED: Every mechanical link in the claim checks out in the code I read, and I could not find a guard, a test, or a UI cue that neutralizes it.\n\n1. Truncated fetch. `apps/web/src/routes/app/dashboard.tsx:47` — `events7 = useQuery({... listEvents({ from: weekAgo, limit: EVENTS_CAP })})` with `EVENTS_CAP = 300` (line 25) and `weekAgo = now - 7d` (line 38). The client just forwards `limit` into the query string (`apps/web/src/lib/events.ts:35,40`).\n\n2. The 300 rows are the NEWEST ones, not a spread over the week. `packages/db/src/repos/events.ts:40` — `orderBy: { id: \'desc\' }`, `take` clamped at line 32. Descending insertion id means the returned page is the most recently inserted 300 events, which for pipeline-generated events tracks `at` closely. So on a high-volume tenant the whole page collapses into the last day or two, and days 1-6 of the window are simply absent from `rows7`.\n\n3. The truncation flag exists and is deliberately surfaced — but only on two of four consumers. `trunc7 = rows7.length >= EVENTS_CAP` (dashboard.tsx:75) drives the "sampled" note on the donut header (line 218) and the hourly-histogram header (line 252), and the donut center renders `floor(rows7.length, trunc7)` → "300+" (line 229). The comment at lines 215-217 states the intent explicitly ("when that window is full the per-kind/hour numbers are a SAMPLE ... so say so"). The two spark series computed from the same `rows7` at lines 84-85 get no such treatment: they are passed straight into the StatCards at line 148 (`eventsSpark.some((n) => n > 0) ? { spark: eventsSpark }`) and line 157 (`criticalSpark...`), whose hints are the unconditional `t(\'dash.vsPrev24\')` ("vs. prior 24 h", en.json:980) — nothing marks them sampled. The `trunc24 || truncPrev` guard at lines 78-79 suppresses only the numeric delta, never the spark.\n\n4. Missing days silently become zero rather than "unknown". `apps/web/src/lib/dashboard.ts:148-154`: `counts` is pre-seeded to 0 for all 7 day keys and only incremented for rows present in the input, then `keys.map((k) => counts.get(k) ?? 0)` returns the zeros verbatim. There is no "insufficient data" sentinel.\n\n5. The rendered shape really is the misleading one described. `AdminKit.tsx:135-146` normalizes per-card: `min = Math.min(...data)`, `max = Math.max(...data)`, `range = max - min || 1`. When the tenant produces >300 events/week, `rows7` covers only the most recent slice of the window (often a few hours).\n- `dashboard.tsx:75` computes `trunc7 = rows7.length >= EVENTS_CAP`, and it is used in exactly two places — line 218 (donut header) and line 252 (hourly header), rendering `dash.sampled` ("By type · latest 300 (sampled)", apps/web/src/i18n/en.json:1001).\n- `dashboard.tsx:84-85` builds `eventsSpark`/`criticalSpark` from the SAME truncated `rows7` via `dailyCounts`, and they are passed to the StatCards at lines 148 and 157 with no `trunc7` guard — the only gate is `.some(n => n > 0)`.\n- `apps/web/src/lib/dashboard.ts:148-154` — `dailyCounts` pre-seeds all 7 day keys to 0 and only increments keys it finds, so days with no rows in the truncated page render as a hard 0, indistinguishable from a genuinely quiet day.\n- `apps/web/src/components/admin/AdminKit.tsx:133-142` — `Sparkline` normalizes min→max over the 7 points, so [0,0,0,0,0,0,N] draws a flat baseline with a full-height terminal spike regardless of N.\n\nReachability is high and the project has already conceded it: commit fb24671 (#105) added `trunc7` specifically because "dashboard 7d event widgets [are] marked sampled when the window is truncated" — i.e. a prior audit accepted that the 300-row window fills in practice. That fix covered only the donut and hourly headers; the two sparklines fed by the same array were missed. Any tenant with ignition/geofence rules and a few dozen devices clears 300 events/week trivially (60 devices × ~5 trips/day × 2 ignition events ≈ 600/day).\n\nConsequence is real but genuinely minor, matching severity=low:\n- The numeric surfaces are already honest — the card value renders "300+" via `floor()` (lines 145, 154) and the delta badge is suppressed when truncated (lines 78-79). Only the trend line lies.\n- The lie is inverted-truth, not just imprecise: a fleet with constant weekly volume renders as six flat days plus a terminal spike, reading as an incident. Conversely `criticalSpark` can vanish entirely (the `.some(n>0)` gate) when the newest 300 rows are all ignition noise, hiding a week that actually contained panic/power_cut events — the more misleading half for a telematics product.\n- The artifact is a 80×24px `aria-hidden` polyline with no axis, values, or tooltip, and the user is one click from the real Events page. ### 113. [LOW] releaseLeases() does a non-atomic GET-then-DEL and can delete a peer's freshly-claimed lease

**Subsystem:** worker / shard leasing · **Location:** `/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/shards.ts:104`

`releaseLeases()` reads the lease key and, if the value equals our workerId, issues a separate `DEL` (shards.ts:102-108). This is the exact compare-and-mutate hazard the same file solves with Lua for renewal (`RENEW_LUA`, shards.ts:22, with the comment 'a non-atomic GET-then-PEXPIRE could extend a lease a peer just claimed in the gap → two consumers on one shard'). The release path was left non-atomic.

**failureScenario:** On SIGTERM the worker calls `stopRenewing()` and then drains consumers (main.ts:459-461). Because renewal has stopped, a lease can expire during the drain. If it expires in the window between the `GET` (which still returns our workerId) and the `DEL`, a peer's leaser tick claims the shard with SET NX in that gap and our `DEL` immediately erases the peer's lease. A third worker (or the peer itself on its next tick) then claims the same shard while the peer's consumer is already running on it — two active consumers on one shard, breaking rule 5 / I2.

**suggestedFix:** Replace the GET+DEL with a compare-and-delete Lua script: `if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`, mirroring RENEW_LUA.

**verifierNotes:** ['CONFIRMED: I read the code and every test that touches lease release.\n\nThe code is exactly as claimed. `apps/worker/src/shards.ts:102-108`:\n\n```ts\nasync releaseLeases(): Promise<void> {\n  for (const shard of this.owned) {\n    const holder = await this.redis.get(leaseKey(shard))\n    if (holder === this.workerId) await this.redis.del(leaseKey(shard))\n  }\n  this.owned.clear()\n}\n```\n\nTwo separate round trips, no atomicity across them. The same file solves the identical compare-and-mutate hazard for renewal with Lua and documents why (shards.ts:19-22): "A non-atomic GET-then-PEXPIRE could extend a lease a peer just claimed in the gap → two consumers on one shard (rule 5 / I2 violation, review MED)." So the project\'s own standard treats this window as a real bug; the release path was simply left on the non-atomic form. There is no `RELEASE_LUA`, no WATCH/MULTI, and no ADR or comment recording the omission as a deliberate tradeoff (grep for RELEASE_LUA/DEL_LUA returns nothing).\n\nThe window is genuinely reachable, not theoretical:\n- `stopRenewing()` is called first on SIGTERM (`apps/worker/src/main.ts:459`) and only clears the interval (`shards.ts:94-96`) — it does not touch `owned`. Because renewal has stopped, the 30 s lease (main.ts:73) is free to expire during the consumer drain at main.ts:460, which is unbounded (each `ShardConsumer.stop()` awaits the in-flight batch, consumer.ts:79-82).\n- With the leaser tick stopped, nothing removes an expired shard from `owned`, so the `GET` at shards.ts:104 is the *only* guard. If expiry lands between the `GET` reply and the `DEL` (and a peer\'s `tryClaim` SET NX, shards.ts:56, lands in that same gap), the `DEL` erases the peer\'s brand-new lease.\n\nTest coverage: none for this path. `shards.spec.ts:53-66` tests atomic *renewal* only; `shards.spec.ts:68-76` and `pipeline.spec.ts:237-247` both first drop the shard from `owned` via `onLost` before calling `release()`, so `releaseLeases()` never even reaches the GET/DEL for a contested shard — those tests pass with or without the guard. `pipeline.spec.ts:178-198` only asserts the key is gone after a single-worker release.\n\nTwo corrections that reduce (but do not eliminate) the claim\'s stated impact, which is why severity=low is right:\n1. "the peer itself on its next tick" would not re-claim: the peer has `owned.has(shard)`, so its tick runs `RENEW_LUA` (shards.ts:77), gets 0, fires `onLost` and stops its consumer (shards.ts:78-81, main.ts:74-80). Only a third worker\'s `tryClaim` can take the shard in that gap.\n2. The durable-effect half of I2 is defended by the consumer fence: `ownsShard()` is consulted before `process()` (consumer.ts:93, 121, 130) and is itself a GET on the same key (shards.ts:15-17), so the peer\'s just-started consumer (started via `onGained`, main.ts:81-86) reads `null` and fences before persisting anything. So the realistic damage is a spuriously freed shard: a lease-thrash window where the peer XAUTOCLAIMs/XREADGROUPs entries into its PEL and then fences (consumer.ts:86-93, 119-123), leaving those entries pending under a dead consumer name until the 60 s `autoclaimMinIdleMs` elapses, plus up to ~10 s of unconsumed shard until someone re-claims.\n\nThe defect is real, unhandled, untested, and inconsistent with the file\'s own documented invariant — just very low probability (requires expiry plus a peer SET NX inside a sub-millisecond gap, at SIGTERM only) and blunted downstream by the fencing check. Fix is a one-liner mirroring RENEW_LUA: `if redis.call(\'get\', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call(\'del\', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`.', 'REJECTED: The code pattern is real but the failure is not reachable in practice, and its consequence is already neutralized by two independent guards.\n\nWhat the code actually says:\n- `releaseLeases()` is indeed a non-atomic GET-then-DEL (`/Users/ernis/Sites/gps_tracker/apps/worker/src/shards.ts:102-108`), while renewal uses a Lua CAS (`shards.ts:22`). The asymmetry is factual.\n\nWhy the scenario cannot realistically fire:\n1. Timing. TTL is 30 s and the renew interval is `leaseTtlMs/3` = 10 s (`shards.ts:39,67`, wired with 30_000 at `apps/worker/src/main.ts:73`). At SIGTERM the remaining TTL on every owned lease is therefore between 20 s and 30 s. The SIGTERM handler is bounded by a hard watchdog: `setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 5_000).unref()` (`main.ts:493`). Drain itself is bounded (`blockMs` default 2 s, `consumer.ts:126`, plus one batch). So `releaseLeases()` (`main.ts:461`) runs ~0-5 s after SIGTERM against a lease with ≥15 s of TTL left. For the GET to still return our workerId while the key expires inside the GET→DEL gap, the process would have to stall 20+ s between those two commands — and a 20 s stall means the 5 s watchdog timer fires on unblock and `process.exit(1)` pre-empts the DEL.\n2. Compounded coincidence. Even granting the stall, the peer\'s leaser tick fires once per 10 s (`shards.ts:67`); its `SET NX` (`shards.ts:56`) must land inside the sub-millisecond single-round-trip window between our GET and our DEL. That is a triple coincidence at microsecond scale, not an operational event.\n3. Deployment reality. `infra/compose/docker-compose.apps.yml:41-44` runs a single `worker` service with no replicas, so a concurrent peer only exists during a container recreate, further narrowing exposure.\n\nWhy the consequence is mitigated even if it fired:\n- The peer\'s own renew CAS returns 0 on the next tick (missing key ⇒ `get` returns false ≠ ARGV[1], `shards.ts:22,77-81`) → `onLost` stops that shard\'s consumer (`main.ts:74-80`).\n- More decisively, the consumer performs a fencing `ownsShardLease` GET *before* applying any batch\'s durable effects (`consumer.ts:93,121,130`, `shards.ts:15-17`). After the erroneous DEL the key is either absent or holds the third worker\'s id, so the peer\'s consumer fences itself (`consumer.ts:105-109`) before touching the trip/geofence/rule engines. The claimed "two active consumers persisting one device" outcome therefore collapses back into the already-documented one-check-wide fencing TOCTOU, not a new I2 break.\n\nSo: real code asymmetry, worth a one-line Lua compare-and-delete as cheap hardening, but as a defect report it is theoretical (unreachable given the 5 s watchdog vs ≥15 s TTL) and already mitigated by the per-batch fencing check. Rejecting per the "unreachable, already mitigated, or purely theoretical" bar.']
